The extraction of Time (Kāloddhara) is characterized by the nature of the word;
above the waist [is the region] of the dress and so forth, belonging to that which dwells near the sacrifice.
Arranged at the main gate and the side doors is the mandala, the destroyer of obstacles.
The lotus at the top is reddish-pink; outside of that are the external lotuses, and beyond those is the white path.

First, when employing the name individually for the armor and the amulet, one should first arrange the middle syllable; then, from this, one should determine the state of the even and odd positions. Afterwards, one should clearly enter the triad beginning with the letter *tva*.
The application [of the suffixes] in present and other tenses regarding actions—|| 4 ||

And here one should point out: the designation of the middle voice (ātmanepada), the designation of the active voice (parasmaipada), and that which possesses the nature of both; likewise, the case endings (vibhaktis) are sevenfold. || 5 ||
And each [of these] has three genders; they should be employed in sequence according to the number two, three, or many. The nominative case is used for the mere meaning of the gender. || 6 ||

And likewise, having purified them with mantras, one should apply the remaining [terms] in the case of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the recipient (*sampradāna*), as well as in connection with the point of departure (*apādāna*). || 7 ||
Likewise, it is beneficial when used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). The locative case should be employed regarding the object:
"Having known [this], there is association with the office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*). It is free from cause. || 8 ||
When a nominal application is observed, then the extraction of the case-endings should be performed by the most learned masters, according to the sense of the genitive case. || 9 ||
The locative case should be employed where there is the sense of the locative;
furthermore, by means of this sequential application, one should practice the transgression [of the rules]. (10)
The grammatical factors (kārakas) should be applied according to the sense with the seven types of objects;
by this, they are not at all [exhausted] by consent alone, but likewise always by way of consumption. (11)

An explanation should be made with effort regarding words and sentences; one should compose it in a concise manner for the sake of those who were previously well-disposed, otherwise it would be improper for men. 12.
In the presence of a prefix, there is no [separate] root; rather, the entire expression is a verbal form.
When there is a common substratum, the ritual act of maintaining [the sacrifice] should be performed by means of two words. (13)
The number should be understood as preceded by two; likewise, due to the weight of the Tatpuruṣa compound, it must certainly be formed by carefully writing down the words. 14.
As long as it has not been correctly and fully grasped by the disciple, O Nalinikhiya,
you must not speak with such critical analysis regarding what has been taught by me in the doctrine.
In that very same way, one should proceed with the contact of the *kārṣī*; [the names] *vela* and *upādeya* are [to be applied].
In a doubtful case, there is a contradictory statement; what was spoken by me is uneven, yet it is equal. (16)
One should act according to the scriptures and reasoning, and not teach according to one's own personal preference;
for when a teacher explains by speaking in contradiction to the scriptures, [he harms] his disciples. (17)
Likewise, O Teacher, there is a fault in the departure [from the path] regarding that which is afflicted in the Sūtra;
however, through the traditional transmission of your own established doctrine and through the teacher’s demonstration of the meaning, [this fault is avoided]. (18)

Having reconciled what is contradictory by interpreting it otherwise, one should truly contemplate the sixfold union; therein, one object is considered as being other than the primordial material substance (prakṛti).
Above that, an unequal altar (vedikā) should be provided, situated near the place of sacrifice;
it is adorned with gates and side-doors, a mandala that destroys obstacles.
The central lotus is red; outside that are the external lotuses. A white path should be made beyond them, and the doors may be fashioned according to one's desire.
Furthermore, one who offers leaves placed upon the ears and likewise filaments [of flowers] is always dear to Gaṇeśa; he is the crusher of obstacles.
In the center, Gaṇapati is to be worshipped, who stands near the excellent Nāda-aṅga;
therefore, Śakra was struck on the head by the medicine and completely overwhelmed.
One endowed with firmness and other virtues of excellence should [employ] this greatly radiant mantra;
thereafter, Vighneśvara and the others are to be worshipped in brief.
Vighneśvara, Gaṇeśa, Gaja, Gajavāhana, Gajākṣa, Gajaśīrṣa, Gāṅgeya, and Gaṇanāyaka—[these are the names of Gaṇeśa]. || 25 ||
The inhabitants of the eastern region [worship] the Lord of Cows (Gopati), who is the sky of the three realms,
possessing a great body, with protruding lips and long ears, and who causes terror to the obstructors.
To the long-bellied one, the most formidable, the deformed, the beloved of Pārvatī—Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati! To the fierce and terrifying one—|| 27 ||
Auspicious, the destroyer of fear, the slayer of fear—these twelve [deities] are to be worshipped, O wife, as they are situated on the right side of the Lord. || 28 ||
Madhusūdana [encountered] Trāsa, Mahānāda, Bhāsura, Utkaṭasvana, Caṇḍa, Sauṇḍa, Mahābhīma, and Ḍamatha. || 29 ||
One should worship those situated in the west, beautiful and kissed by the evening twilight;
they are the source of Brahmā, the navel of Brahmā, the cessation, and the dissolution in the final destruction.
Delighting in dance, fickle, a cutter, fond of action, the end-maker, the staff of time, and the destroyer— these reside in the northern direction. (31)
These should be worshipped with flowers, perfumes, water for the guest-offering (arghya), and seats;
then, having worshipped according to the detailed rites, one should place the pitcher as before.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part of that;
for the remaining [mantras], one should likewise perform the recitation and the fire sacrifice with a tenth part.
Having offered the full [oblation], the consecration must be performed by one desiring success;
for everywhere, his power is irresistible even to the gods.
Then the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed after the Guru has been worshipped with devotion;
it is prescribed that he be honored with elephants, horses, vehicles, and the like, as well as land and gold.
When this is done, the spiritual perfections (siddhis) indeed arise for men;
their intellect shall be directed toward water everywhere, and they shall not be afflicted by malignant planets.
"Ṣaṇmukha [is the deity] in all undertakings of ritual action and in the great accomplishments.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter on the worship of Gaṇapati in the *Mahātantra* known as the *Kālottara*, consisting of six thousand verses.
Īśvara said:
I shall fully explain the maṇḍala by which the accomplishment of speech (vāksiddhi) arises. || 38 ||
One should perform the worship of Īśvara at night, joined with the Kāladāha Mantra; by means of that Mantra, it should be performed like the worship of the Moon and the Sun.
The three-syllabled supreme mantra should not be given to just anyone;
one should instruct it with the Praṇava, using the mantra of six recitations.

Having meditated upon her who resembles a kunda flower or the moon, who has three eyes, possesses a beautiful seat, is of her own essential nature, has a gentle countenance, is seated upon a lotus, and is radiant with a crown; 41.
Adorned with a garland of fifty letters and decorated with strings of pearls and blood—such is the Blessed Lady Vāgīśī; may she grant me success in speech. (42)
Then, being pure, one hundred thousand recitations should be performed mentally;
one should contemplate [the mantra] entering from the head down to the *kanda*. (43)
One should contemplate the garland of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa';
one should always remember the life-creepers as resembling a collection of crest-jewels.

Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands with the mantra, the practitioner should then place the three syllables in sequence upon the head, the secret place, and the heart. (45)
One should not perform the ritual placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) by merely reciting [the names] once;
however, at the time of receiving the mantra, one should have a mandala prepared there.
The lotus, divided into four parts and one part for the moon, is beneficial;
it should be provided with a pathway, a band, and adorned with creepers and foliage.
Then one should fashion four-petaled lotuses, eight of them there;
outside the path for the travelers, the doors shall be two squares (padas) wide.
Those very same [measures] for the lotuses, together with the cheeks, constitute the side-doors; likewise, there is the corner-binding and the double-band.
The white lotuses are fresh, their pericarpis are made of gold, and their filaments are variegated. || 50 ||
Page 6 is missing.
One should fashion a variegated *koṇabandha* there, consisting of two squares;
the lotus is white in color, and its pericarp (*karṇikā*) is made of gold.
There are sixty-four filaments, yellow, red, and white;
one should establish stability in the regions of the base, the middle, and the tip.
A red pathway is recommended, adorned with various leaf-patterns;
one should complete the doors in accordance with the [directions of the] world-protectors.
Within the space between the sky-lines, one should indeed fashion a wheel resembling the sun;
it should be bound with spokes at the corners, and yellow or white is beneficial.
Thus has been fully explained the supreme support of Śiva known as Bhadra;
it is employed in the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites for the sake of attaining auspiciousness.
Now, the procedure for the lotus is briefly described by me:
the lotus is of two kinds, namely, the unattached and the attached. (57)
O son of Pārvatī, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; it is always beneficial when unattached, yet for those seeking liberation, it is eternally harmful when attached.
Each of those should be known as twofold by the Guru who understands the ritual:
namely, the child, the youth, and the old man, according to their names, for the sake of attaining the fruit. (59)
Having reflected thus, Padma should then proceed in due order;
he should cast the lines in every direction upon the lotus-field. (60)
Likewise, there are sixteen smoky-colored [circles] and thirty-two of them by number;
five of these are to be fashioned as circles, equal in size within the lotus-field.
There, in the first [lotus], the pericarp is provided with nine [petals] at the tip;
in the second, however, the filaments are twenty-four in number.
The third [layer] is always the petal-joints, shaped like the frontal lobes of an elephant;
the fourth consists of the tips of the petals, and the fifth is the celestial peak (vyomakūṭa).
At its end, the sky-line (vyomarekhā) should be established as neither thick nor thin;
this is called the "joined lotus" (saṃsakta-kamala), and now the "joined" (saṃsakta) is further described.
Unattached, one should extend the *dhala* toward the intermediate directions;
by omitting two parts, one should increase the *dhala* by an eighth part.
One should worship that joint according to the detailed sūtra and the petals of the tamāla;
by following the sequence of right and left, there shall then be the "increased lotus" (vṛddhapadma).
Alternatively, one should rotate it like a half-moon within the joint;
when the thread reaches the tips of the two joints, then it becomes a "young lotus" (bālapadma).
One should rotate the joints and sutures from behind according to the measurement;
with a sharp tip, that lotus [tool] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 68.

The "old lotus" (vṛddhapadma) is for liberation; the "child" (bāla) is for the eight supernatural powers (siddhis); and the "youth" (yuvan), when employed according to its petals, is taught for all ritual actions.
One should make it fourfold in its rotation, continuous and devoid of empty space;
however, one must avoid leaving a gap for a line of empty space at the end of the tip of the swing.
Thus, by way of brief indication, the eight-petaled lotus has been shown;
it should be understood as common to all, except for the maṇḍala of Vighneśa.
Listen to me as I describe the mandala known as the Nine Naves:
the original field should be eight cubits, or even ten cubits.
One should again draw [the design] all around with parts established according to the Vedas;
indeed, there should be an eight-part division all around, and in the center, there shall be a lotus.
A pathway (pathikā) should be made as a street (vīthikā), and the door should be half the measure of a lotus (padma).
It is provided with a neck (kaṇṭha) and a sub-neck (upakaṇṭha); the molding (paṭṭikā) begins from where the neck is excluded.
Thus, one central lotus, provided with pathways and gates, has been described to you in brief; outside of that, a pathway is prescribed.
That [line] measures five parts, while the one extending all around is ten parts;
then, O son of Kṛttikā, the work should be performed in the ten directions as previously described.
According to the ritual procedure for the eight lotuses, it is provided with paths and gates;
outside of that, there is a five-pada path adorned with petals.
The door and the ear (corner) should be like a lotus; the ear-ornament should be one square (padika);
the cheek should be made one square; thus, three doors are clearly established in the cardinal directions.
The tripod formed by the corner-bindings should be like a double-vajra;
its cause is a white lotus, while the eastern lotus is yellow.
In the southeast is the red-colored one, standing on the right with a blue lotus;
in the southwest is the yellow-colored one, and the white one is situated in the direction of Varuṇa (the west). || 80 ||
In the northwestern corner it is smoky-grey; likewise, in the north it is red-yellow;
in the northeast, it resembles a pearl or is white, like a fresh lotus. || 81 ||
Alternatively, it may be as white as a lotus or even reddish-white;
it pervades the sky like Śiva and is beneficial for the ritual of the nine gates.
The ninefold name of Śiva is declared to be that which is called Prāsāda;
Śiva is to be worshipped in the central lotus, and the world-protectors (lokeśas) in the others.
Having diligently worshipped the weapons in the outer path with devotion,
[one obtains] the merit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
In the worship of this maṇḍala, they do not equal even a sixteenth part;
he is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (85)

In rites performed for specific signs or for the sake of desired results, the Mahāmaṇḍala—known as such and bestowing all perfections—should be constructed for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation; this I shall now describe.
The original site, measuring eight cubits, shall be divided into twenty parts;
in the center, there is a lotus of two squares, and a pathway is beneficial for the traveler.
In each of the directions and likewise in the intermediate ones, one should fashion eight blue lotuses;
by the measurement of the central lotus, there are twenty of them here. (88)
Devoid of joints and seams, with blue stone slabs;
behind that is the path for travelers, and above that is the Svastika.
Then, having divided that portion into two, eight,
and so on, one should fashion svastikas there according to the injunctions of the Guru’s command.
The walkways are as described before; on the exterior are gates and a lotus as previously detailed, along with side-chambers, corner-connections, and decorative friezes.
In the center of the lotus is [the deity] resembling snow and the kunda flower, with a pericarp and yellow filaments;
its petals are unattached, auspicious, and conceived as being like the sky, like the void itself. 92.
The corners are red in color, while the pathways have the luster of gold;
the blue lotuses are dark-hued, and their pericarp-like centers form the shape of a pericarp.
There should be svastikas of various colors, as well as pathways and leaf-patterned borders; and having filled them with powders of many different colors, [one should proceed]. (94)
The Great Maṇḍala, known by that name, is dear to the heart of Śiva;
it is recommended for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and especially for initiation (dīkṣā). || 95 ||
One obtains all desires through the worship of the great maṇḍala;
I shall now describe the five lotuses for the dedication of the vows.

And for the sake of attaining the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, the *liṅgoddhāra* (the extraction of the linga) must be performed on a square field measuring five cubits, divided on all sides by lines representing Indra.
One should arrange a two-petaled lotus in the center, followed by a pathway for travelers;
then, one should fashion a set of four lotuses in the cardinal directions, just like the central one.
Outside of that are the pathways for travelers, with gates and doorways two paces wide,
joined by ears and sub-ears at the junctions of the various corners.
The central lotus is always fully opened, with its filaments falling from the pericarp; the [lotus on the] left is yellowish-white, while the one on the right has the luster of lapis lazuli.
The northern [region] has the luster of Darada and the luster of Kunda; the arm of Varuṇa is [there].
The first and subsequent pathways have a red luster and resemble gold. 101.
The gateways are images of Lokeśvara, with Śikhivāhana [at the top];
the entire five-fold maṇḍala grants the accomplishment of all desires. (102)
I shall describe the mandala that grants all desires and fulfills every wish: O auspicious one, at the tip of the fourth [line], there is a lotus extending ten units on all sides.
The travelers are outside; the doorways are two units [in width], and one should turn the faces, together with the ears, according to the measurement of a lotus.
Then one should fill the corner-binding (koṇabandha), which is unattached and slightly reddish;
the pathway (vīthikā) should be like gold and adorned with leafy creepers.
A white-colored lotus, endowed with manifold splendors, bestows all desires and is highly praised for a temple of great mind. 106.
By worshipping the Prāsāda, one attains all desires;
it bestows all desires upon men and is honored in all rites. || 107 ||
This very mandala is recommended here for the destruction of obstacles;
however, [it is used] on the pathways and at the svastikas for the purpose of driving away misfortune.
Because it destroys misfortune, it was then taught for the destruction of misfortune by Śiva, the God of gods and the Supreme Self. (109)
Having made the city four cubits square and two cubits round,
the pathway shall be one cubit wide, and the door-frame shall be one cubit in measure.
The circle previously described should be in the middle, measuring sixteen finger-breadths; there should also be circles in the cardinal directions, accompanied by lotuses.
There are five white lotuses, and the space between them is beneficially dark;
the corners have the brilliance of fire, and the pathways possess the luster of gold.
The gates are the world-protectors... [missing 11, 12, 13,
and 14 pages] ...having the luster of a lotus, a jasmine flower, and the moon, [and] a staff with the radiance of a black antelope skin.
The root, resembling fire, has been described by me as the weapon of Rudra.
The Brahmāstra is to be known as the lotus; [the] characteristics [are as follows]: [missing pages 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24] || 115 ||
Salutation! Having performed the placement [of mantras] once upon the hands, the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) is thereby accomplished.
By performing the placement once from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head, one becomes pure. (116)
He should then perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the body from the head down to the feet;
after performing the bodily placement (dehanyāsa), he should thereafter commence the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). || 117 ||
Worship, recitation, fire-sacrifice, and the construction of the temple must be performed externally;
his meditation should likewise be external, not otherwise, in the form of the latent tendencies that cause obstruction.
For rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), white is prescribed, while red is praised for the rite of subjugation (vaśya). || 119 ||
For the rite of immobilization (*staṃbhana*), yellow color is [beneficial], while for attraction (*karṣaṇa*), tawny (*kapila*) is beneficial;
likewise it should be for the rite of delusion (*mohana*); having understood the ritual action, one should reflect upon it. (120)
Having awakened the *praṇava* with the intellect, one should once offer a seat with a flower;
from the limit of incapacity to the limit of capacity, one should fashion it there through pervasive extension.
Above that, one should conceive the supreme form by means of the thirty-two syllables,
[extending] from Īśvara up to Śakti, whose body is composed of the Kalās.
Then, one should perform the supreme invocation with the king of mantras,
having invoked according to the previous rule, just as will be described.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the limbs of Brahmā and having worshipped thus with devotion,
one must perform the preliminary service (pūrva-sevā) of the root mantra, as well as the sprinkling (seka) and the purification (pūtikā).
The practitioner should recite the Aghorākṣa mantra an equal number of times;
having taken recourse to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that amount.
O Six-faced One, when one offers guggulu resin with the clarified butter of a tawny cow, the accomplishment of the mantra is then perfected and brings about the desired state. || 126 ||
One should accomplish [the goal] through those who are superior, inferior, or middling, without disregarding their words;
and one should accomplish even those things not desired by means of a non-terrible form for the sake of success.
One who desires grains and those various objects of desire shall surely attain them;
by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one will certainly achieve success for the sake of accomplishment. 128.

Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment through recitation and oblation, the middling [attainment] results from half that number of guggulu oblations, while the lowest results from one hundred thousand.
One shall accomplish it; there is no doubt here. The threefold attainments are always [attained]; in this very same way, one should likewise arrange the pacification of the threefold portents. (130)
In this very same way, one should perform the pacification of all calamities;
in this very same way, one should perform the pacification of immediate calamities. || 131 ||
In the pacification of all calamities, there is no other protector on the surface of the earth;
likewise, among the Siddhāntas and other systems, there is no other protector than that which belongs to Śaṅkara.
There is no mantra other than Aghora that bestows success upon reaching the Kali age;
Aghora is the mantra that grants success—of this there is no doubt or alternative conception. (133)
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice the Aghora mantra—whether standing, waking, sleeping, walking, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse. (134)

One whose mind is offered to Aghora becomes a partaker of liberation; otherwise, one who is not a celibate student becomes a celibate student, and one who has not yet performed the ceremonial bath becomes one who has performed it. 135.
Merely by remembering him, the destruction of all sins occurs;
by reciting [his name] five times, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 136 ||
By reciting it seven times, one attains the fruit of all sacrifices;
and by reciting it twenty-one times according to the rule at the conclusion of the worship, [one obtains the same].
One obtains the fruit of worship and shall attain what is spoken in the scriptures;
having abandoned all other doctrines, one should practice the doctrine of mantra.
Discourses have mantras as their root; therefore, the mantra should be supreme.
Furthermore, those who contemplate mantras must perform the recitation (japa) of the Aghora mantra therein.
The warding off of celestial, atmospheric,
and terrestrial obstacles must be performed with the Aghora weapons, as well as the prevention of sudden portents.
These two king-mantras are situated above the sun:
the terrible thirty-two-syllable mantra, and especially the Aghora-weapon mantra.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice these two mantras;
indeed, the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) for both mantras must be performed.
Then Śiva himself shall burn away all obstacles at the proper time. The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) exists in a threefold state: whispered, mental, and spoken aloud.
O son of Pārvatī, know that mental recitation (mānasa) is the supreme and sattvic form of japa; know that whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is the middling and rajasic form. (144)
However, that which is to be cultivated as inferior is declared by him to be *tāmasa*,
because it pertains to the performance of rites that are inferior, superior, or middling.
This must be performed with great effort, preceded by the Aghora weapon;
for those two who have become [so] through effort, they shall be supreme in mantra through their exertion.
Having completed the preliminary service, one should then accomplish the siddhis;
his rites succeed, O Destroyer of Krauñca, and not otherwise. (147)

When there is non-duality of knowledge, that enjoyment is desired as the supreme accomplishment; the middling is the power of moving through space (khecaratva), while the lowest is [attained] in the region of Janapada.
One shall accomplish even the lowest of low siddhis, such as summoning and enchanting; there is no doubt in this matter through the power of the King of Mantras. 149.

He who attempts to accomplish [the goal] for the sake of success without knowing the King of Mantras is like one who, while suffering from hunger, seeks to satisfy his guests with the flesh of a corpse. || 150 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should always accomplish the Aghora [mantra];
for whoever among the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas have attained perfection in mantras, [it is through this]. || 151 ||
All of them shall come under his control, remaining subject to that one who has achieved the terrible siddhi;
yet those who have attained success through mantras may at some point meet their end in the course of time. || 152 ||
For the sake of accomplishing the non-terrible mantra, all those of inexhaustible and immeasurable splendor remain unassailable and possess unfailing power. || 153 ||
The mantras of one who is always devoted to worship are accomplished;
the siddhis are eternally accomplished for those who are constant reciters of mantras.
Mantras bestow their fruits upon those whose minds are fixed on their accomplishment;
therefore, one should practice this triad: worship, fire-oblation, and recitation. (155)
But having known the supreme form of Aghora, the great practitioner attains knowledge and yoga, being entirely free from the portion of the knowable. || 156 ||

Brahman is eternally of the nature of the self and consciousness, free from conceptual construction and formless; it is devoid of all means of valid cognition, self-evident, and inexpressible. || 157 ||
Through faith, austerity, devotion, and by means of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth;
through contact with great souls and by the realization of the sacred ford of knowledge (jñānatīrtha). || 158 ||
Through instruction, through such practice, and through well-performed observances, they worship the supreme form, which is like that of the Lord of Existence (*sadaspati*). (154)
This is not otherwise, nor is it non-dual; it is neither substance nor quality.
Neither Brahmā nor the other gods worship it eternally.
With half of that, those who consider themselves wise satisfy [the gods] day and night;
yet, due to great delusion, they sink down, they struggle, and they die. || 161 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the partless [Brahman],
by the mere remembrance of which one shall not undergo the three births.
One should worship the god Aghora; one shall become a partaker of liberation through Aghora.
He who remembers Aghora at all times within his heart, in all states of being, [attains the highest goal]. || 163 ||
"One attains the supreme state, characterized by no return.
Thus [it is said] in the venerable *Kālottara*, the great tantra of six thousand [verses]. 164.
The Aghorakalpa is completed.
Īśvara said:
"One should perform the Rudraśānti or the Mahāśānti by means of a sacrifice. (165)
O Mahāsena, the sacrifice of weapons (astrayāga) is now briefly described by me;
the mandala previously mentioned must be prepared for the destruction of misfortune (ariṣṭa).
O son of Kṛttikā, the worship of Rudra should be performed in reverse order, whether it be five cubits, four cubits, or even eight cubits.
The Vasus, Agni, the Saṃkhyās, and the Rudras—these one should employ for the propitiation of Rudra;
as well as Rudra himself, Vṛṣabha, Avimukta, and Asambhava. (168)
And including Puruṣa, one should place these five lords upon Prakṛti;
then, on the northern petal, one should worship those five Rudras in their proper order. (169)
Viśvākhyam, Mahāviśvam, Karālam, Vikṛtam, and likewise Tvaṃte—these five, known as Vikṛta, abide within the Puruṣa. || 170 ||
There are four known as Piṅgala who are fixed in the wind-leaves;
likewise, there is one named Ekaśveta, and the fourth is named Madhu, who is black. (171)
Ananta, as well as Pañca and Śuṣka, along with the group of waters (Payogaṇa)—these mighty Rudras are stationed in the water at the principle of Time (Kālatattva). || 172 ||
Karāla and Vikarāla are in the southwestern petal of Māyā;
they are situated in the southern vessel within the four-thousandfold Vidyā. (173)
One who knows reality should place these four: the one called Head, the one named Cloth, the one called Hand, and the fourth, the one called Battle-Black, in Laṅkā. 174.
One, two, and three Rudras, ending with Jagat, are situated there along with Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra; furthermore, there are three more Rudras. (175)
And at the end of the six periods, the Rudras shall be present in the east during all the ritual acts;
therein, the great element, the Bhūta, approaches as the means for the system of the Paśus. (176)

O Śikhivāhana, having worshipped all beings and likewise the appropriate time, Umā and Maheśvara are to be worshipped in the center; Śiva, whose nature is the ultimate reality (tattva), is to be worshipped there.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with white flowers, fragrant substances, and ointments such as sandalwood, one should honor the mudrās with milk-rice and ghee.
Then one should worship the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvaras) with the hair of the crest (*śikhā*);
since those are infinite, hear now from me the doctrine of the nine principles regarding the disciple. (179)
From the *praṇava* up to the *dhruva*, the seat of Śiva (*śivapīṭha*) is within the region from the fire to the earth; and from there up to the *tatpuruṣa*, the seat is Sadāśiva. || 180 ||
Prior to the contact [of the breath], Aghorā, whose form is light, descended from the seat of Īśvara toward the direction of contact. || 3 || [The form of the worship of the lotus... || 181 ||

And those who reside outside that seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), as well as those who abide in the state of night-stalkers at the very end of the subtle steps of the mind and fire—[these are the ones to be known]. || 5 || [182] || 183 ||

The seat (pīṭha) ending with *dhanā* is likewise situated within the Puruṣa; from the word *pākṣa*, it stands as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the seat, extending to the end of the quarters of the Praṇava. || 183 ||
"Śīśānyāḥ || 1 ||" Thus, this great sacrifice of the words (padamahādhvara) is to be fully honored by mere placement (nyāsa); thus, through the division of the words, [it becomes] nectar. || 184 ||
All the auspicious ones stationed at the edge of the city are enumerated within the circular perimeter of the letter Śa, brilliantly illuminated by the Praṇava. || 185 ||
All of them, with faces turned inward and well-established, are seated in the eastern seat, situated as they were before; they are to be worshipped and honored. || 186 ||
All Rudras mentioned previously in the ritual manual (karma) are to be praised with the word "Brahman" along with clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, fruits, and so forth. || 187 ||
Rice, barley, black grains, and sweetmeats for eating—these constitute the first group of foods, as does milk-rice (pāyasa). The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is likewise [included]. || 188 ||

On each pedestal, it should be applied as prescribed; the sacrificial offering consists of nine parts, adorned with the beauty of the earth, the mountains, and the hooves, along with *dūrvā* grass and black [sesame]. || 189 ||
Sesame, clarified butter, and the substance called amṛta, mango leaves—these should be offered; likewise, the accomplished Jvālājāvajrī and fragrant flowers. || 190 ||
Leaves of the milk-tree (*kṣīrataru*), fuel-sticks, rice, barley, and so forth—one thousand oblations for each of these, along with clarified butter, for each Rudra. || 191 ||

That [mantra] should be given with effort; in its absence, it may be recited by those [initiated] as prescribed. A thousand repetitions of each individual word constitutes the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). || 192 ||

One should avoid those who have resorted to the left-hand path (vāmācāra). Those who have resorted to the left-hand path are censured in the scripture once [the goal] is accomplished; they are [only] for secret practice. || 193 ||
Those who are to be avoided should always be shunned—those who have fully embraced the Siddhānta, who are pure in conduct, firm in their vows, and [capable of] restraint. || 194 ||

O Goddess, those who are difficult to restrain are capable of bestowing grace upon the gods; having first known [the disciple] to be pure through his teacher, one should thereafter begin the cooling rite (śīti). || 195 ||
It should be performed day after day, or whenever it has arisen;
indeed, these thirty-eight deities have been proclaimed, and by them this [rite] is desired. || 196 ||
In reverse and in direct order, with Rudra and Vyomaśiva,
and by means of the word "rākā," the pedestal consists of nine parts.
That should be worshipped in the forward order (anuloma) by Rudra and likewise in the reverse order (viloma);
one should offer seven, five, or three oblations, or even a single oblation for each.
Thus the daily rite has been declared; for specific occasions, one should offer oblations as before. For each of the divine omens, however, one thousand [oblations] should be offered.
For omens occurring in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), there should be a corresponding additional oblation;
for those on the ground, a propitiatory homa (śāntihoma) should be performed at the stations of the Rudras.

In all portents, and especially in great portents, when one hundred oblations have been offered, those who are free from all diseases or whose souls have been released from the grasp of the planets [shall attain peace]. (201)
For those who have been seized by calamities, whose selves have been crushed by the Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas), and who are afflicted by malevolent spells,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa). || 202 ||
And the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed daily with nine jars, using one hundred and twenty oblations consecrated by mantras.
The consecration should be performed by assigning the mantras with one less [syllable];
it should be done day after day, or one should recite [the mantra] and shake [the vessel].
That prepared sacrificial porridge (caru) should be given for the consecration;
by consuming it from a copper vessel, one is not afflicted by any obstacles. || 205 ||
In this moment, the supreme bowman has described the vision of the eyes,
and the distinction between the Rudras and their stations has been demonstrated.
Number, the division of its own atoms, and the substance characterized by the oblation have been described in the first section; in the second, the hymn of praise is set forth. (207)
That Blessed Lady brings forth the third section of mantras; indeed, these three sections are declared by means of prose, with the third being told in prose. (208)
Following the section on the division [of the ritual], the section on praise is now declared.
I shall proclaim the Rudra-śānti, which is auspicious and accomplishes all goals. (209)
Spoken by Rudra himself for the benefit of human beings, all obstacles perish upon hearing these [mantras] which destroy sin. (210)
Bad dreams, diseases, and even the planets in the ten directions [are overcome] by the one of many forms, the all-encompassing one, and the supreme one whose form is the universe. || 211 ||
Having prostrated before the God of gods, the remover of all sins, who is accompanied by Pārvatī and indeed by Nandīśvara; || 212 ||
I shall proclaim the Rudra-śānti rites, which destroy Vetālas for men who have been afflicted in temples and dwellings of the gods.
For those in whom there is no conception in the womb and no loss of lineage, where those born perish and do not cause any distress. (214)
Wherever desire arises, from that [desire] come houses upon houses;
the fetus falls prematurely, or one is born as a *kuṇḍa* (an illegitimate son). || 215 ||
They are afflicted by famine and by terrible national calamities;
where the guilds are in conflict and even brothers are at odds with one another. (215)
When the father, mother, and daughter-in-law have all passed away, and the house has become like a plantain tree, one sees the sage in a dream; yet the seed does not sprout in that field.
If cattle, horses, slaves, and laborers residing in the house become rebellious, one should perform a rite for peace there. (217)
When struck by a thunderbolt, the spinal column is shattered;
and the vital organs, though not pierced, bleed profusely. || 218 ||
The gods and even the trees were dancing and laughing;
the trees blossomed and bore fruit many times out of season. (219)
Meteors fall and terrible earthquakes occur;
by these and other such inauspicious and dreadful omens, [the world is foretold]. (220)
Having become single-minded and disciplined, one should apply oneself to peace therein.
How shall I explain, according to the truth, the origin of the Rudra-peace rite? || 221 ||
Surrounded by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and numerous other spirits, all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity [approached him]. 222.
They petitioned Hara, the Lord of Gods, together with Brahmā:
"O Lord of Gods, it is known to you that the subjects are suffering from pride. (223)
O Lord, by means of planets of irresistible power— neither by enumeration nor by qualities—
grant him peace that liberates from all planetary afflictions.
Having heard the words of the gods, Hara, the lord of the three worlds,
commanded all his attendants to quickly bring the planets along with their various qualities.
And the Blessed One is irresistible, especially the guardians of the world;
indeed, all the protectors of the people and the protectors of the realm are invincible.
O Lord, the hosts of bhūtas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas, as well as the kūśmāṇḍas, the fierce and wise ones, the yakṣa-protectors, and those who follow his grace; || 227 ||
And the guardians of the temples of the gods, the hosts of spirits, night-stalkers, Kālakarṇī, Mahākālī, and whatever other harmful household deities there may be— 228.
Epilepsy as well as insanity, diseases of the eyes and demonic seizures,
heart disease, diseases of the mouth, diseases of the belly, and the wasting away of old age; || 229 ||
Diseases of the head, diseases of the limbs, and most terrible afflictions—these and many other maladies have been thus described. (230)
Those planets, together with their hosts, having been brought near for the sake of pacification,
prostrated themselves again and again and made a petition to the Lord of Gods.
If they are unable to endure even your splendor, how much less can they look upon you?
"Command me, O Mahādeva; what is to be done by your command? (232)
Mahādeva, his eyes bloodshot with anger, said to them:
"Why are human beings suffering, and by whose fault or for what reason? (233)
One among them spoke these words in the presence of the Lord of the World:
"This is our livelihood here; indeed, this Brahmadatta is our master. (234)
Those planets which seize in this world men who are evildoers, who are excessively greedy for wealth, and who are intent on killing; (may they be appeased). || 235 ||
Seeing Rudra, those men— whether joyful, sorrowful, or those whose wickedness has perished— enter into him, performing various rites such as funeral ceremonies.
This has been told to you, O God; be gracious, O Blessed One.
Command us, O Best of Suras: what further must be done hereafter? (237)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the three-eyed Supreme Lord,
the granter of boons whose vehicle is the spirits, spoke this Rudra-śānti.
But he who, having heard this Vidyā of Umā from the Guhyaka... [verses 32–39 missing] ...239.
One who is pure through the sound of celibacy and does not speak is considered a practitioner. || 240 ||
Therefore, one should likewise avoid such a person as previously described;
he too is called a "teacher" (deśika) in the Tantra, though he is merely a seeker of success (siddha-sādhaka).
The vow of the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is arduous, whereas for the householder (bhautika), it is forbidden [to engage in these]:
approaching the wife of one's teacher, theft, and sexual intercourse during auspicious times.

For a householder, it is considered proper to avoid the practice of shaving, the consumption of clarified butter, flowers, fragrant substances, fine perfumes, beautiful dwellings, and physical strength. (243)
Having gone to enjoyments, they do not become corrupted; food is the cause of strength.
A square of one cubit with four lines is the mandala at the edge of the Veda.
However, for the sake of providing food, the duty toward the teacher must always be performed;
it is taught that for the practitioners and others, [the offering] is diminished by one line each.
(19) Wearing hair or shaving it off is both commended according to one's desire;
for ascetics wear matted locks, being embodied beings marked by [their] vows. (246)
One should wind the matted locks, but one should not wrap the shaven head;
for those locks should be made either straight or in the form of a braid.
The *kanaka* and other [types of] *vṛtta* should have their *jaṭās* made uneven by one, three, five, and sixteen [units], resembling the coils of a serpent, by one who knows [the rules]. (248)

But the others may be according to one's wish; as for the established system of the scriptures, there are [variations in] the knowledge of the principles (tattva), the letters (varṇa), the digits (kalā), the words (pada), and the locations (sthāna). || 249 ||
Having well-prepared the site, its layout should be determined by the predecessor;
then a foundation for the ashes must be constructed, whether it be solid or even made of brick.
The strength should be one span in length, and there the height [of the base] should be eight finger-breadths;
the height of the upper garment (uttarīya) should be made to measure twelve finger-breadths.
It should be four finger-breadths wide and joined in its center;
alternatively, a gourd may be used, measuring sixteen finger-breadths.
One should carefully avoid a staff that resembles ash or wood;
it should be made equal in length to one's own body, and its base should be like the size of a thumb.
Alternatively, [one may offer] a bamboo, khadira, or śirīṣa staff measuring one cubit;
[having done so], he does not turn back from his goal.
If one strikes the head [of the deity] seven times with the staff of Rudra while it is manifest,
that planet-grasper shall be cooked in the Raurava hell for seven thousand births.
"And furthermore, he who, knowing me, should transgress this most terrible [command]—having spoken thus, the Blessed One stood before the planets. (256)
Having established [the fire] in the sacrificial pit, the Lord spoke this Vidyā;
having performed this, the Great Goddess Bhavānī stood before Brahmā.
Salutations to the one who is beyond intellect and invincible; salutations to the supreme refuge.
She is the syllable Om, the syllable Vaṣaṭ, as well as Brahmā, Svāhā, and Svadhā. || 258 ||
Sāvitrī, Bhūtasāvitrī, and Rudrasāvitrī;
likewise Rudrāṇī, Brahmasāvitrī, and the goddess Sarasvatī. || 259 ||
Umā, Kṛṣṇā, and Śivā are indeed eternal and reside within the heart,
among gods, asuras, and humans, and in both the stationary and the moving.
Having thus praised the God in his presence, they departed for their own worlds.
The hymn of Kalā has been told; now the division of the maṇḍala is being described.
In worship, one should employ the word "namas"; in the oblation (havana), that which ends in "svāhā" is beneficial;
in nourishing (āpyāyana), one should apply "vaṣaṭ", "ṣṭau", and "vauṣaṭ". || 262 ||
One should perform the application of the birth [sign] in the place of the two circles;
thus the ritual action has been declared, beneficial according to the tradition regarding the location. (263)
Oṃ, salutation to Rudra. Oṃ, salutation to Avimukta. Oṃ, salutation to Mahāvikṛtarūpa. Oṃ, salutation to Puru... [264]
Salutation to Śāya. Thus, in the vessel of Īśāna: Kṛto Rudra... Oṃ, salutation to Viśvarūpa; Oṃ, salutation to Mahāviśvarūpa. || 265 ||
Homage! 001 Oṃ, homage to the one of terrifying form! 001 Oṃ, homage to the one of deformed form! 001 Oṃ, homage to the one of greatly deformed form! || 266 ||
In the northern vessel, regarding the principle (tattva) of Puruṣa, there are the Rudras ending with Pañcarūpa: Oṃ, salutation to Ekapiṅgala; Oṃ, [salutation] to Śveta... || 267 ||
Salutation to Piṅgala. 001 Oṃ, salutation to Kṛṣṇapiṅgala. 001 Oṃ, salutation to Madhupiṅgala. 001 Oṃ, salutation to Niyata— || 268 ||
In the vessel for the limbs (vāvayavapātra), there are four Rudras: Om, obeisance to Ananta; Om, obeisance to Rudra; Om, obeisance to Śuṣka. || 269 ||
Homage! 001 Oṃ, homage to the host of waters (payogaṇa). 001 Oṃ, in the principle of Time (kālatattva), there are four belonging to Varuṇa. Oṃ, homage to Karāla. 001 || 270 ||
Oṃ, obeisance to Vikarāla. Thus, these two [mantras] are for the Māyā-tattva at the western face. Oṃ, obeisance to Sahasraśīrṣa. 110 || 271 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the thousand-faced one. Oṃ, salutation to the thousand-rayed one. Oṃ, salutation to the thousand-liṅga one. || 272 ||
Thus, on the right petal, regarding the reality of the four thousand sciences:
Oṃ, homage to Ekaṭā; Oṃ, homage to Bīja. Oṃ. 273.
Salutation to Svāhākāra. 001 Oṃ, salutation to Svadhākāra.
001 Oṃ, salutation to Vaṣaṭkāra. Thus on the leaf of the fire [Vahni]. 274.
The eight Rudras are situated on the leaf of Īśvara. Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Rudras. Oṃ, obeisance to the Sovereign of Time. Thus [ends section] 275.
In the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva, on the six eastern petals: Om, obeisance to the one who bears a single form (ekarūpadhāriṇe). Oṃ, O four-faced one (caturmukhi), you are Rudra. || 276 ||
O God of gods, Viśākha! Slay, slay! Crush, crush! Act, act! Puri, puri! Suri, suri! O Rudraśānti! || 277 ||
p.
21) Recollecting [this], [one should say]: "Obeisance to Vighneśvara, the lord of the Piśācas of untimely [onset], who is dark and tawny. 001 Thus [ends the section on] Umāma— || 278 ||
The two lords [are situated] in the pericarp within the principle of Śiva: Oṃ, to Vyoma-vyāpin; to Śiva, whose form is space and who pervades all. || 279 ||
"To the infinite, the protectorless, the supportless—[I offer] incense"—thus, in the center, with the essence of Śiva, [he offers it] to the foot upon the pericarp. || 280 ||
Obeisance to Śiva, the eternal Yogi who abides on the seat of Yoga, who is beyond all permanence, and who subsists on nothing; Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya Sarva- || 281 ||

To the one who is the source for the sake of auspiciousness, to the head of Īśāna, and to the face of Tatpuruṣa—thus [he worships] on the eastern petal; Sādākhya and Aghora [are worshipped]. || 282 ||
To the heart, Vāmadeva; to the secret Sadyojāta form—Oṃ, salutations again and again! To the most secret of secrets! To the slayer of the cow... || 283 ||

For the sake of wealth; for the sovereign of all accomplishments; for the one whose form is light—in the Īśvara-tattva, at Agnidula; for the one who is devoted to the Supreme Lord; for the motionless... || 284 ||
Therein is the insentient void; the void, the pervasive, the pervasive, the formless, the formless, the primordial, the primordial, the light, the light. || 285 ||
Light, light! Formless! In the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), on the southern petal:
Ananta, ashless, ashless! Beginningless, manifold! || 286 ||
Dhū dhū dhū oṃ bhūḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ suvaḥ | oṃ mahaḥ | In the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva), on the petal of Nairṛta: Anidhana Nidhana Nidhanod- || 287 ||
O Bhava, Śiva, the Supreme Self of all, Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Sadbhāveśvara—in the vessel of Varuṇa, within the principle of Time (kālatattva). || 288 ||
O you of great splendor, lord of yoga, release, release! O first one, first Śarva, Śarva! O Bhava, Bhava, born of existence, bestower of happiness upon all beings! || 289 ||

"O you who bring all things into presence!"—thus, in the northwest petal, within the principle of necessity (niyatitatva), [he is] beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; unworshipped, unworshipped, unstudied... || 290 ||
O you who were previously praised, O you who were previously stationed, O witness, O witness! Act, act! O moth, O moth! O tawny one, O tawny one! O knowledge, O knowledge! Thus—291.
In the principle of Puruṣa, on the northern petal: || 1 || Śabda Śabda Sūkṣma Sūkṣma Śiva Śiva Sarvada Sarvada Oṃ Namo Namaḥ. Oṃ Śivāya || 292 ||
Salutations, salutations! "Oṃ" refers to the primordial reality. On the petal of Īśāna, one should constantly recite the Rudraśānti; thus, one is liberated from all sins. || 293 ||
O Six-faced One, in all calamities and all portents,

if a person does not subsequently perform pacification rites— such as the installation, worship, and initiation— at the commencement of the ritual sequence, he is deprived of the fruits of his sacrifices and charitable works. || 295 ||
When there is the attainment of recovery from disease, during rites for regional peace and the like,
and in cremation grounds where men constantly reside— (296)
Likewise, for the rites of subjugation, eradication, and killing, one should perform eight hundred repetitions;
in these cases, one must never wait for the physical time [of the victim]. (297)
Thus, in the glorious *Kālottara*, the great tantra of six thousand verses,
the chapter on the propitiation of Rudra— the conduct of Śiva.
Īśvara said:
The conduct of Śiva for those who have been initiated is now declared in its proper sequence. (299)
Furthermore, what is to be avoided and what is to be performed by those established on the path of Śiva on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights? || 300 ||

On all occasions of Vyatīpāta, on the increase of a day, on the decrease of a day, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), at the two solstices (ayana), and at the six mouths of the Aṣṭamī (ṣaḍaśītimukha). || 301 ||
The worship, fire-oblation, recitation, and subsistence on a single night-meal should be doubled;
one must practice protection toward all beings and show affection toward ascetics.
Compassion toward all beings, patience, truthfulness, and lack of fickleness—speaking what is untrue for the sake of one's guru or the gods does not result in fault. (303)
Without punishment and without companions, there is neither going nor lying down;
he always wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads as a bracelet, and his dwelling is uneven and free from dust. (304)
One should wear [the amulet] with one, three, or five faces as available;
those with two, four, or six faces are recommended, provided they are unblemished, with a bulbous base and sharp edges. || 305 ||
One should never wear a rudrākṣa that is cracked, infested by insects, devoid of its bulbous base (kanda), or scarred by the marks of a crow's beak. (306)
Or, one should wear [the image of] the four-faced [Brahmā] on the tip of the right arm;
thus, O dear one, even one who is not a celibate student becomes a celibate student, a son of Brahmā, and a Snātaka.
By wearing rudrākṣa beads, one is indeed glorified in the world of Rudra;
it burns away the sins of speech, mind, and body, just as fire consumes fuel. || 308 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should always wear the rudrākṣa;
if it is not worn, there is great fault, and spiritual accomplishments remain far away for him.
The wearing of Rudrākṣas should be performed by both those who have been initiated and those who have not;
however, a golden ring must always be worn on the right hand.
It should be fashioned with rubies or else made of sapphire;
indeed, it should be worn as an earring adorned with various colors such as gold and other materials.
The first [measurement] should consist of nine sounds and ten [units], with three threads starting from the teacher;
when it is encircled by three threads, that circle is rubbed and well-rounded.
One should lead [the cloth] twice as wide by means of a waistband up to the region of the breasts;
from that, one should make it twice as wide again, with its knot formed by three windings.
The sacred thread (*upavīta*) for kings and others consists of its specific strands in the proper order;
they should maintain it merely for the sake of ritual worship, for they do not wear it above the shoulder.
The name Śiva belongs to the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas), while the name Deva belongs to the Cāndrapas;
for Vaiśyas the name is Deva, and for Śūdras it is accompanied by the word Gaṇa.
The designation "flower" is beneficial because it leads one toward its source;
one should not abandon one who is helpless, weak, frightened, or foul-smelling.
The raising up of cows that have sunk in mud or similar substances must be performed;
it is declared here that the status of being an Ācārya belongs to all four castes.
And for all the castes, the twice-born [brahmin] is the benefactor through his actions;
for the three [higher castes], the kṣatriya is so by two [means]; the vaiśya and the śūdra are [benefactors] only by birth in their own [caste]. || 318 ||
One should avoid the office of the *hautr* priest from those such as artisans;
likewise, the act of favoring [the disciple] should be performed by all four preceptors.

The state of being a twice-born who observes the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharmitva) is proclaimed to be fourfold: the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the ascetic (yati), in that order. (320)
The state of possessing the duties of the householder stage of life belongs to these three and no other;
for them, the practice of celibacy is prescribed for that duration.
There is indeed a distinction between the stages of life (āśramas), but no distinction exists in their ultimate goal (niṣṭhā).
One enjoys the fruit of one or both; liberation is common to both.
The religious student (brahmacārī) is said to be of two kinds: the temporary (bhautika) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika). The temporary student is to be known as threefold; I shall describe them briefly.
The *viprāsnātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *vidyāvratasnātaka*—for indeed, each of these three types is a *bhautika*. (324)
Upon the completion of the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata), his [status] is declared as that of a householder;
the second is called the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), whose conduct lasts until the end of the body. || 325 ||
Wearing a girdle, with matted hair, carrying a staff, or shaven-headed, he should be a pure mendicant;
he should dwell constantly in the teacher's family, self-restrained, and speak only the truth. (326)
One should bathe at the three times of day, free from anger, patient, and practicing celibacy;
this is the turning back for a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) resulting from the recitation of ten thousand Aghora mantras.
When Vṛṣeśvara has been worshipped and one has departed, there shall then be liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
One should perform bathing, worship of the gods, fire-offerings, giving of gifts, and libations to the ancestors. || 328 ||
One should either bring about the death of one's own wife, or else maintain eternal affection for her;
O son of Pārvatī, the householder should be understood to be of these four types.
Dwelling in the forest, wearing fire as one's garment, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, sleeping on the ground, wearing deerskins, and refraining from accepting gifts. || 330 ||
Bathing three times a day, performing fire oblations, worship and meditation day and night,
and the restraint of all the senses— this is the way of life for one dwelling in the forest.
The renunciation of all ritual actions, dwelling in the forest or wearing bark garments, seeing with equanimity toward all things, and remaining unshaken by pleasure or pain. (332)
Purity both external and internal, devotion to meditation in the forest, and the relinquishing of the pleasant and unpleasant—from these, the [proper] way of life is described. (333)
p. 25) This tetrad has been described, and each one is fourfold.
Thus [ends] the glorious *Ṣaṭsahasrikālottaramahātantra*. || 334 ||
In the Tantra, the chapter on the stages of life (āśrama-paṭala), the Lord said: "I shall once again proclaim the fourfold domain of Śiva. (335)
Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Sāvitrī are the Gocarās;
the Kula is to be known as the Gocara, and by it those who have been looked upon are to be known. || 336 ||
Those who are marked with the sectarian sign (cihna) are Śaivas; all others are considered heretics (pāṣaṇḍinaḥ).
One should, moreover, visualize the body of Śiva as fourfold within one's field of perception.
That which is expressed by Mantra belongs to the Śiva-kula; that which is expressed by Nāda belongs to the Śikhā-kula.
That which is known as Bindu, Ardhacandra, and Jyotsnā is declared to be Sādākṣya.
The state of being within the range [of perception] should be understood as extending from the non-auspicious (āśiva) up to Īśvara;
however, when there is prior cognition of Śiva and so forth, it is then no longer mere consciousness (cinmātra). || 339 ||
In the Śiva-āgama, the knowledge of the nature of the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) conjoined with the seed-syllable is to be known as consisting of eternal bliss; that Kula is designated as Śiva.
The power of Nāda, praised, has arisen from the supreme state of Brahman;
for it is pierced by the needle of Nāda as far as the end of the twelve.

Having uttered the mantra, that which is declared as internal by means of the *śikhā* [mantra] within the *kalā* should likewise be known as the *śikhākula*, by virtue of its support in the principle of *nāda*.
Form resides in the principle of the point (bindu) and in the state of Sadāśiva;
the investigation of the object, by virtue of the power of the fetters of the bound soul (paśu), occurs in that which is designated as light (jyotis).
But that family known as Sāvitra, which is mixed with all [the others],
consists of Śiva and Śakti in their manifest (sakala) form, and below that is the nature of Īśvara.
For in each respective case, because he is the enjoyer therein, that family belongs to him;
Śiva is the crest-lock (śikhā), and likewise the light—the Sāvitraka family is to be known.
The fourfold distinction of the livelihood for each one is now declared:
the Prājāpatya, the Mahīpāla, the Ākapota, and likewise the Granthika. (346)
These divisions have been fully described within the sphere designated as Śiva;
likewise, the Kuṭikas, Vetālas, Padmas, Haṃsas, and the Śikhākula.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Bakas, Kaṅkas, Gopālas, those known as Jyotis, the Tuṭikas, Māṭharas, Gulikas, Daṇḍins, and others. (348)
(26) Regarding those born under the influence of Savitṛ, hear now their prescribed mode of life:
non-violence, service to the teacher, study of the Vedas, purity, and self-restraint. (349)
Indeed, this vow of Prajāpati must certainly be maintained;
for the sake of the destruction of the son, one should perform acts of hostility along with rites for pacification and the like. (350)
Because they protect the earth, those who rule the land are indeed arrows; for if they do not strike down others on the ground with a single glance, they gather them like pigeons.
Those pigeons whose life depends on that [flesh], however, are the arrows;
for they suddenly abandon it once they have made a large, firm knot. (352)
Those who have abandoned their huts on the banks of rivers and oceans and remain there for the sake of the fire-eating deity are considered *granthika* practitioners. || 353 ||
Those who dwell in huts, devoted to the worship of Śiva, accompanied by their wives, attached to sacred fords (tīrthas), and subsisting on whatever is obtained, are to be known as Kuṭīcakas. 354.
Those practitioners who are endowed with great enthusiasm, who are self-controlled yet attached to impurities, are the ones who accomplish the goals of sovereignty, desire, and wealth. || 355 ||

Those known as Sādhakas are like lotuses; they are always devoted to the practice of begging for alms, endowed with the yoga of knowledge, and established in the conduct prescribed by the Vedas. || 356 ||
Those who are called *haṃsa* practitioners, whose consciousness has arisen spontaneously through celibacy, truthfulness, and by means of whatever [means] they have obtained; 357.
Those who are considered Dhṛtarāṣṭras have conquered the entire world;
they move about in concealment, whether possessing knowledge or observing vows and dharma. (358)

But those who are intent solely on their own self as their goal are like herons; desiring to be practitioners, they remain resorting to a body of water for the sake of attaining superior siddhi. (359)
Those who subsist on seeds and water-melons are the Kaiṅkas, the practitioners;
they travel here together with cows and dwell in cow-pens.
Those cowherds who consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are indeed practitioners;
they emaciate their own bodies through penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
Eating only a mere morsel, those practitioners were desirous of success; having devoured Śamarī as their wife, they made the earth their household.
Those practitioners who are pure and devoted to the life of a monk, taking only a single morsel of food at intervals of eight *truṭis* equal to one *samāna*, [attain success]. (363)
Those practitioners, intent on the mortification of their own bodies, remain at night in the *vīrāsana* posture with pills produced from bulbs, roots, and fruits. || 364 ||
Those who carry staffs are called practitioners; all this has been declared to you in general terms, whether they abide in specific [stages], have become [liberated], or are even householders.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on the Sphere of Experience, in the glorious *Mahātantra* of the Six-Thousand-Verse *Kālottara*. 366.
Īśvara said:
Regarding the practice of eating alms-food—the student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha) are each of two kinds according to their role as teachers (deśika). || 361 ||
I shall tell you everything regarding what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided by those two:
during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should avoid weapons, but turmeric need not be avoided;
likewise, one should avoid passion for women, perfumes, singing, instrumental music, and dancing.
Except for that which pertains to Śiva, one should avoid everything else here with great effort. || 369 ||
Eating twice a day, giving gifts, and abandoning perfumes are beneficial; one should avoid garlands, ornaments, and scents, as well as the performance of sacrifices.
In times of calamity, even a beautiful vehicle, weapon, or other such [equipment] may not be seen.
[Missing page no. 39] || 371 ||
The alms-bowl should be made of either copper or leaves, with a height of ten finger-breadths and a depth of eight finger-breadths.
One should avoid the palāśa, the honey-leafed trees, the kadamba, the mango, and the campaka; however, one should avoid the excellent aśvattha, the viśā, vātākṣī, and the kesar.
He should beg for alms from all four castes, but he should avoid one who has been accused of a crime;
likewise, the practice of begging for alms regarding those born of outcaste status follows the prescribed rule.
Having placed the weapon in the staff and the heart in the bowl, he should go out for alms while remembering Śiva;
he should accept the alms that fall into the bowl, but discard what falls on the ground. (375)
One who has turned back from worldly life should not remain for a long time;
he should diligently practice silence, or else [remain so] until his alms-bowl is full. (376)
p.
28) Or else, alms consisting of grains of rice should be prepared in great abundance;
having placed them in a pure and level spot, let the alms indeed be brought forth. (377)

The wise one should recite the mantra for the body, beginning with the hands and feet, as before; then, having sprinkled it with water from the heart-mantra, he should offer it to Śiva and again to the Guru.
One should have food prepared by another, consecrated with the three-syllable mantra; thus it quickly becomes as described, and having consumed it, one shall become a conqueror of death. (379)
One should eat while maintaining silence and should not cause excessive disturbance;
thus has the wandering for alms been described as a characteristic common to all.
There is no merit equal to alms-giving; there is no austerity equal to alms-giving.
Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords and whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices [is attained thereby]. (381)
Whatever merit is found in all types of giving, and that which is found in rites such as the Cāndrāyaṇa,
a man who subsists on alms shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten millionfold.
When the cooking is finished, if a guest turns his face away, then all the gods and ancestors turn their faces away from him as well. (383)
When the time has arrived, it should be given with effort and without hesitation;
for such a person uplifts ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants.
Among all worthy recipients, the guest is indeed the supreme recipient;
whether he be deficient in limb or complete in limb, of noble conduct or even by birth alone. || 385 ||
He who is worthy of worship without hesitation shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
he who, when the time has arrived, avoids begging from afar.
Taking all the fruit of his merit, that guest departs;
it is as if one were to apply [the result] without reflection when the time has not yet matured. || 387 ||
Indeed, he is said to be a slayer of a Brahmin who is pure after a hundred transformations;
knowing this, one should always diligently engage in the practice of begging for alms.
The perfections (siddhis) are accomplished for him who subsists on alms and has his senses restrained;
O Śikhidhvaja, all other forms of receiving gifts are said to be excluded, with the exception of alms.
Thus ends the chapter on the conduct of the preceptor engaged in the stages of life, in the glorious Kālottara Mahātantra, the Six-Thousand [Verse] [Treatise]. 390.
Kārttikeya said:
"And as for the two types of gurus that have been mentioned, they are the *bhautika* and the *naiṣṭhika*, respectively. (391)
But the distinction between those to be favored [by me] has not been understood by me in its true nature. (392)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the truth concerning liberation and worldly enjoyment as they exist:
the supreme teacher is of two kinds, namely the celibate student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha). || 393 ||

These two—initiation (*dīkṣā*) and establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*)—are the causes for power and authority; however, they are the manifestations of those whose minds are turned away from liberation, not of those solely intent upon liberation. (394)
The celibate student (brahmacārī) is to be known as the teacher for householders;
indeed, for those of the preceding castes and stages of life who abide in their respective duties. || 395 ||
For ascetics who have produced the knowledge of reality, their state of asceticism is considered common to liberation, even when they are supported by chariots drawn by householders. (396)
The householder alone is honored by those who seek the fruits of sacrifice;
for others besides the householder, there is no entitlement to enjoy such rewards. (397)
Therefore, a householder who seeks both worldly enjoyment and liberation should be treated with great respect;
by merely bowing to such a person, one obtains the fruit of donating a thousand cows. || 398 ||
By prostrating at the feet of one's own guru, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
through that, one attains everything that has been given to a devotee of the Śiva-liṅga.
When he is satisfied, may the entire world, including all moving and unmoving beings, be satisfied;
when he is pleased, may the God of gods, Sadāśiva, be pleased.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the bearer of the Śiva-linga, whether among the Buddhists, Vaiṣṇavas, Pañcārthikas, Sauras, Kālamukhas, Kāpālikas, and so forth. (401)
Only a Śaiva may hold all offices; a non-Śaiva may never do so.
Here, the bound souls (paśus) are to be understood according to the distinctions among their latent impressions (vāsanās) and their essential natures (tattvas).
I shall explain the classification of those who have been initiated (dīkṣita), which originates from the Ṛgveda:
both the householder and the student (brahmacārī) are considered to be of two kinds among the initiated. (403)
O Śikhidhvaja, in the absence of the father, the sons shall be the heirs; they shall share the wealth equally, and the forest-born [goods] especially so. (404)

How is it that, in the case of one who has no son, the father shall take the inheritance, and in his absence, the mother? This applies likewise to the Śreṣṭha, the Haniṣṭha, and others born of the same progenitor.

In their absence, the paternal uncles, or likewise others who offer the rice-balls (piṇḍa)—whether they be born from the father’s side or when they are born from one's own lineage—[should perform the rites]. || 406 ||
Due to the absence of paternal kinsmen, however, the other [heirs], those born of the maternal side, [shall take it];
in their absence, the king shall take the property from both sides. (407)
In this way, the maternal grandfather and others are traditionally considered the creditors of the father and others;
however, a married woman who has offspring belongs to the lineage of her husband's family.
One should diligently seek the inheritance arising from the paternal side;
in brief, the master should take the wealth produced by the slave. 409.
In this manner, from those village-dwellers who are likewise devoted to their own existence and who have offspring, one should indeed take only a sixth part.
At the time of exportation, regarding the goods, the king is the one entitled to the share and no other;
he should present the highly valuable elephants to the sovereign.

Wealth from a Brahmin who has been excluded from the four [classes] may be accepted; likewise, that which arises from the water used for ritual rinsing (upasparśa) by fishermen and others may be accepted. 412.
And for the purpose of producing the *tantuplāvī*, one should extract it without the *veṇuplāvī*;
thus, one should divide the eighteen-fold nature according to the understanding of the scriptures. (413)
The intermediate scent is conceived as being external, following the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa); it does not exist otherwise.

Thus has the inheritance of the householder been described; now that which arises from the student is declared. Regarding the inheritance arising from a student, it belongs to the student's own lineage. 415.
And because of the absence of one's own lineage, as well as that of another's lineage, heirs are thus described; one should avoid those who do not bear the marks [of their order]. (416)
Because it arises within one's own continuum, the substance is not led away even by enjoyment;
moreover, that which is devoid of enjoyment is not beneficial for more than thirty years. (417)
Having been proclaimed according to the rules of documentation by the king, who holds the wealth [in trust], the witnesses must then examine it once both parties have given their consent. (418)
In disputes concerning verbal assault, witnesses need not be examined;
however, one should deliberate upon the core of the claim in a legal proceeding.
O Six-faced One, I shall once again explain to you the deliberation concerning those who are students (upakurvāṇakas) and who carry out the commands of Śiva.
Having abandoned and even accepted wealth, land, and so forth, he became a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and then entered the stage of a householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
p.
31) Their division of inheritance, however, should be calculated like that of householders;
one should determine the respective shares for the mother, sons, and brothers. || 422 ||
One should examine the legal dispute here, in its entirety and preceded by witnesses, by means of the threefold instruments of knowledge regarding the eighteen titles of law. || 423 ||
These analytical investigations have indeed been presented here in brief;
now, one who is endowed with learning, youth, and noble birth is considered inferior. (424)
Therefore, one who was initiated earlier should be saluted with effort like a guru;
he should be circumambulated by the senior [initiate], or the senior should greet him like a guru.
He should be worshipped with supreme devotion day after day as one's own guru; likewise, his wife should also be worshipped with diligent effort, for she is identical to him.
One should never cause the atoms [of the mantra] to be grasped by the wife of a guru for any purpose;
the three pledges (samayas) must not be given to her, nor should she ever be made to wear the sectarian marks (liṅginī).
One should never bow down to them, nor should one ever look upon them naked;
the elder brother is always to be honored, and thereafter one should seek out the scriptures.
Alternatively, one should listen to a scripture from any [source] for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action;
one should always worship it as if it were the Guru and avoid any sense of diversity [between them]. || 429 ||
The one who exhorts, the one who awakens, and the third, the giver of liberation—one should worship all of them like Śiva, for they are the givers of liberation to human beings. || 430 ||
That which impels living beings toward Śiva, the supreme cause, is called the "impeller" (codaka); such a teacher is the foremost leader and most excellent. (431)
The Guru is the bestower of liberation, the awakener, and the revealer of the scriptures;
indeed, the awakener must always be honored with great effort. (432)
Thus, this which resides with the Guru has been briefly stated according to the injunction;
so it is said in the *Kālottara-mahātantra*, the six-thousand-verse [work] concerning the Guru.
The sixteenth chapter on Discernment, consisting of forty-three verses; the Lord said: [434]
I shall now fully explain the *aṃśaka* (astrological division) which bestows fruits upon practitioners;
indeed, an investigation of the *aṃśaka* of mantras must be performed here. (435)
Without their constituent parts, seeds are devoid of fruit;
just as a seed that is sown out of season is never seen to yield fruit. (436)
Having scattered and sown seed in saline soil that is devoid of fruit,
one should never cause [a disciple] to receive a mantra that is likewise deficient by ten syllables. (437)
Therefore, I shall explain the threefold division of the *aṃśakas*; by knowing this, one becomes a perfected traveler (*siddhagata*).
Having written the *mātṛkā* on the ground, [the letters] are to be devoid of the *kūṭas*. (438)
Having analyzed the syllables of the mantra, one should separate the *anusvāras* individually; likewise, one should perform the analysis of whatever name belongs to the practitioner.

One should employ the designations of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* in sequence at the beginning and likewise at the end of the mantra for the practitioners. One should count these names according to their order.

If at the beginning and likewise at the end of a mantra there is an auspicious *aṃśaka* that grants success—such as one starting with "Siddha" and ending with "Siddhi"—it becomes effective at that very moment. || 441 ||
One should consider that which begins with *susiddha* and ends with *susiddha* as being like a *siddha*; however, one should avoid from afar that which begins and ends with *ari*. || 442 ||
The *siddha*, *susiddha*, *ari*, and *sādhya* [mantras] are likewise situated at the beginning of a mantra as being established in success (*siddhi*), and similarly at its end. (443)
The *siddha* [aspect] brings about success; the *saṃdeha* [aspect] is indifferent; the second is the *udāsīna*.
The *svasiddha* bestows fruit quickly and certainly destroys enemies. (444)

One should avoid one who is completely overwhelmed by the enemy of death, which is like the jaws of Death; however, one who is being overcome by the enemy of the Siddhānta, such as the Susiddhānta and others, is again auspicious.
Having understood this single part, O Six-faced One, one should impart the mantra— beginning with the Prāsāda and Praṇava and consisting of the syllable Māyā— to the disciple.
One should assign a portion to each of the nine-fold self and the deities;
for these are considered the sovereign lords of the king of mantras, the bestowers of grace through knowledge.
One should not assign a share in those matters for those who are capable in all tasks;
or else, the wise man may assign a share in another manner.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śakra, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas, as well as the Daityas, Vidyādharas, and Rudras, are to be known as pure portions of Him. || 449 ||

One who bathes at dawn, is devoted to the twice-born, practices purity, is self-controlled, compassionate, and is deeply absorbed in the knowledge of Brahman as the Self— such a person is to be known as a portion of Brahman.
Deceptive, yet endowed with courage, firm-minded, fond of women, and envious;
