one who knows hundreds of means for accomplishing tasks—such a person should be known as having a Vaiṣṇava portion. (451)
A man who is devoted to Rudra, industrious, heroic, a traveler to the abode of the Piśācas,
fond of the Great Vow (mahāvrata), and wise, should be known as one who possesses a portion of Rudra.
One who is skilled in song, dance, and the like, yet not devoted to them;
one who possesses such sovereignty and is attached to stories—he should be known as Paunandanaśāntaka. (453)

One who subsists on milk, suffers from wind-related ailments, has no fondness for rice mixed with pieces of meat, possesses fixed eyes, and desires the daughters of the Nāgas—such a man is to be known as one whose portion is the Nāgas. (454)
Adorned with ornaments such as bracelets and necklaces made of blackwood,
endowed with courage and possessed of all limbs, he is to be known as one who possesses a portion of the Lord of Yakṣas.
A lover of song and dance, beautiful with garlands, garments, ornaments, and perfumes, and desiring that sovereignty—such is the best of men who possesses a portion of a Gandharva. (456)
Flesh-eating, smelling of blood, fond of wandering at night, and with eyes terrifying due to the knitting of his brows—he is to be known as having a portion of the Rākṣasa nature. (457)

A man who has deep-set eyes, agitates others with his words, is intent on finding the weaknesses of others, and is fond of talking about worldly existence and its tales, should be known as one possessing a portion of wretchedness (dainya). || 458 ||
One who seeks the thirty-eight accomplishments (siddhis) through the practice of binding and collyrium, whose mind is absorbed in that, should be known as born from a portion of a Vidyādhara. (459)
He who is wise yet fearsome, pure yet fond of foul-smelling meat, noble yet mean, and afflicted by intense anger— he is said to possess the portion of a Piśāca.
The pure portion has been fully described; now the mixed portion is being told:
it is adorned with the tips of divine nails, smooth, and embellished by a halo of light.

Furthermore, his ankles were hidden, his fingers and toes were well-proportioned, his feet were like the back of a tortoise, his shanks were perfectly rounded, and his thighs were like the trunks of plantain trees at their knees.
Broad at the slopes of the hips and curved by the three folds of skin,
it is a vast abode of Lakṣmī extending as far as the waist, which is free from fine linen.
He had a neck marked with three lines like a conch shell, lips red as the *bimba* fruit, and lotus-like arms hanging down;
his prominent nose was perfectly straight, and his eyes were tremulous and restless.
With his inner radiance, he has a pure face marked by a pair of eyebrows like a bow;
he is beautifully adorned with a broad forehead and a parasol-like head. || 465 ||
(34) With the great peacock-feather fan as his crest and blue hair upon his head, he is endowed with the crane-like intellect and strength of sentient beings, as well as patience and joy. || 466 ||
Endowed with enthusiasm and joy, a devotee of Rudra who turns back [from sin] and possesses a mixed portion of grain will achieve success in all undertakings on that day. || 467 ||
On the full moon of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, those established in the doctrine of absolute non-duality [should worship];
he, however, together with the Mothers, should do so in the middle of the two fortnights at Karṇoṣṭhya.
Having understood this, one should bestow a portion and a mantra that is beneficial for him;
the mantra is said to range from a single syllable up to six syllables. (469)
From seven syllables up to five hundred, there may be a Vidyā;
from seven syllables up to twenty-two, there may be a Bālā. (470)
Beyond that, she is a maiden (kumārī) until thirty-two years of age;
beyond that, she is to be known as a young woman (yuvatī) up to three hundred years of age.
From three hundred syllables down to five,
and from there up to one thousand syllables, these are proclaimed as the firm vidyās.
Beyond one thousand recitations, this knowledge is proclaimed as the *Daṇḍaka*;
know that it is a hymn (*stava*) consisting of two thousand [verses], and it is perfected by being recited even once.
The morning twilight is beneficial for children during recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;
at sunrise it is for young maidens, and during the [first] watch of the day it belongs to those established in youth. (474)
At midday, worship is for the elders; in the afternoon, for the aged; at twilight, for those with staffs; and when the night remains, worship is for the others.
At the conclusion of the worship of the mantras, the recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and so forth are beneficial;
however, he who performs them otherwise will be obstructed by the lords of obstacles (vighneśas).
Not even a slight portion of what he strives to accomplish will succeed;
furthermore, for all [the deities], the food offering (naivedya) consists of milk-rice with ghee and curd.
Various kinds of modakas, sugar-candies, and many other sweets, when prepared with effort at the proper time, grant success; this is no false word. (478)
The two wings, white and black, consist respectively of the letters from *ka* to *ha*; however, the first wing is said to be like a calf deprived of its three [teeth]. (479)
One should perform the placement of the measures (mātrā) without the anusvāra and visarga. || 480 ||
Short, white, even, long, black, indeed...;
a girl, a maiden, a young woman, an old woman, the one who brings about thought.
The lunar days (tithis) are to be known as fivefold, established in three ways for each fortnight. || 482 ||
Birth, gain, and destruction—these five [states] occur in succession, one by one;
likewise, there are the rising, the twilight, the grasping, and the motionless.

When [the moon] has risen, one should perform rites such as pacification (śāntika); likewise, when it is in the dust-constellation (bhasita), one should arrange for universal attraction (viśvākarṣaṇa), immobilization (staṃbha), and so forth, at that time.
O Son of Pārvatī, the *grāmita* [mantra] is recommended for causing hatred and eradication;
having understood the time when the sun has set and is setting, one attains success. || 485 ||
For each individual period, the emergence of six ghaṭikās should be known;
therein, the intermediate time should be understood as existing in three ways.
Rites such as pacification (śānti) and others are accomplished through the flow of the iḍā;
the attraction of the universe, delusion, and so forth are successfully achieved through the piṅgalā. 487.
One should perform acts such as killing and expulsion while situated at the equinox;
one should diligently understand that each [act] is fivefold according to the movement of the channels (nāḍī). || 488 ||
Because earth, fire, air,
and space flow downward from it, it is known by the name "Pṛthivī" (the Broad One).
From those two, the upward-moving fire flows; from their middle, it is said, comes the wind, which exists in the side cavities, pervading everything and likewise the lower regions.
Stambhana (paralysis) is prescribed on the path of the earth element; śāntika (pacification) is desired in the water element;
and vaśya (subjugation), ākarṣaṇa (attraction), and so forth, are accomplished by the fire element—of this there is no doubt. (491)
Wandering by way of the path of the wind, the battle is indeed through the void;
thus has this been declared in brief regarding the movement of Time.
But without this, my child, nothing at all is accomplished;
therefore, one should practice the knowledge of time with every effort. (493)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the constituent parts (*aṃśaka*), in the great tantra *Kālottara*. 494.
The sixth verse (p. 36):
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme true nature.
It bestows incomparable good fortune, prosperity, beauty, and sons; it should always be resorted to by those desiring well-being, as it increases longevity and nourishment. (496)
Mantra-meditation, the maṇḍala, and likewise the application of mudrās—these five types, in brief, I shall now describe according to the ritual manual. (497)
Having extracted that very [principle] which is Citrabhānu, Śiva, Kāla, endowed with Great Power (Mahāśakti), and possessing both beginning and end, as well as its modifications; 498.
The second [mantra] is "Tāraka Kānta Gaurī," which should be provided with three words and made to end in the dative case, expressing the complete fulfillment of Gaurī.

In that regard, among the triad, one should not utter the first [mantra] at all up to the end of the Ṣoḍaśī; from Īśvara up to Śakti, however, one should perform the formal rite with one's own heart-mantra.
The mantra of Gaurī has been fully explained; now the mantra of Śiva is being told. One should extract the syllable ŪHA, as well as KĀLA, and the seed-syllable of Śiva.
One should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga), conjoined with the seed-syllables (jāti) and pervaded by the long-syllabled breath (prāṇa);
here, one should indeed place the seat (āsana) arising from the six [limbs] with the Praṇava.

O child, the ritual placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) is performed here with the heart-mantra, as well as the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth; this has been described according to the Yāmala tradition. Now hear the Ekavīra system.
Pervasive and joined with creation, the fire and illusion (vahnimāyā) are indeed the Śoṅga;
this seed-syllable consists of Śiva and Śakti, yet it is devoid of the heart and other [limbs]. 504.
I shall now proclaim, in due order, the meditation and the mantra of that which is known as the supreme seed of seeds, the calf, which bestows all desires. (505)
Starting from two finger-breadths up to as many as twenty-four finger-breadths,
it should be made according to the actual measurement in a house, whereas outside [the house], it follows the measurement of the temple.
An image made of gold is most excellent; those made of brass, copper, or bronze are also praised.
One made of white sandalwood is auspicious, as is one made of devadāru wood.
The unmanifest [mandala] should be carefully constructed, provided with five lumps (piṇḍas) and accompanied by Śiva;
there are circles in the corners, and above them shall be the fifth.
Lālitā, Subhagā, Gaurī, and Kṣobhaṇī are indeed the Śaktis;
they are located in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu, with [the fifth] above, while in the circle [of the mandala], it may be otherwise. (509)
One should place Speech (Vāk), Will (Bhavēcchā), and Knowledge of Action (Kriyājñānī) in the directions starting from the east;
she who is situated on the left side is joined with the arrangement of the seat (pīṭha).
One should make the unmanifest (avyakta) form auspicious (śiva), devoid of the lines of the *lakṣma*;
this is proclaimed as the unmanifest form of the two Śivas. || 511 ||
It should be known as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, especially for women;
therefore, I shall describe its manifest form, which is common to all.
She may have two eyes or three eyes, she may be pure or filled with apprehension; she may stand with even feet or uneven feet, and she may have two or four arms.
Whether she is situated upon two lotus seats or established in the ritual action, Gaurī should be installed there just as she is; the first [form] is endowed with two arms.

The deer, the eye, the thread, the bud, the needle, the lotus petal, the small bell, the arrow, and the supreme [vajra]—these may be held in the right hand, while the other [left hand] displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). || 515 ||

In the visualization of Gaṇeśa, one should offer the following items in sequence, one by one, starting from the left: a book, betel, a staff, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā), and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Through the eightfold division of each of the eight hands by means of the other forms situated upon them, there are sixty-four varieties of the Lord.
As it has been stated: "Carrying two [staffs] on each side, they possess four hands; [the variations arise] from the divisions of the Vedas, the eight [world-protectors], and the mountains. (518)
For every *aṣṭaka*, there are pairs numbering eight times four (thirty-two);
through their mutual multiplication, the number of *muktās* proceeds. (519)
One should conceive of her as either visible or invisible, or manifest;
she should be understood as being like the *liṅga*, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Gaurī, whose form is unmanifest, who causes Śiva—who is himself unmanifest—to act;
or the Supreme Goddess, whether manifest or unmanifest, who makes Śiva manifest.
Alternatively, two manifest forms endowed with the [proper] characteristics should be fashioned:
Gaurī shall be eight tālas in height, and Śiva shall be nine tālas.
It should not be short, nor should it be made by a Śākya, nor deformed; it bestows auspiciousness.
Alternatively, the form of Ardhanārīśvara should be made according to the prescribed measurements.
(Thus) meditation has been fully explained; now I shall indeed describe the mudrā.
One should visualize the lotus seat and the mudrā as previously described. (524)
The Liṅga-mudrā is declared for Śiva, and the Āvāhanī-mudrā for both;
for Gaurī, however, the Śakti-mudrā or the Yoni-mudrā is prescribed.
One should interlace the fingers with one another and place the two thumbs between them;
when both index fingers are raised, this is the Śakti-mudrā, which bestows auspiciousness.
O Six-faced One, the agitator who binds all together is preceded by mantra;
I shall now duly explain the maṇḍala in its proper sequence.
One should construct a square measuring four cubits on all sides, divided into sections;
in the central cell, one should fashion a triangle.
Above those three, there is a half-moon, which is doubled by doubling the curvature;
the door-section consists of two units, being twice the size of the unit-section.
In this manner, one should diligently arrange the fourfold [set];
the corner region from the two doors is considered to be two units, like a vajra.
In this [mandala], the two ears of the two doors for the expiation (prāyaścitta) are made by oneself;
in the center of the triangle is a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
It has the luster of the color of a white kunda flower or the moon, is triangular, and possesses a red radiance;
it is shaped like a half-moon, yellow, and has the brilliance of gold.
The doors are yellow and black, and the corner-vajras have the luster of collyrium;
having thus completed the mandala according to the rule, one performs the consecration.
Alternatively, O Six-faced One, one should fashion the Sarvatobhadra mandala; one should construct the mandala as before during the consecration ceremony.

The rite, beginning with the consecration as the fifth and ending with the hoisting of the banner, should be performed like that of a temple of Śiva; O dear one, when this restoration of the dilapidated is completed, one obtains the fundamental fruit.
Then, having installed the Goddess with devotion, one should worship her there according to the rules, either upon a well-adorned sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or elsewhere, with sublime hymns.
One should cause a horse to be fashioned there, representing the supreme and non-supreme Śakti-tattva;
thus should this visualization be performed by practitioners upon images and other such objects. (537)
That [deity] should be meditated upon by the foremost of practitioners during the ritual for the sake of attaining success through good fortune;
having bathed [the image] with the five nectars and the like, and having anointed it with saffron and other substances.
Red garments should be offered, especially flowers; likewise, fragrant white flowers and other perfumed ones. (539)
As for incense, black agallochum or musk combined with camphor should be offered;
likewise, sugar-candies and many other pure offerings should be presented.
One should cause [the patient] to drink milk mixed with sugar-candy, or whatever roots, tubers, fruits, and so forth may be pleasing to the mind. (541)
One should offer betel-leaf together with various enjoyments;
facing north, one should worship the Supreme Goddess. (542)
Having performed worship, O son, one should diligently perform the recitation (*japa*) of the supreme [mantra] every day—either eight thousand, or a thousand, or even a hundred times. (543)
In the same manner, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed, O limb [of the body], as a tenth part [of the recitation];
however, according to one's own capacity, there should likewise be recitation (japa) for Śiva and fire-oblation for Śaṅkara.

In a place with the luster of a lotus, one should construct a forest grove; in its absence, one should do so before [the deity] in an auspicious pit measuring one cubit, provided with three tiers of girdles.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit once with the water from the arghya vessel;
likewise, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the oblation materials grant success, and not otherwise.
One should conceive of the fire of knowledge situated there within the lotus of the heart;
having placed it upon the path of the *suṣumṇā* and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
And likewise, having meditated upon Guharī in her form, one should cause the full oblation (pūrṇā) to be offered;
for thus she becomes the fire of power (śakti-agni) in all rites, whether daily, occasional, and so forth.
O son, by making offerings into the fire of knowledge, one attains all desires;
day after day, one should perform the oblation with *jāti* flowers.
With *caṃpaka* flowers, or *palāśa*, or *karavīra* soaked in ghee;
or with blue-lotus petals, or with auspicious *bilva* fruits, or with mandāra flowers. || 550 ||
The oblation (homa) should be performed with betel nuts, nutmegs, saffron, or kesara;
it should especially be performed with camphor and sandalwood.
An oblation of Kapila-ghee combined with guggulu is likewise recommended;
an oblation of dūrvā grass is likewise praised, and an oblation of parched grain (lāja) is especially so. || 552 ||
An oblation (homa) is beneficial when performed with *kanda* flowers, and especially so with *jāti* flowers;
however, one should always avoid performing an oblation with *sumanā* flowers or those that cause madness.
Furthermore, a Homa of Dūrvā grass, Amṛtā, and clarified butter, mixed with honey, is recommended;
likewise, a Homa of white mustard seeds and the buds of the Brahma-tree (Bilva).
Then, with tender leaves produced from those [plants] and likewise with tender branches,
one who knows the fire-oblation (homa) should perform the oblation for the purpose of attraction;
for in the case of subduing, the stalk of the *nāgakeśara* flower is prescribed for the oblation.
A white [cow] increases prosperity, while a red one is praised for curing blindness;
however, a black cow, possessing a lustrous hue, is indeed recommended for rites of black magic (kṛṣṇakarma).
The *pūrṇāhuti* should be offered afterwards, and then one should apply the *tripuṇḍra*.
One should present the oblation (*homa*) to the Goddess, bowing down again and again.
One should calculate the retrograde sin up to the root of the asterism;
an image should not be fashioned there, nor should the ritual dismissal (visarjana) take place. || 559 ||
One should perform that [rite] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the mandala, in the fire, or in the water-jar (kalaśa);
afterwards, the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) should be given, and the field is expelled outside.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should diligently recollect the imperishable Śakti through the practice of nyāsa seven times, and then offer libations to the preceptor and the others.
One should always worship five, seven, or eight virgins with diligence;
O Śikhidhvaja, women who are united with their husbands should be worshipped with great effort.
Whatever has been offered to the Goddess, one should cause that to be given to young maidens;
one should give it to the devotees of Śiva, and never eat it oneself.
Thus has this, together with its secret, been proclaimed by Subhagā according to her desire;
one seeking victory obtains victory, and one seeking sons obtains sons.
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
and even an unfortunate woman shall attain unimpaired good fortune.
And the king attains victory with undiminished majesty;
he shall sport over the entire earth, including all nine divisions together with the oceans.
By reciting [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times, the desired accomplishment arises;
for one who brings even the planets and so forth under control, what need is there to mention [subduing] the dānavas and others? (567)
Thus, this preliminary service must indeed be performed by the practitioner;
having conferred initiation upon women or men, he should cause [the mantra] to be bestowed. || 568 ||
O child, one should not entertain any doubt regarding this practice of mantras;
one should perform the initiation through the ritual digits (kalās) by means of a hundred oblations in the proper sequence.

In this manner, five oblations (kalā) should be offered; when one has the capacity, one should employ the full oblation (pūrṇā). This applies likewise to those of equal intellect, as well as to the spiritual sons (putraka), the aspirants (sādhaka), and the teachers (ācārya).
The application for all [the levels] should be performed; however, in the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva), the previous [method] applies.
In Īśvara, there is enjoyment for the practitioner (sādhaka); in Sakala, there is the state of the teacher (ācārya). || 571 ||

Having understood this, one should diligently effect both dissolution (laya) and enjoyment (bhoga). However, if a Guru performs initiation without knowing dissolution and enjoyment, [it is fruitless].
The teacher, together with his disciples, shall be cooked in the Raurava hell;
therefore, the preceptor should perform the initiation with great care after having ascertained [the disciple's fitness]. (573)
At the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā), the rules of conduct (samaya) should be proclaimed to the female practitioners and teachers,
to virgins, to those versed in the Vedas, to Brahmins, and especially to the gurus.
One should carefully avoid censuring the scriptures, the teacher, and other practitioners; one may engage in jesting with them, but never show contempt. (575)
One should mentally renounce the theft of property, as well as fickleness, greed, and the transgression of the teacher's commands. (576)
One should always diligently cause [the disciple] to grasp the perfected mantra from every aspect.
There is no restriction regarding time here, nor should one entertain any doubt in that regard.
Red garments should be worn, as well as collyrium and barley-meal.
The eyes should always be smeared with collyrium, the feet dyed with lac, and fragrant flowers should be worn upon the head with great care. (579)
The mouth should be provided with betel; the neck should be adorned with necklaces;
bracelets should be worn on both hands, along with earrings and finger-rings.
Fragrant and red garments should always be worn; sexual union is to be honored during the day, as well as on every festival day. (581)
During her menstrual period, she should diligently perform the internal sacrifice;
she must not consume the remnants of another's meal, for by doing so through the mouth of her husband, she incurs sin.
One should avoid giving gifts such as arrows and seats in the Pādmake [kalpa];
having seen the Guru, one should diligently prostrate at his feet from a distance. (583)
Worship should be performed three times a day, or even once;
as long as Gaurī has not been worshipped, eating is not beneficial.
Having worshipped her with betel, garments, perfumes, and other offerings, one should wear them;
at the time of dawn, one should always worship Bhavānī with devotion. (585)

A practitioner of mantra should never perform various tasks involving the physical form [of the deity], such as breaking things, grinding, using the hearth, sweeping, or [cleaning] the threshold. (586)
One should not touch with one's feet a maiden, a woman, a child, a weapon, fire, a twice-born man, a teacher, an elder, a sickle, or blood. (587)
O Śikhidhvaja, worship with the left hand must be avoided;
O child, oil, meat, and the like should be shunned on every sacred festival day.
Especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, on the full moon, at the sun's passage into a new sign, during eclipses, and at the junctions of the sixty-four-year cycles (ṣaḍaśītimukha).
A special worship must be performed; one should always honor the preceptor.
On the third day, a vigil should be observed, and likewise, worship should be performed on the fourth.
The food offering (naivedya) given by the Goddess should be presented to the young maidens;
one should avoid performing worship in the presence of those who have not received initiation.
In the absence of maidens, women should be employed as attendants;
they should be fragrant and auspicious, and likewise, the fourth worship should be performed.
That which was given by the Goddess... [53 to 87 missing] ...593.
In the eighth part, there are two parts of speed; through a twofold increase, the wind becomes double. || 594 ||
One should likewise imagine the earth-element as before;
in this manner, one should imagine [the elements] up to the twentieth part, ending with feces. || 595 ||
One should fashion the *māyā* (the illusory veil) extending to twice the measure of the end;
it should have two or three stories (*tala*), with *ālindas* (porches) and walls according to the external count.
One should fashion it with one quarter, or half a quarter, or three-quarters;
or with a quarter plus a third, or two quarters. (597)
Having given Indra the outer portion, or [the portion] of Ghanā, one should arrange the six groups (ṣaḍvarga) upon their respective foundations as before. || 598 ||
Whether shaped like a needle, a flame, or a temple, this head-ornament is known to be of three types: inferior, middling, and superior.
The eighth [category] consists of the suffixes *vibhakta* and *kta*; the triad beginning with *uttama* is the triad of *amatraya*.
Listen to how the supreme state, which is free from pride and has double the height, is attained. || 600 ||
That which is less by one part from the apertures is declared to be middling;
that which is terrifying, fierce, and not diminished is indeed the best.
It should be known that three *ratnis* is the medium [size], while two *ratnis* is the superior;
thirty *labvis* is the movable [measure], extending from the northeast to the northeast and from the southeast to the southeast. 602.
Having planted one equal portion, until its auspicious emergence. || 603 ||
Tāla is said to be of two kinds: technical (yaugika) and worldly (laukika).
It may consist of three, four, or even five tālas. (604)
The height is declared to be equal; this is stated to be the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha).
Above the pedestal, a lotus is to be placed, occupying one-fiftieth [of the total height].
The height of the lotus should be three parts; that height should be divided into three:
one part for the elevation of the petals, and the upper part for the pericarp.
Having done thus, the measurement for the pedestals (pīṭha) by means of the canopy (vitāna) has been declared;
for the Goddess, it is said to be threefold, in accordance with the Śiva-liṅga.
It should be equal to the portion for worship, or twice, thrice, fourfold, or fivefold that portion; or it may be three-quarters of the portion for worship.
p.
44) When the meaning is different, this [division] should be made in the ninth part;
and worship should be performed in the fourteenth, or having divided it into one hundred parts. || 609 ||

For one who has lost his wealth, there will be [suffering] reaching as far as the ears; for one with a deficient limb, leprosy and wasting away; and for one who possesses marks such as the conch and the discus, [there will be prosperity].

O Brahmin, there is no doubt that one should not cause the limbs of the Brāhmaṇas—who are the Vedas and the Sūtras and are the lords—to be marked with the weapons of the deities upon their bodies. || 611 ||
If [the syllable] has indeed fallen upon the limbs, there is no doubt in this matter;
the Brahmin should treat the trident and the wheel of imperishable syllables like a slave.
He should avoid all ritual acts, such as recitation, fire-offerings, and giving of gifts. || 613 ||
One should avoid touching the teacher (deśika) in the same way as one would touch a trident;
however, the wheel is said to be like a servant, so one may touch the preceptor (ācārya) closely.

Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and charity are prescribed as fruitless [if performed] according to the measurement of the Liṅga; however, O Goddess, they are fruitful when performed according to the measurement known as Niṣkala.
And for all images, [the mantra is] Hariḥ Om. (p. 45)
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms, and possesses a serene countenance.
We worship the elephant-faced one, who is the sun to the lotus of the unborn, the great day and night for the elephant-faced ones,
the many-tusked, yet to his devotees the single-tusked.
May there be auspiciousness; here is the description of Gaṇeśa:
Gaṇeśa has a human form, with the ears of an elephant and the face of an elephant. (611)
With a large belly and a massive body, possessing a single tusk and three eyes,
he had fierce eyes, protruding lips, and wore a serpent as a sacred thread.
Adorned with a crown and a basket, and decorated with all ornaments, he is endowed with four arms; in his right hands, he holds a goad and a tooth-stick.
One should place a foot and a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka) on the left side as the support;
the hand should likewise hold a sweetmeat, joined with the tip of an elephant's trunk.
Having meditated upon this form of Gaṇeśa, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra:
[he who is] saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, having the face of an elephant, and wearing a crown. || 615 ||
Accompanied by a basket, holding an elephant-goad, a sweetmeat, and a beautiful noose—this is the form of Gaṇanātha, whose eyes are like fire. || 616 ||

One should meditate on the elephant-faced one, who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms; he holds a noose and a tusk in both his right hands, while in his left hands he holds a *kuśa* blade and a *laḍḍuka* sweetmeat.
Now I shall describe in detail the form of the Lord of the Gaṇas, who has a serpent as his sacred thread and protruding lips, and who is the very embodiment of the Gaṇas. || 618 ||
Having two eyes and two arms, with short necks and large bellies, they have short feet and round eyes; their eyebrows are arched and full of playful grace.
Some there have the appearance of green, some likewise the appearance of yellow;
some there have the appearance of black, and some likewise the appearance of white.
Some resemble white, some are filled with smoky colors;
they are joined in mixed hues, combined with coral and dancing.
Some were joined with jewel-pitchers and clad in tiger-skin garments;
some had deformed bodies, while others sat intent upon their tasks.
Some held swords and shields in their hands, and likewise some carried staffs;
some bore snakes, and others likewise bore serpents.
Some indeed wear variegated garments, and likewise carry food-balls and nooses;
such is described as the form of the Bhūtas, with a height of five tālas being considered most excellent. (623)
Having two arms and two eyes, with a short neck and in the full bloom of youth;
her hair tied up like a crest, she is auspicious with her pure teeth as her weapons.
He should be white, wearing a sacred thread and clad in white garments;
with a purifier (pavitra) held in his hand, he should be seated there on the left side, adorned with various ornaments.
One was endowed with a prominent nose and possessed of earrings;
another was girt with a belt of muñja grass and wore a black antelope skin.
Those of dwarf form are said to be equal to five tālas;
this supreme form of Gaṇa is declared to be three times five tālas (fifteen tālas).
Śloka-je: Four-armed, three-eyed, of elemental form, with the face of an elephant;
red-bodied and blue-faced, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread. 628.
Adorned with a waist-string, a small crown, necklaces, and armlets, it is joined with a forehead-plate and provided with a binding for the belly.
Adorned with a jeweled casket crown, with anklets and finger-rings;
others indeed possess fruitful deeds, being delicate, beautiful, and pleasing to behold. (630)
One should place half of one's own horn held up by the right hand;
on the other right hand, one should place the supreme axe.
Then, in the left hand, he holds a fruit that is ripe, while in the other [hand] he holds a noose;
it is joined with a half-moon face and endowed with three arms and so forth. || 632 ||
Prajāpati said: "The mantra is seen as having two forms within Gaṇeśa, who is of a single form. || 633 ||
She is endowed with a boar’s face, possesses beautiful breasts, and is in the prime of youth;

her two right hands hold the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), while her first left hand bestows boons (*varada*) and her other left hand holds a staff (*daṇḍa*). 635.
The form of Vārāhī has been described; now the form of Indrāṇī is being told:
she has two eyes, four arms, is peaceful, and possesses full, elevated breasts. (636)
Adorned with a crown of jewels and equipped with bracelets on both [arms],
she holds a vajra and a śakti in each of her right hands.
Endowed with a golden complexion, possessing beautiful breasts and a lovely smile, she is complete with all ornaments and possessed of webbed feet. (638)
The form of Indrāṇī has been described; now hear the form of Cāmuṇḍā:
she has four arms, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses a luster like a dark cloud.

She has one face and three eyes, possesses beautiful fangs, and is endowed with hands that grant fearlessness; she wears bracelets, holds a trident in her hand, and bears a skull in her hand—she is auspicious.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of small bells, she holds [the weapon] in the left hand of all the Śaktis in the eastern direction. 641.
One should display some distinction, such as extending the arm like a bracelet,
or performing the action of touching above the waist, or perhaps with the arm hanging down like a pendant bracelet.
O Four-faced One, one should especially fashion them according to one's desire;
thus has the description of the Śaktis been told, and now the form of Dharaṇī is being described.
The extraction of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra is taught for the sake of one's son;
furthermore, the Goddess of Speech is praised by means of the Vāksiddhi-stotra mantra. (644)
All other fruits whatsoever are accomplished through his grace;
one should apply oneself to the realization of the words "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One. || 645 ||
One should also apply the word "Dakṣiṇāmūrti" in that very place;
"medhapradaḥ svāhā" is declared to be the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 646 ||
In one's own [mantras], the heart and other [limbs] are proclaimed as pure;
they are, in sequence, the utterances *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with a serene countenance,
resembling the Gaṅgā and the moon, adorned with earrings, and bearing matted hair upon his head.
Clad in a tiger skin and endowed with four arms,
he holds a rosary of pure crystal and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) in his right hands.
In the left [hand], there is either fire, a campaka flower, the gesture of granting boons (varada), or the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya);
or else, it is joined with a book; thus, according to the tradition, there are three eyes.
Having thus meditated upon the God, the Lord of Gods, who is yoked to a great bull and accompanied by hosts of sages, he is honored in all undertakings.
(He is in) meditative absorption;
his body is smeared with ash and is pale white; he wears a crescent moon [on his head]; and his lotus-like hands shine with the Jñāna-mudrā and a rosary in his two right hands. 652.
Delightful with his yogapaṭṭa, seated upon the throne of exposition, the Sage, served by the most excellent of men, is exceedingly serene; [his left hand] with its serpent... || 653 ||
May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, clothed in an elephant hide, protect you constantly;
may Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Śyāma, Sthita, Kaupīna, and Varṇaka [also protect you]. 654.
Bhāradvāja is considered to have red eyes, while Dhūmrabhāga has three eyes;
one should place one or two of these at the end of the sixth [syllable] and the end of the tenth for the two animals.
The second [vowel] conjoined with fire (the letter *ra*), joined with a vowel, and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, is called the first *praṇava*. This is the meditation on the Sun. 656.
The fifth seed-syllable is said to be joined with two *mān* [mantras], conjoined with *ya*, and united with the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*). || 657 ||
The sixth seed-syllable, ending with the letter *bha*, is here called the six-syllabled mantra;
it is joined at the beginning with the Praṇava and joined at the end with an obeisance.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by the mere recitation [of the mantra].
When joined with the *nāda* and other elements, the limbs of Brahmā are envisioned. (659)
This has been declared as the root mantra; now hear the seed-syllable of Uṣā:
the fifth letter from 'a' (pa) should be taken, conjoined with the bindu and nāda.

He was mounted upon a white elephant that had itself been mounted by another; he possessed the luster of a pomegranate flower and stood in the center of a circular orb of great brilliance from shimmering jewels.

One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having two arms and one face, clad in red garments, with his two hands holding a white lotus with its stalk that extends across his shoulders and throbs with light. (662)
The Vrata of Vināyaka:
Now I shall describe specifically the Vrata of Vināyaka; listen.
When the sun has entered Scorpio (vṛścika), one should begin on the day of the Agni constellation (kṛttikā). || 663 ||
Having likewise tied the protective thread (rakṣābandha) on the right hand of the men,
one should especially tie the thread on the left hand of the wife.
One should thus bind the seventh and the fifth sūtras as a triad;
the seventh with seven colors and the fifth with five colors.
Combined with three triple-strands of three colors, it should be held as a single color when obtained;
it may be made of fine silk, woven cloth, or cotton thread.
(49) First, the cleansing of the teeth, and after that, the purification of the tongue;
likewise, bathing is prescribed, and then the wise man should attend to his place of practice. || 667 ||
Having wrapped [the image] in a white cloth, wearing a clean upper garment,
and having covered it with a multicolored cloth, he should likewise wear a white turban.
One should worship the teacher first and afterwards worship Gaṇeśa;
one should offer food offerings and the like, including cakes and various fruits.
Having offered a coconut, one should then offer betel-leaf;
thereafter, one should present the mantra-flower and bind the protective thread.
One should especially fasten twenty-one threads;
having offered a prayer to Gaṇeśa, there shall be no interruption in the ritual action.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] every day for twenty-one days,
and likewise for twenty-two days, during the birth asterism of Gaṇeśa.
In this manner, during the month of Kṛttikā or indeed Mārgaśīrṣa,
when conjoined with the hundred constellations, it becomes most excellent on the sixtieth day.
At sunrise, at midday, and at dusk, there shall be [the three types of] exertion:
superior, middling, and inferior; this is now the rule.
If one obtains [the time] taught by others as being joined with yoga, one shall obtain that fruitlessly;
however, if the conjunction of those two is not obtained, this day is prescribed.
At the time of sunrise, however, a journey is said to be auspicious for one hundred constellations and days;
this is especially so when the sun rises in the constellation of Gaṇeśa’s birth. || 676 ||

Six, four, and three nāḍīs [of the day] at the time of sunrise constitute the "glorious" (dyuta) period; one should consume [the food] during these equal nāḍīs. This is declared to be the primary [period] for the birth asterism (janmarkṣa). || 677 ||

One should worship Gaṇeśvara on one's birth star, provided it is not joined with a hundred stars; at the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), one should perform the rite sixty times, while avoiding the other lunar fortnights.
On the day when the lunar mansion is conjoined with the rising [of the sun], one should observe the vow;
when the festival of Īśvara has arrived, one should perform the Vajra [vow] beginning from that very day.
One should observe the vow common to both gods and humans;
then, joined with fasting, one should worship Gaṇeśa.
At sunrise, one should recite the root mantra of Gaṇeśa one thousand and eight times;
at midday, however, one should perform circumambulations and one hundred and eight prostrations.
One should perform one hundred and eight recitations joined with the striking of the letter *ya*; one should especially worship [the deity] at the time of evening, particularly so. (682)
An oil-consecration should be performed, as well as one with ground āmalaka;
a wise person should perform the consecration with turmeric, all-pervading perfumes (sarvagandha), and other such substances.

One should perform the consecration with the five products of the cow and with milk, and especially with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as with water scented with perfumes, water with fruits, and water with flowers.
The ceremonial bathing (snapana) is joined with nine [substances], and the consecration (abhiṣeka) is performed gradually with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and black fragrances.
Having thus painted it, adorned with all its limbs and beautified with various flowers, and having decorated it with various garlands and cloths spread upon the altar; || 686 ||
Having prepared pure rice, milk-rice, and especially cakes and the like, in quantities of half a *kuḍava* each, according to the number twenty-one; || 687 ||
And having performed the ritual prostration, one should offer twenty-one portions of unhusked rice and flour paste, along with mung beans.
One should offer various kinds of food together with pieces of sugar-cane, mixed with clarified butter, immersed in curd, and combined with honey and sugar. 689.
Then, having offered various roots, one should offer pieces of sugarcane,
combined with oil-mixed betel nuts and various distinct flavors.
One should employ either white birch bark or plain paper, combined with camphor and strewn with powdered rays of light. || 691 ||
Having specifically offered this to the god Gaṇeśvara at the conclusion, one should afterwards present the mantra-flower; one should always worship with the eight flowers.
And for the sake of desired fruits of action, and especially for the sake of prayer:
one who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom; one who desires a field shall obtain a field. (693)
One who desires wealth obtains wealth;
one who desires a son obtains a son; and for one who desires enjoyment, enjoyment shall arise.
For those seeking the warding off of all diseases, there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
and for one seeking the destruction of all enemies, there shall be the destruction of all enemies. || 695 ||
Seeking the destruction of great sins, [he recites] the destroyer of great sins;
seeking the destruction of the five sins, [he recites] the destroyer of the five sins. || 696 ||
Having brought forth Kumāra from his own being, one should observe the *garuḍīvrata*;
having effected the release from Gaurī’s curse, one should observe the *viṣṇuvrata*. (697)
Having performed that which originates from Pulastya-gat, one should observe the vow of Brahma;
however, Indrajit obtains the vow originating from Indra.
In all such cases as these, one obtains whatever fruit is appropriate; furthermore, if it is a vow for men that is desired or performed for a specific wish, one shall obtain that very result.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the vow of Vināyaka in the Bhīmakāraṇa-pratiṣṭhā-tantra. || 691 ||
Nakedness, wearing a loincloth, binding a waist-thread, wearing wet clothes, and carrying a tail— these are proclaimed as the five types of nakedness.
By eating the food of a Śūdra and by constant association with a Śūdra for one full month, one attains the state of a Śūdra in this very life and shall subsequently become a dog. (693)
In the evening of Uttarāṣāḍhā in the month of Āṣāḍha, it is praised;
if Raktāṅga should arrive first, it is said to be the most excellent for nourishment.
If a white-bodied [child] arrives first, it is called middling nourishment;
if a black-bodied one arrives first, it is called inferior nourishment. || 695 ||
Likewise, they bear a dark-complexioned Śakti who is naked,
seated upon their laps, slightly red, and adorned with all ornaments.
She has the face of Digaṃbara and others, is endowed with two arms, is renowned as Vighneśvarī and so forth, and is beautiful in all her limbs. (697)
Likewise, he holds a lotus in his hand; it is secret with the right hand.
He has the form of a bull, with one face, four feet, and [the body] from the belly down to the tips of the hooves. 699.
A white-colored bull, possessing sharp horns and great strength, is the four-footed embodiment of the Vedas; its two horns are the form of Agni.
The Ādityas are indeed the cow-urine, Rudra is likewise the mouth, and the form of Agni is [the fire]. || 701 ||

He has the form of an elder, three eyes, four arms, tawny eyes, and is mounted upon a bull; he possesses a gentle form, was spoken of by Śiva, wears garments of the fourth color, and is accompanied by Śivā.
Wearing yellow garments, holding a spear in his hand, he is the very embodiment of the fire of Śiva;
likewise, children, the elderly, and the young are all of the nature of fire. (703)

The form of the "child-fire" (bālāgni) has been described as praiseworthy; likewise, the "eternal-fire" (nityāgni) is said to be for the elderly, while the "youthful-fire" (taruṇāgni) is for festivals. — Gāruḍa, 704.

One should always worship the form of Śiva-Agni during the rites of installation, festivals, and daily rituals, whether it appears as a child, a youth, an elder, or its own essential nature, and whether it is offered oblations or given sacrificial fees. || 705 ||
Now, [I shall describe] specifically the various forms of the aforementioned numbers of fires,
as well as their respective places of application.
I shall explain them in due order and in brief; listen again without doubt. Among those fires, the Śivāgni is first.
The second is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the third is the Dakṣiṇāgni;
behind them are the Āhavanīyas, and their end is the Lord of the Quarter (the West).
Among those three divisions, the names of the Lord of the Directions were indeed spoken by the speaker of the five names; in two of them, however, there is only the name Mahānana.
The name has thus been declared; now hear how one may attain his form:
he has aged limbs, three eyes, and is endowed with four arms. (710)
It was joined with the speech of Piṅgalā, endowed with a flaming crown,
possessed of the face of a wise man, consisting of itself, and accompanied by the granting of boons.
Furthermore, he who carries an axe and a deer, or else a spear, a voice, and a rosary in his left and right hands, and whose two hands grant boons; 712.
O Brahmin, that which is directly composed of Śiva is remembered as the form of Śiva-Agni;
thus, the form of Śiva-Agni is declared to be called Gārhapatya.
And Śivāgni is that fire extracted from a thousand parts,
red in color, with two faces and a body beautiful with six faces.
Clad in white garments and adorned with all ornaments,
one [foot] among these three is positioned with the tip bent upward.
The right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), while the left is endowed with the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*);
O Prajāpati, the two hands hold the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, each placed in the left [hand]. (716)
He shall have a fierce form mounted upon a ram and be likewise accompanied by Śakti;
thus is the Gārhapatya fire described, and now the Dakṣiṇāgni is spoken of.
A thousandth part of what was previously described arises as the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
there [is the deity] with two faces and six arms, wearing white and black garments. (718)
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, possessing six eyes and a tawny radiance, he has fierce fangs, a massive body, and a face slightly smiling. || 719 ||
In the right [hands], he holds a terrifying *bhaya*, a *sruva* ladle, and a sword; and in the left, he repeatedly displays the *varada* mudrā, a *kūrca*, and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). || 720 ||
Having ascended the dawn, the three-vessel [fire] together with Svāhā constitutes the form;
now the form of the Dakṣiṇāgni is clearly described by me.
I shall describe the form of the Āhavanīya fire, preceded by its origin:
from a thousandth part of the Dakṣiṇa fire, the four-faced one (Brahmā) was produced.
It has two faces and three feet, is endowed with two nostrils,
possesses three girdles, and is further characterized by six eyes and a tawny complexion.
[One should meditate on the deity] with four horns, mounted upon a bull, possessing a luster equal to the rising sun,
endowed with seven tongues, three of which are on the left.
I shall now declare their locations in the right face and the tongue:
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā. (725)
The seven tongues are proclaimed to be exceedingly red and multiform;
these names are now being told, and I shall now describe their locations—listen! (726)
What should the subtle [line] be like in the middle, in the north, and in the south?
In the forenoon, one should first apply the [lines] in the direction of Rudra (the northeast) from the city.
As before, one should meditate upon the goddess Svāhā conjoined with Rūpa;
in this way, there shall be the Āhavanīya fire, and as before, there shall be the Lord of the Quarter.
And from a thousandth part of the Lord of the Quarters, there arose Kevalāgnisamudbhava;
he has two eyes and two arms, and Caṇḍa is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Clad in white garments with a second white garment as a divine ornament, he is known as Kevalāgni; then Mahāsena is spoken of.
With a tenth part of the fire alone, [one should worship] Udbhava on the great seat;
he has one face and two arms, and is mounted upon a ram or a bull.
Clad in red garments and endowed with three crests, it has four peaks and three eyes; [this is] the *sruva* in the right hand. (732)
(54) Known as Mahāsana, he [saw] the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the form of fire. || 733 ||
The form of Indra has been described previously; now hear [the forms] of Vahni and the others. [The nature of] Dakṣiṇāgni... || 734 ||
Among them, O Brahmin, the form of Fire is now described:
she has two arms, two eyes, and hair that is curly and adorned with jewels. (735)
They are red in color, wearing red garments, red garlands, and red unguents;
they have white sacred threads and white upper cloths.
One should meditate upon the *sruva* ladle as being in the right and the *sruva* as being in the left; likewise,
the form of the *āhavanīya* fire is thus described as "vahyārī," and now the form of Yama is stated.
While staying in the east, the fire is in the east; however, when the twice-born is situated in the east, one becomes facing west after reciting the fire-mantras a hundred times. || 739 ||
If one performs an oblation in the ear, one is overcome by diseases;
an oblation in the nose brings suffering; and an oblation in the eye leads to the destruction of the sacrificer. (740)
If one performs the oblation at the location of the crest-lock (śikhā), the king’s kingdom will perish;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the evening oblation.
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, however, is the nose;
where there is blazing, that is the eye; and where there is ash, that is the head.
Wherever the tongue is ablaze, there one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in this manner:
[to the deity] who resembles blood, has six eyes, two faces, and tongues— || 743 ||
The hand is the *śakti*, the eyebrows are the *sruva* ladle, the eyes are the *mālā*, and the nose is the *tomara*. || 744 ||
Others [use] a ladle of clarified butter for the people.
It is red, endowed with five faces, and resplendent with seven tongues of flame.
Ten-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments, clad in red garments, and seated upon a lotus. || 746 ||
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and endowed with ten weapons;
then [the goddesses] Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā follow thereafter. (747)
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and Ratnāvatī are the three who reside in the upward-facing [direction] within the golden [city]; likewise, Śeṣā resides in the intermediate direction. (748)
The locus of the Śaiva Āgamas is indicated as being threefold and is proclaimed as peace (śānti);
it is the cause of creation and dissolution for her who is mounted upon the vehicle of the Unborn (Aja). 749.
At the time of the consecration festival, there are likewise three fires:
the fire of consecration (pratiṣṭhāgni) has an old form, while the fire of the festival (utsavāgni) is in the prime of youth.
The Dakṣiṇāgni fire is proclaimed to be the form of the offerings (bali) and the form of Agni;
the sacrificial pavilion is the nature of hundreds of thousands of fires, and the mouth is the *sruva* ladle. || 751 ||
Holding a noose, a battle-axe, and a sword, she bore the vajra in her hand;
she bestows the fire, the boon-granting gesture, and the goad, while holding all weapons and limbs in her hands. || 752 ||
The left arm is the fire that generates form;
having invoked and worshipped the Āhavanīya fire everywhere, one becomes Śivāgni. || 753 ||
"If there is no distinction, what could I do? Tell me that, O Navāgni. The Lord said: [754]
Having thus invoked the crops, there would be a distinction of directions, each with its own specific fruit;
I shall describe them in due order—listen, O Savya! (755)
There shall be the destruction of enemies in the southern direction, while in the south-west there is the eradication of disease.
In the west there shall be an increase of crops, and it becomes the station of Dārī and Āyu;
in the north there shall be an increase of wealth, and in the northeast it bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Between Indra and Īśāna, it shall be the bestower of all siddhis.
[It is located] in the house of Karaga, which consists of the six flavors and the earth, at the foot of the sun. || 758 ||

The sixteen new [units] shall constitute nine *pada*s; together with the three *pada*s of the central (*madhya*) new altar-base (*navavedi*), there are nine *kuṇḍa*s within the five *pada*s of the Śiva-maṇḍapa. || 759 ||
Having performed the ritual procedure, [he should divide] the portions starting from one square up to the interior of the pavilion of sharp and vast intellect; in the center is the altar. || 760 ||
Indeed, from nine parts there arise three [sides] all around, and three portions in the middle;
the front is the side of the qualities (*guṇabhuja*), while the other is truly well-rounded. || 761 ||

One should construct a six-pointed lotus and an eight-pointed sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the sequence beginning with the abode of the Lord of the Gods; [this is for] the subjugation of those who have strayed through pride. || 762 ||
p.
56) A cord of four crores in every direction, with a triple girdle, or else a double one, possessing the qualities of the elements and beings. || 763 ||

Even in the midst of the Mothers, O Vyāsa, fashion the Yoni with the letters of the Mother-alphabet (mātṛkā) belonging to the side of fire, like a sacrificial post rising upwards; and [fashion] that which arises from the length of the Tāra. || 764 ||
Praising with his fingers toward the fire, he, well-versed in the nine-times-nine [mantras], [placed] one in the middle of the nine. || 765 ||
One step at a time; with nine new [steps] by way of the body, there shall be the ritual of oblation (homa) for nine new deities. || 766 ||

O Ajita, in the case of fire, one should perform the oblation (homa) facing south in the eastern [fire] and likewise facing north in the others; in all other cases, one should face east while performing the homa. || 767 ||
The Seer: Having first laid out the initial thread according to rule, one should proceed through the center with the *bindu* while singing, and then [form] the pair of fish. || 768 ||
Having drawn a thread across that [space] between the two walls of Śyāma and Malidhī, which were thin, the four corners were marked by drops of oil. || 769 ||
It would be a field [of merit]. The fierce mothers, the progenitress, and the other fire-pits—this which has arisen from the fire is the singular, desired goal for ascetics. || 770 ||

Indeed, the spreading of the seat, the performance of the fire-rite, the sacrifice to the ancestors and the gods, and the worship of the guru—these are performed with water from the vessel named Śaśin. || 771 ||

Those belonging to the Piśācas, Bhūtas, and various Grahas and Rakṣasas, who are joined with the Sūtras, should be worshipped by the worshipper in the forest according to the fourfold method. || 772 ||

From the point five parts out from the front [of the field], one should draw the lines for the corners and the Vedāṃśa (one-fourth) rotations; this is the triangular enclosure of the triangle. [Verse 773] Vṛtta.
By turning the base of the *kuṇḍa* one-sixteenth [of its width], a circle is formed; [this results in] a hexagon.
By turning one-sixth on both sides, one-sixth of the hexagon is [formed]. || 774 ||

The wing-shaped pit (pakṣakuṇḍa). When the measurement for the girdle (mekhalā) of the circular pit is divided into four parts, there is one [part] for the pericarp (karṇikā) measuring one and a half units. || 775 ||
And the descent into Nyā, as well as he who is Sadāśiva within the Kuṇḍa;
the heart of Sadāśiva, Śakti, Śaktī, Hṛdī, and Śiva. || 776 ||
There is nothing between the two; the wind has entered the very sky.
Therefore, with every effort, it is said that the fire arises from the heart.
One should bring an image situated in one temple to the temple of another. || 778 ||
In that regard, one should perform festivals and so forth along the royal road;
thus it is said in the *Sūkṣmatantra*: [the measurement of the girdle]. (779)
The fist of the performer is formed by the middle joint of the right ring finger;
its width at the tip of the thumb is two fingers (aṅgulas) less than a fist.
In the middle of the front [face], it is one *aṅgula* wide according to the *ratni-gāyatrī* measure;
at the base of the front [face], it is one *hasta* wide and two *bhānu*s (twelve) *aṅgula*s.
That [measurement] of the eastern [side] is indeed extended; its count is one cubit. By that indicated measurement, the excavation (*khātaka*) is [determined].
It is declared that it should be level in this manner; half of the dwelling may be dug out for the wind, or it may be excavated down to the edge of a pit, or indeed entirely free from any excavation.
O Kāśyapa, or alternatively, the measurement of the girdle is stated in another manner:
one should divide the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) into twenty-four parts.
That [foundation] should be one part; the body [of the temple] should be two, three, or four times that.
The measurement of its width and height should be such that the girdles of existence (bhavamekhalā) come into being.
If the two girdles were each six finger-breadths in width, then what would be the extent of the girdle according to the Kāmika? [In that case,] the girdle would be as wide as the sacrificial altar.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be level in all respects according to the prescribed measurements; the sacrificial seat (viṣṭara) is likewise described. Now hear concerning the depression (nimna) and the churning (nirmathana). || 787 ||
One should dig there a pit of equal measure, level and covered like a cloud;
one should not join womb to womb, but should cause it to be fashioned with a lotus.
One must not make [the fire-pit] either deficient or excessive; if it is so, it brings destruction to the performer.
This is the characteristic of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) according to the Vidyeśvara [Tantra]. (789)
One should worship facing north in the southern, western, and eastern [directions];
or, facing east or north, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the western direction.
In other cases, having turned [the fire] toward the east, one should perform the oblation and complete the *homa*.
This is the measurement of the girdle for the initiation of knowledge (*vidyādīkṣā*). || 791 ||

Regarding the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*): in the primary fire-pits dedicated to Vāyu, Soma, and Īśa, as well as in the optional fire-ritual—wherein the exclamation *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed—I shall now describe the girdles and other [components]. (792)
In this matter of the girdle (mekhalā), according to the shape of the pit (kuṇḍa),
the girdle from top to bottom should have a width of three finger-breadths.
Then, one should have the deity fashioned with fist-sized jewels for the hands,
according to the sequence of the various fire-pits and their respective girdles.
Each one joined individually, up to the end of the eightfold [arrangement], is known as the characteristic of the girdle (mekhalā) and also the characteristic of the womb (yoni). || 795 ||
It should be five finger-breadths in length, three finger-breadths in width, and one finger-breadth in height; the womb (yoni) should be shaped like a leaf, according to its literal meaning.
One should have it made one cubit in size; this is said to be the source for others. The characteristic of the navel— || 797 ||
The length should be two finger-breadths greater; the space for the star should be one finger-breadth, and one should make its height half of that. Thus is the yoni described.
Thus, the characteristic of the navel is said to extend up to eight finger-breadths;
its width should be five finger-breadths, and its height half of that. (799)

The width should be divided into five parts; the central portion shall become the pericarp (karṇikā). On both sides of that pericarp, a portion equal to one-quarter [of the width] shall become the petal (dala). || 800 ||
Thus it should be one cubit long; for the others, however, one should add one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in width in due order, and the height should be one finger-breadth. || 801 ||
One should apply it in this very manner up to the end of the eightfold [arrangement]. Such would be the characteristic of the *nābhi*; now the *juṣṭaka* will be described.
The pit should be within the girdle, while the enclosing sticks (paridhi) are likewise on the outside;
one should make the seat (viṣṭara) one cubit long and one finger-breadth thick.
One should have it made eight cubits in length; understand that its finger-breadths (hastāṅgula) are likewise [measured].
Thus is the "viṣṭara" described; now hear concerning the depression within it.
Having especially established the preceptor with a joyful mind,
one should, by the command of Śiva, present the five-limbed ornament to the teacher.
One should cause two new upper garments and a turban to be offered;
and there, one should honor the officiating priest with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
But even if no *hotṛ*s are available, the preceptor should perform all the oblations;
he should carry out everything prescribed for the fire-ritual, beginning with the formal installation of the fires (*agnyanyādhāna*).
In the absence of curd, milk should be taken; in the absence of honey, however, clarified butter (ghee);
in the absence of clarified butter, honey should be taken; and in the absence of milk, one should take curd from the house.
If all perfumes are unavailable, one should instead take sandalwood;
and if even flowers from sacrificial trees are not obtained, one should use sugar and karavīra.
If leaves are not available, one should gather bilva leaves;
if fruits are not available, one should take the plantain fruit.
Regarding the thousandfold ablution (*sahasrasnapana*), one should take a sacrificial tree and extract its pith.
Prajāpati said: || 871 ||
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Protectors of the World, tell me, what indeed are the sacrificial trees?
The Lord said: The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Vaṭa, and likewise the Śamī. (812)
Khadira, palāśa, and likewise vaikaṅkata, bilva, and madhūka—these are remembered as the ten sacrificial trees (yajñavṛkṣas). || 813 ||
One should cut the side and the split side of the beautiful [wood];
this is the characteristic of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. || 814 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain; listen to the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
They should be made of *vaikaṅkata*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, or indeed *bilva* wood. (815)
The udumbara, the nyagrodha, or the pālāśa, as well as the śamī;
or also the tinduka, the madhuka, the pāṭalī, and likewise the vakula. || 816 ||
Having taken that according to its availability, one should mark its characteristic;
it should be three finger-breadths wide, located at a distance of eight mātrās from the edge of the Veda.

One should extend the middle thread, which is four finger-breadths thick and four finger-breadths wide; know that the length of the face is taught to be [the same] number of finger-breadths. || 818 ||
But a single portion of its qualities is designated as "cloudless" (abhra);
likewise, by means of the two-fold and non-two-fold measure, it is so on both sides of the tablet.
The face should be fashioned in this manner; the ear should be five finger-breadths [in length], and one should know its width to be equal to that. The altar (vedi) should consist of seven mātrās.
Having made it square and even, one should likewise place two finger-breadths in its center; thus is the well-rounded bilva described, which should be prepared with great care.
Having dug from the base up to the tip of the *balā* plant, measuring half a finger-breadth,
one should fashion two bands around the *bilva* tree according to that measurement.
In that same manner, the wise one should draw a depressed area described as having eight petals;
around the altar, there should be a band made of barley and rice.
Having dug from the base upwards with an upward-facing opening, one should attach a copper pipe;
or else, one should fashion a beautiful excavation by means of skillful artifice.
Furthermore, one should fashion the *gaṇḍikā* according to the measurement of two fingers;
having shaped it like the form of a water-pot (*kalaśa*), its circumference should be twelve fingers.
At the base, one should again fashion a block (gaṇḍikā) in the shape of a water-pot;
one should carefully make two bands, with the circumference reduced by ten [units]. || 826 ||
In its lower part, however, there should be a lotus shaped like an elephant's trunk;
thus the characteristic of the *sruc* has been declared, and now the characteristic of the *sruva* is being stated.
Make it twenty-two finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths at the base;
gradually taper it from the base to the end of the neck.
The width of the neck is said to be six fingers;
its length is seven fingers, while the width at the front is six fingers.
One should fashion the tip like the shape of a nose, with two ends joined together;
one should make the handle circular—this is said to be the characteristic of the *sruva* ladle.
If those two, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, are ancient, the wise one should wash them with pure water;
he should sprinkle them with the *astra-mantra* and retain them for the sake of ritual action.
The sage considers the pair of Veda-parts to be the elephant's temples;
in the ancient [tradition], there are the cheek-joints (*gaṇḍagaṇḍa*) as well as the minor altars (*upavedikā*) and the altars (*vedikā*).
[The dimensions] of the neck, face, and so forth, in sequence; its cheek-width [is specified], and furthermore, the hollow [of the handle] is measured by the cheek, as is the *sruva* ladle. || 833 ||
Starting from three cubits up to the height of an *uddhṛtakāntaka*, one should divide that width into two parts and [construct] according to the measure of one part. (834)
A central shaft (śūla) should be fashioned, and likewise at the tip of the foot;
its width should be two finger-breadths and its thickness one finger-breadth.
Starting from one finger-breadth (rasāṅgula) up to the limit of fourteen finger-breadths (manvaṅgula),
a wise man should have the circumference of the arch-pedestal (toraṇāṅghri) constructed in nine [proportions].
A wise man should have the archway (toraṇa) constructed from trees suitable for sacrificial purposes;
such an archway is indeed proclaimed as auspicious and is said to bring about well-being.
The height should be sixteen finger-breadths and the width half of that; its thickness is said to be one-third of that; one should thus procure the wooden planks. || 838 ||
In this other manner, the width and height are stated;
one-fourth of that which is high is called the *tāra*. (839)
The highest of the high has been declared; half of the lowest is the end. Thus the height has been described; one should reduce that by two in width.
O Prajāpati, it has been stated that there are nine abodes for the times of fruition;
now, however, the expansion is being described in another manner.
Furthermore, one should calculate it as five parts or one part according to reason; having divided the height by four, one should place that [result] together in one place.
One should fashion the crest with two parts; the parasol shall consist of one part.
Likewise, the Śrīvatsa, the pair of fish, and the Svastika should be on the right.
One should fashion Mātaṅga, Pūrṇakumbha, Kuṅkuma, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Daṇḍaka—these eight forms—with appropriate measures and according to the sequence of the ritual. 844.
If it is made without a parasol, one should consider it no fault;
likewise, the banner, the bull, and the lamp are said to be the male linga (pulliṅga). || 845 ||
The Śrīvatsa and the two Svastikas are said to be feminine up to their limit;
the fish, the mirror, and the jar are remembered as neuter. (846)
The eight auspicious signs have been described; now the characteristics of the *kūrca* (grass-bundle) are stated:
its length should be twelve finger-breadths, and its width one finger-breadth of a *kauśika*.
The thickness is said to be one finger-breadth; thus one should fashion the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala).
Peace is achieved by nine, seven, or five [fingers]; perform those with three or one.
In the form of a clockwise coil, the knot should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
the tip should be known as auspiciously one finger-breadth, and the stalk should be twelve finger-breadths. (849)
The characteristic of the *kūrca* should be thus: if there is one, one should place a knot; endowed with these characteristics, it is called a *pavitra*, which is Brahmā. (850)
Having grasped the pair of openings and placed the root of one at the front, one should join them in a clockwise direction; thus it is released by the index finger.
In rites for the gods, there should be two parts; in rites for the ancestors, however, an odd number;
in rites for the sages, with three parts—one should perform these using only masculine forms.
The characteristics of the purifiers have been declared; now hear the rule for the garland of *darbha* grass.
A forest of twenty finger-breadths [in length] is made with seven or five *darbha* blades from the fire-altar.
One should fashion a circumference of two finger-breadths with the front edge on the right;
having set it aside after discarding one, two, or three finger-breadths, make it even.
This has been declared as the darbha-garland; now prepare the characteristics of the darbhas.
The darbhas should be known to be of three kinds; hear now their distinctions.
It is declared to be of three kinds: female, male, and neuter;
the *tālaka* [seal] is situated in the middle of the leaf, joined to the sides like a leaf.
That which has a broken or split tip is known as neuter (napuṃsaka). For male rites, one should take male darbha grass; for female rites, one should take female [darbha].
One should avoid neuter [grass] there; it should be prepared for the purpose of malevolent rites (abhicāra).
The characteristics of the darbha grass have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the fuel-sticks (samidh).
It should be twenty-two finger-breadths in length and one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth in thickness;
in the northern tradition, it should be accepted as being devoid of skin, and the wise man should discard any that are not so.
One should carefully avoid wood that is curved or dried out at its base;
thus has the characteristic of the sacrificial fuel (samidh) been declared, and now the measure for the oblations (āhuti) is stated.

Taking a śloka-measure of curd, milk, and clarified butter; a śukti-measure of flower-essence; a śukti-measure of sugar; a handful each of parched grain flour and fried rice—having thus taken them... || 861 ||
If the *kanda* and *guñjā* are cooked, there shall be a *niṣka* and another *niṣka*.
Likewise, sesame, black gram, mustard, green gram, bamboo, and rice [yield] wealth. || 862 ||
What indeed is the end? And in Vāṃśinī, the beloved one whose limit is hidden;
we shall go toward that which is not inferior, or from there, with fuel as fierce as fire. || 863 ||
Having gathered them, they should be four finger-breadths long, with a circumference extending from the middle finger to the little finger, and made of smooth reeds. || 864 ||
One should gently place the mekhalā; having made the tip four finger-breadths long, one should grasp the kuśa and darbha grass with the thumb and ring finger. || 865 ||
One should cause a long tuft to be made; one should know the thunderbolt to be the first. || 866 ||
The second is said to be the spear; the third and fourth, however, are the sword itself; the fifth is the ready noose, and the sixth— || 867 ||
And likewise the *kuśa* grass; one should know that the mace is the seventh, while the trident is remembered as the eighth; and the discus is the ninth. || 868 ||
The tenth lotus has been declared; it is known as the "Ten Weapons," which wards off all enemies. || 869 ||
One should have it made of gold or else of copper;
or else, one should have it made from the heartwood of sacrificial trees.
One should first make the *kulāṅgula*, the second the *dharmāṅgula*,
the third the *pañcāṅgula*, and the fourth the *tryaṅgula*.
One who considers it to be made according to the measurement of finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula) should describe the noose, the lotus, the spear, and the goad. || 872 ||
The four [suffixes] ending in -t are known as feminine, excluding *kav*;
those ending in *-an* are renowned as masculine, while the chin (*cubuka*) is neuter.
Having described [the deity] endowed with ten weapons, now hear of the one with five weapons:
the chisel, the serpent, fire, the bell, and the eye, in this order. (874)
The characteristics of those known as the five weapons are now stated:
one should take the height as before and divide it again as previously described. (875)
One should fashion the *tāra* as before and perform the *ghana* as before;
for the temples (*prāsāda*) and the bull-enclosures (*vṛṣāṇī*), one should protect the *gośṛṅga* of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
For Prākāranandin, there is indeed an auspicious bull-shrine;
it is circular for one seated comfortably, while the standing-liṅga is square.
The characteristic of the remainder has been stated; the sign of the reclining posture is proclaimed.
Having first placed the enemy [in the east], one places Revatī in the southeast (the domain of Agni). (878)
Pūtanā is on my south-western side, in the direction of the spirits;
Vakramuṇḍī is in the west, and likewise Nicara is in the north-west.
In the north, however, there is Meṣadeva; likewise, in the region of Śaṅkara, there is Śaṅkara. All possess the form of Skanda, yet there is indeed some distinction.
In the case of the cause, it is accompanied by Bhīma;
the height of the *liṅga*, however, should be divided into three parts starting from the base. || 881 ||
In the midst of the garments and ornaments, above them, various flowers—skillful for the worship of the God—are placed. 882.
The earthly [element] is characterized by fragrant flowers and so forth, along with the roots and fruits of the *skanda* plant;
the watery [element] is characterized by liquids, milk, curd, cow urine, and the like. (883)
In the southeast (Āgneyī) are golden, red, and other [ornaments] for the day;
in the northwest (Vāyavyā) are the parasol and the sacrificial rite which causes the wind.
The musical instrument called *nāhasaṃgeya*, as well as the bell-sound and the like—these are declared in the scriptures to be the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*). || 885 ||
The invocation has been explained previously, and the procedure for installation has been proclaimed;
[namely] the five-fold service (pañcopacāra) and the ten-fold service (daśopacāra).
First is the invocation, and the second is the offering of a seat;
one should give the third with water for the feet, and the fourth is the water for sipping.
One should perform the fifth, the placement of the arghya; the sixth, the consecration (abhiṣecana);
the seventh, the offering of cloth and fragrance; and one should worship with flowers as the eighth.
One should offer the ninth [offering] of incense and lamp, and the tenth as the food offering (naivedya);
in the eleventh, one should present the bali, and in the twelfth, the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
On the thirteenth day, one should perform the Śrī-bali; on the fourteenth, song and instrumental music; on the fifteenth, dance; and on the sixteenth, the marriage procession.
Thus, these sixteen [rites] are connected with ritual action, beginning with the marriage ceremony;
[one should hold] the right hand bent at four finger-breadths [from the wrist].
Having taken up a handful of flowers, listen then to this:
the five purities (pañcaśuddhi). || 892 ||
(65) First there should be purification of the self; second is the purification of the place;
third is the purification of the ritual substances; and fourth is the purification of the *liṅga*. || 893 ||
The fifth is the purity of the mantra; thus the five purities are declared. Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, thereafter follows the purification of the body. (894)
Having washed one's feet in a space measuring one cubit, one should then invoke the Earth; after that follows the purification through bathing.
