The wise one should wash [the eyes] with the Astra-mantra while gazing with the Hṛdaya-mantra; then he should protect them with the Kavaca-mantra, and perform the opening [of the eyes] with that very same mantra.
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should perform the purification of the Liṅga;
one must not discard the flower previously offered to Īśa.
All mantras, especially those beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, should be employed in sacrifices; this is declared to be the purity of mantras. (898)
He who knows the fivefold purity is fit to perform the worship;
for [otherwise], due to the movement of the teeth, palate, and lips, there is the destruction of the mantra's power through impurity. (899)
There is no purification of the mantra nor its projection upon the utterance of the syllable *nāradānta*;
likewise, one should especially worship Īśāna within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
One should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east, Aghora in the south,
Sadyojāta in the west, and Vāmadeva in the north.

The heart should be worshipped in the southeast (pāvaka), while one should worship the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest (nir-ṛti). The armor (kavaca) is in the northwest (vāyu), and the head is in the northeast (vaiśāna).
Having worshipped the Astra weapon in the south, one should worship Dhana with Īśāna; this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear about the second enclosure.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin on the eastern petals and so forth; this is declared as the second enclosure. Now hear about the third enclosure.
One should worship Gaurī in the north, and one should worship the Bull in the east;
having fully honored Gaṇeśa in the south, one should indeed worship Guha in the west.
Having worshipped Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa,
and Mūrtinātha in the corners starting from the southeast according to the prescribed rite, [he should proceed].
The third enclosure has been described; now hear about the fourth enclosure.
One should assign Indra and the other world-protectors to the directions beginning with the east.
Having worshipped Brahmā in the southwest (Nirṛti) and Ananta in the domain of the northeast (Īśāna),
the fourth enclosure is thus completed; now hear concerning the fifth enclosure.
From the eastern petal-tip onwards, one should place the deities beginning with Vajra and ending with Pakaparyanta;
in the center, one should place the seven [deities] of Āśādhipa and Gaṇeśa.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍī are the seven Mothers (Saptamātaraḥ).
To the right and further to the right, [he should worship] Vīrabhadra and Vināyaka;
the best of preceptors [should do so] with incense, flowers, and other offerings, using their respective names.
"The five obscurations have been declared; one should worship all the deities.
Thus it is said in the *Kāraṇa*:
"The worshipped, the worshipper, the act of worship, and the fruit—these are supported by the *ādhāramūrti* (the foundational form). || 912 ||

For the sake of the pervasion of the mind, one should contemplate the pervasive state of the upward-moving breaths, which are the abode of the mere inward-facing [consciousness], with the face and hands directed toward the interior of the belly. || 913 ||
Adorning his body with ornaments, [purifying] the castes, and constantly employing skillful means, the wise man, having refined himself, should worship Śambhu. || 914 ||
Saffron, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, uśīra root, and likewise white mustard seeds,
when combined with water, are called the most excellent *pādya*.
Uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds,
combined with water, are declared to be the middling *pādya*.
Water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra grass is called the "inferior" (kanyasa) water for washing the feet;
one dhanarāṇa of each ingredient is the best, while half of that amount would be middling.
Half of that is to be known as the smallest portion; these three substances for the foot-washing (pādya) are uśīra, jāti, and karpūra, along with tuḍītī, pūla, and vaṅgaka.
Water mixed with *muraṇa* is the most excellent for sipping (*ācamanīya*);
it should be combined with cardamom, *lavaṅga*, camphor, and *murajāti*.
The medium *ācamanīya* (water for sipping) is prepared with water alone;
the inferior [variety] consists of cardamom, *lavaṅga*, and camphor together with water.
The measurement for these has been declared as before:
a bath with eight *droṇas* of water is called the smallest;
the middling should be known as double that, and the best should be triple.
Water mixed with milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken grains, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds— this is called the supreme *arghya*.
An offering of barley, mustard seeds, and rice grains constitutes the medium *arghya*;
an offering of water and *śāli* rice grains constitutes the inferior *arghya*. (924)
The measurement of these, however, has been proclaimed as before. Camphor, saffron, tamāla leaves, rhinoceros horn, and the three fruits—
along with sandalwood, uśīra, and iron— are said to constitute the supreme fragrance.
Uśīra, sandalwood, camphor, and the three fruits. || 926 ||
The middle grade of fragrance is said to be that which is combined with khaḍga;
the inferior grade of fragrance is said to be camphor, both in its natural and solidified forms.
The materials for the *arghya* offering— jāti, *āra*, white *karṇikāra*, *tulasī*, *keṇasaṃbhaka*, *arthaka*, *dhattūra*, *udayamārūpaka*, and *brahma*. || 928 ||
With *śamyaka* flowers, blue lotus (*utpala*), jasmine (*mallikā*), and *bilva*, *bṛhatī*, *piṇḍītakī*, and *mātakī*—these are recommended for Nandā. || 929 ||
The Punnāga tree, together with Varta, Palāśa, and Pāṭala, is worshipped.
Its color is fourfold: white, red, yellow, and black. || 930 ||
The white [lotus], the white-flowered [lotus], the *punnāga*, the *śaṅkhapatra*, the *mallikā*, the *naṃdyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, and the many-stampered [lotus]. (931)
Dvikarṇīkaraṇa, Jāti, Lakṣmī, Vakula, as well as Śvetārka, Mālatī, Droṇa, Asatī, and Śvetalodhraka. || 932 ||
Piṣṭakāsī, sakusuma, bhadra, and likewise mahā—
these white flowers should be designated as sāttvika.
The red lotus, the palāśa, the red water-lily, and the pāṭalī;
likewise the mausalī, the dhuttūra, the bṛhatī, and the karavīraka. || 934 ||
The *vyāghrī*, the red *mandāra*, the *paṭṭikā*, and likewise the *vedikā*—these red flowers should be designated as belonging to the *rājasa* quality. || 935 ||
Śaunakya, karṇikāra, campaka, hema, dhattūra, āragvadha, koraṇḍa, sairika, and girikarṇikā. || 936 ||
These mixed flowers are indeed black and characterized by tamas;

that which bestows liberation is declared to be sattvic, while that which leads to growth is likewise rājasic. For the sake of accomplishing both types of mixed results, one should offer leaves that grant an abundance of flowers.
The *brahmapatra*, the ascetic’s staff, the *dhātakī* together with the goddess, the *apāmārga*, *kuśa*, *dūrvā*, the five *bilva* fruits, and likewise the *śamī*. (939)
Tulasī, Nṛpa, Jambuka, Nāganandikā, Ekapatrāraviṃda, and likewise Viṣṇukrānti. (940)
Therefore, one should designate other [flowers] as belonging to the quality of darkness (tāmasa) rather than the blue lotus;
for a flower equal to the blue lotus has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
One should offer the *naṃdyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, white *arka*, white *padmaka*, *punnāga*, *paṭṭikāṣāḍha*, and *mālatī* at sunrise.
Paṅkaja, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, vyāghāta, karavīraka, utpalī, pāṭalī, and droṇa—these, O Prajāpati, [should be used] at midday. || 943 ||
One should cause the campaka, vaijikāpatrī, dhuttūra, bahukarṇikā, mālatī, and mallikā to be offered during the evening twilight.
The *jātinīlotpala* flower for half a watch, as well as the *bilva* leaf and the *kadaṃbaka* flower. || 945 ||
One should cause *dvikarṇī* and *bhadra* to be offered during the half-watch;
all other flowers should be caused to be offered at other junctions of time.
One should avoid fruit that is over-ripe, unripe, or still in the bud stage. || 947 ||
One should collect flowers that have fallen naturally, avoiding those infested with hair or insects, those covered by spiderwebs, and those gathered by others. (948)
One should especially avoid flowers that have been left overnight;
the characteristics of flowers have been declared—now hear the characteristics of incense.
Regarding the materials: sandalwood, resin, *kunduru*, saffron, *medha*, black iron, and camphor, respectively. (950)
Having taken eighteen parts of Pūṣa, five parts of Bhūta, and one part each of Agni, Śūnya, and Ambara,
he should grind them together and soak the powder thoroughly with honey.
Vyomapakṣaṇi, the resin of the ṛgbāṇa tree mixed with camphor and saturated with honey, is declared to be the most excellent incense. (952)
Combined with sandalwood and uśīra, mixed with a small amount and saturated with honey;
this portion, as previously described, is called the medium incense. || 953 ||
Guggulu mixed with ghee is called the lowest incense.
Having taken up the incense vessel, the wise one should cause it to be offered according to the prescribed rite. (954)
In the bell, with the left hand, one should hold glowing embers;
this is the characteristic of the lamp according to the Kāraṇa [Tantra]. || 955 ||
The lamp should be made with the ghee of a tawny cow for the white, red, and black [offerings];
however, if ghee is unavailable, it may instead be made with pure oil.
Ghee from a tawny cow is considered the best; that from others is recorded as middling;
goat-ghee is inferior, and likewise pure oil.
One should cause a camphor lamp to be offered, fashioned into a wick, which bestows all perfections, according to the sequence of the sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa types.
The flame with nine finger-breadths is the best, that with eight is middling, and that with two is the lowest; thus is the lamp proclaimed.

One should not have the body made from a tree grown from a seed, nor should one make it a lamp for Śiva; even when wealth is lacking, it must be indestructible, or otherwise provided with fragrance if it is scentless.
At the time of dusk, for the sake of the deity’s withdrawal,
one should perform the evening protection ritual, holding incense and lamps.
The gem is named Vāsudeva, the needle is composed of Soma,
the tongue is Sarasvatī, and Indra is the deity of the stalk.
The trident, which has the three forms as its deity and brings about the destruction of the asuras, moves;
it is said that the presence of the gods occurs at the sounding of the bell.
In the center of that incense burner,
the handle is declared to be Īśvara, and likewise the two feet are Prajāpati.
The nine powers constitute the nine lamps; they are the mothers of the seven-islanded earth.
In the five lamps are Nivṛtti and the others; in the single lamp is Sarasvatī.
The conch has the moon and other deities as its presiding deities; the belly has Varuṇa as its deity; Pārvatī resides on the back; and likewise, the two Aśvinīs reside on the two sides.
"All sacred fords are at the tip of the conch"—since these are the presiding deities, how could the preceptor not perform worship, setting aside day and night? (967)
The moon and the sun abide as the eyes of the minds of all beings;
by means of the mind one rejoices, and by means of the mind the mental vision is divided.

O Prajāpati, while performing the worship, one should look with the eyes at nothing other than that very [object]; for as long as the worship has commenced, so long should the movement of the eye and mind remain fixed there. (969)
Since other moments do not exist as sense-faculties after having come into being, nor do those [faculties] exist as such beyond [the moment],
therefore, by that very act of worshiping the Lord of Gods, there is likewise no worshiping of anything else.
O best of the twice-born, at whatever time the activity of both the mind and the eyes is focused on a single object, at that very moment one should perform worship with a concentrated mind.
At the time of the disappearance of the moon and sun, liberation is attained at that very moment;
however, worship should never be performed during a solar transit (saṃkrānti) or at the equinoxes (viṣuva).
The transition from one fold to another is called *saṃkrānti*;
however, when it occurs on both sides of two cloths, it is proclaimed as the equinox (*viṣuvat*).
The upward-moving breath (ūrdhvavāyu) is also proclaimed as prāṇa, and the downward-moving breath (apāna) is called the moon;
by effecting the restraint of these two, one brings about the destruction of the vanished moon and sun.
The consecration (abhiṣeka) and the ritual action are always performed together with mantra-flowers;
indeed, all flowers are offered back [to the deity] with the mantra. || 975 ||
The mantra-flower specifically becomes the Destroyer of Tripura;
through sprinkling, there is excellence and purity, and the letter *ṇa* becomes the eye. (976)
Through the method of supreme purification, it is indeed called "sprinkling" (prokṣaṇa). Salutation to Rudra, the source of the world, for the commencement of the dance. || 977 ||
Salutations to the one whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, who pervades all;
"Ma" is the mantra that is the seed of Rudra, and "Huṃ" is for worship, by which Hari is worshipped.
Ādāna, Dāya, Mūrti, Īśvara, Hari, and Hara—these are worshipped for the sake of Śiva; silence is said to be the bath, and [this] is called japa. (979)
The supreme Liṅga of Dhyāna, worshipped there, removes even the most stubborn sins;
it is Maṇikarṇī, the Bhāgīrathī residing in Vāraṇasī, who wears matted locks.
Salutation to him who acts as Vīrabhadra in the alms-begging with the skull of Brahmā;
that which is the singular earth is the supreme heart of Viṣṇu. 981.
The Foot: The three parts of the single form are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
[namely] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 982 ||
The fifth syllable is remembered as that which ends with *ya*, is followed by *bhā*, then *va* joined with the third vowel, then *la* endowed with the fifth vowel, and finally ending with *m*. (983)
The Āgneya [fire-mantra] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is not [neutralized] by pure ashes.
It stands against fever, epilepsy, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas. (984)
Merely by the application of ash, I become composed in mind;
the bath with ash is ten million times more meritorious than a bath with water. || 985 ||
I shall describe the ash in the form of a deity, specifically that of Maheśvara:
it has three eyes, a crest, a fierce appearance, three hands, and increases one's virtues. || 986 ||
Three-legged, with three eyes, his body smeared with ashes, performing the grand display of the *tāṇḍava* dance, terrifying, and adorned with red flowers. || 987 ||
Having meditated upon the Lord as red in color with the mantra, a person shall obtain peace;
likewise, he obtains a necklace and an ornament that bring prosperity and are pure.
The daily ash-bath is declared to be essential for the world.
For Brahmins, the *tripuṇḍra* mark should be six finger-breadths in width;
for kings (Kṣatriyas), it should be four finger-breadths; and for Vaiśyas, three finger-breadths.
For Śūdras it shall be two finger-breadths, and for women likewise one finger-breadth;
just as the water of the Gaṅgā is pure, so too is the smearing with ashes.
It illuminates the face; it eternally illuminates that which is accumulated. Because it destroys all sins, it is proclaimed as "bhasma" (ashes). || 992 ||
The fire-related bath (āgneya) with ashes bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
it is the debt-free bath for householders and the fire-related bath for celibate students.
The form made with ash on the forehead using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers—that indeed is the *tripuṇḍra*, and it is the destroyer of all sins. (994)
The ash-bath is considered pure, a means of purification, the destroyer of disease, and a source of excellent liberation; it is equal to the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā.

It removes all poisons, destroys anger, and brings great peace; it wards off Rākṣasas and Piśācas, as well as debts from one's home; it bestows contentment, nourishment, and complete subjugation. || 996 ||
Worthy of worship among men in this world, bringing happiness to all people—Pārvatī and the Rākṣasa (Śiva)—these very things are purified by Śiva alone. || 997 ||
The ashes, which are the burners of desire and serve as ornaments, eclipse the majesty of the abode of the Three-Eyed God upon the forehead-paṭṭa of the painted gods.
Those are the bad definitions. A well possesses ten times the merit of a pit; a river possesses ten times the merit of a well; from that, [the merit of the ocean is] ten times greater— || 999 ||

Success is attained through the two rivers and the small water-pool. A circle with five faces and an upward-facing mouth is in the east; a triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍraka) is in the eastern direction;
a trident is in the southern region; and a square is in the west. 1001.
In the northern face, the six-faced one is said to be shaped like a lamp;
he stands upon a peacock, possesses ten hands, and is endowed with six mouths. || 1002 ||
The wing-eye [should be] with six segments, joined with twelve segments, and adorned in sequence by six garlands; and the spear [is] at the mouth of the waters—|| 1003 ||
In the right [hands], he holds a sword, a vajra, a trident, and the Abhaya gesture;
in the left, a forest of vajras, a shield, and a peacock-feather fan.
And [the mantra] "ja me varaṃ ca"; Subrahmaṇya;
and the boy with a bracelet granting the boon of fearlessness in his right hand. || 1005 ||
The other palm should hold a vajra and a sword;
he is adorned with a crown and tiara, and his two ears are shaped like lotus petals—this is the first [form]. || 1006 ||
That youth was established by Varuṇa and Vāyu. [The materials were] sandalwood, *cāmpaka*, *bilva*, *mādhūka*, and likewise *panasa* and bamboo for the deity. || 1007 ||
And wood from a sacrificial tree, or from a four-cornered [tree], or from a *jātī* tree, a *kramuka* tree, or even a *munivṛkṣa* tree. || 1008 ||
One should grasp the staff, the side, and the end of the staff;
the base of the serpent (nāgamūla) should be three tālas long, becoming gradually knotted and slender.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is the goddess Pārvatī; the staff (daṇḍa) has Rudra as its presiding deity; the handle (yaṣṭi) is joined with Skanda; and the secondary staff (upadaṇḍa) is Vināyaka. || 1010 ||
The garland is conjoined with Brahmā; the pedestal indeed has Vāyu as its deity;
Vāsukī is the rope for the gods; and Janārdana is the bull. || 1011 ||
The fly-whisks are Candra and Sūrya, the parasol is Sarasvatī, the lamp is Lakṣmī, and the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) is the bell. || 1012 ||
Bamboo, Palāśa, sandalwood trees, Bilva, as well as Khadira, Nyagrodha, royal coconut, betel nut, Tāla, Śamī, and Ceṇāka. || 1013 ||

(73) For the selection of the Lord of Gods, whose banner bears the bull, ten thousand *daṇḍas* have been prepared from whatever is produced among these: the *mādhūka*, the *vakula*, and that which is most excellent. || 1014 ||
The three shafts of that [bow] should be made from *aśvattha*, *cūta*, and *madhūka* or *jambū*;
and the staff (*daṇḍa*) and the secondary staff (*upadaṇḍa*) for the purpose of binding should be made from *nyagrodha* or *panasa*.
The nine, eight, four, and one cubits constitute the entire length in the portion of all the elements;
half of that is equal to the width of the peak, and beyond that are the two tails.

For the fifty-second [deity], a bull should be fashioned according to the middle rule—wherein the characteristic is that a chowrie and a lotus-seat are depicted, with two lamps on either side. || 1017 ||
The width of the other [side] is then reduced by eight parts;
this is the measurement of the bull. Likewise, the height is exactly three parts.
This [body], from the throat to the tail, is praised as belonging to him.
The characteristic of the elements; the eightfold bondage; the threefold bondage. || 1019 ||
The door is divided by the quality-parts (guṇadhātu); one part is divided by the quality-parts. On the left is one part, and on the right are two parts. 1020.

One should place [the disciple] in the middle of the Śiva-sūtra; for at the time of initiation (dīkṣā), there is authority [to do so] by means of Yāmā and Pitṛpatnī. Thus says the Dīkṣākāra. || 1021 ||
O Śivā, because of this, one should not [abandon] these sons;
however, in the case of others, when their bodies are threatened by kings, thieves, fear, and so forth, [one may do so]. || 1022 ||
The ritual service to the Guru, the deities, and the fire (gurudevāgnikārya) constitutes an obstacle to the daily obligatory rites (nityakarman).
However, the occasional rite (naimittika) should be performed at the conclusion of the daily rites, provided there is no conflict.
Even if it is combined with the daily [rite], if it is not performed at the proper time,
there shall be neither the daily worship nor the fire-ritual, nor the daily festival nor the new festival.

Regarding the offering of the bali-oblation during the *snapana* rite for a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), one should know that oil is first [used], while the second is said to be jaggery (*gulam*). 1025.
One should know the third to be bhairika; the fourth is remembered as guggulu;
the fifth is sīsaka-siddhi; the sixth is called sīna. || 1026 ||
The seventh is indeed sarjasāra, and the eighth is known as lākṣāraṅga.
With what are tribandha and [the others] conjoined? || 1027 ||
Now hear the application known as "the double-binding," which involves the left hand, the lamp, the throat, the belly, and the great belly. 1028.
Karmaja, Vedaśāstra, Vedā, Viṣṭaghnī, and Brahmavid—these are declared to be the eight Bhū-dāsīs; they have two eyes and are endowed with two arms. (1029)
Resembling pure crystal, with hair like a brush and possessing fangs,
she is clad in yellow garments, holding a trident in her hand and granting fearlessness. (1030)
The Bhūtādīvas have been described to me as possessing great strength and prowess;
they are two-armed, three-eyed, dark-complexioned, and in the full bloom of youth.
She carries a vajra in her right hand and likewise displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her left;
she is endowed with beautiful garments and wears a crown adorned with red flowers.
Adorned with all ornaments, with a slightly smiling face, possessing full and rounded hips, and beautified in every limb. || 1033 ||
He wore a white sacred thread and was adorned with ornaments of pearls;
with a beautiful neck and excellent arms, he possessed an exceedingly handsome form.
This is known as the form of Indra; this supreme one is the form of Agni;
that which arises from purification is the Yakṣa; and in Bhola is the form of Mālinī.
Pūrṇabhadra, Vetāla, Kaṇḍukuṇḍali,
and the one known as Narendra— these are remembered as the eleven Yakṣas.
They have two arms and two eyes, are adorned with jeweled crowns, endowed with various colors, and are graced with red garlands. || 1037 ||
With serpents as their sacred threads, their eyebrows knitted and fleeing in all directions,
they were clothed in fine silk garments and possessed beautiful limbs.
And with white garments as upper cloths and faces slightly smiling, I shall now describe the form of all the yakṣas as well. (1039)
The medium [proportion] is known as nine tālas; listen now to that nine-tāla [measure]:
Citrasena, Mahāsena, Samitra, and likewise Sumukha. (1040)
Sukha, Sarvanāga, Suraja, and Pañcagītaka—these are renowned as the Gandharvas; they have two arms and two eyes. || 1041 ||
Yellow-white, black, smoke-colored, resembling saffron,
dark-red, and variegated— these are, in order, the complexions of the Gandharvas.
Adorned with simple crowns, decorated with jeweled earrings, endowed with all ornaments, and wearing red garments as upper cloths. || 1043 ||
Clad in yellow garments, with beautiful eyes and a prominent nose,
he likewise performs the art of music with the tāla, the vīṇā, and the flute.
He should apply two [dots] each with saffron; all [the goddesses] are auspicious when accompanied by the *tāla* rhythm.
With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), they remain intent on the playing of the instruments. (1045)
Now hear what was said by Bhayagrīva to Kālanetra of great strength, concerning that which is known as the Gandharva vehicle. 1046.
The water spoken by Sugrīva, Viśikha, Devamardaka, the famous praise of the Yātudhānas, and the red and black pigments. || 1047 ||
White in luster, resembling saffron, dark, and of a tawny hue;
likewise, reddish-brown like sindūra and of a smoky color. || 1048 ||
Gradually endowed with their respective colors, they have two arms and two eyes;
they possess red ear-ornaments and are slightly provided with fangs.
Equipped with the base of a staff and adorned with all ornaments,
wearing red and yellow garments, she is indeed terrifying to behold.
Clad in a black tunic and endowed with a flashing gaze, he is called a *yātudhāna*; such is described as the form of a *cāraṇa*.
The sword-path and one's own path, the eternal knowledge of Brahman, the exceedingly modest, the well-flowered, the contented, and that which is free from suffering. (1052)
The Cāraṇa is renowned for having eight forms; she has two arms and two eyes, and her colors are blue, red, yellow, fair, and smoky-grey.
The colors of the Cāraṇas are indeed blackish-brown, tawny, and likewise black; they are also endowed with large bellies. || 1054 ||
Clad in a white tunic, auspicious and wearing a dark blue turban,
she holds a staff in her hand and is ever intent on arriving.
The *cāraṇa* is thus described; the form of a *rākṣasa* is said to be [the following]:
*kravyādā*, *śroṇatākṣa*, *kañcuka*, and *yajñaśatrukā*. (1056)
They hold the knowledge of Brahman in their hands, they are playful, and they are slayers of heroes;
they resemble crushed collyrium, have two arms, and have two eyes. (1057)
Exceedingly fierce, with sharp fangs, upward-pointing hair, and a large belly; intensely red, endowed with throbbing [energy], and joined with her seat and throne. || 1058 ||
Possessing intensely red hair, with arched eyebrows and graceful movements, they held staffs in their hands; they were formidable and fond of exertion at that time.
With broad arms, a massive body, and great strength and prowess—such is described the form of the Rākṣasa; now hear of his pure appearance.
Having the form of an old man, with three feet, endowed with wrinkles and grey hair, possessing two hands and two eyes, and provided with only a lamp. || 1061 ||
He wears a white sacrificial upper garment and is likewise draped in white cloth;
his two locks of hair are bound together like a parasol, with a staff held aloft by the left and right hands.
With hands holding purifiers (pavitra), peaceful, and devoted to the respective meditations,
the form of the ancestors is said to be endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Seated upon a white-faced [being], he has one white face; his two hands hold a lotus stalk with its bud attached to his shoulder, and he is radiant with light. || 1064 ||
He stands upon a jeweled lotus seat, adorned with garlands and ornaments, two-eyed, and possessing all the auspicious marks. || 1065 ||
He has two arms and two eyes, with beautiful hair and a crown;
he may have a jeweled crown or even a diadem-crown. || 1066 ||
Endowed with a halo of light, bearing a shimmering white lotus, possessing the radiance of a *kunda* flower, with yellow eyes and peaceful gaze.
Whether seated or standing, together with the Śaktis in the left [hand], it is known as the form of the Moon; now hear the characteristics of the sages (ṛṣis). || 1068 ||
Agastya and Pulastya, Viśvāmitra and Parāśara, Vālmīki and Jamadagni, and likewise Sanatkumāra; || 1069 ||
These are declared to be the sages; now hear their forms:
the twice-born [Brahmā] is endowed with beautiful hair and a crown, and has two arms and two eyes. (1070)
He is endowed with a red complexion, wears a white sacred thread, and all [the attendants] wear long garments; he is joined by his calf above.
Some were clothed in bark garments with their stomachs tightly bound by rags; some there wore matted locks, while others had shaved off all their hair.
All of them were marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra), their bodies smeared with sacred ash,
all possessed long beards, and had long, white nails.
Some are joined with books, possessing peaceful forms and smiling faces; they are known to have the appearance of monks. Now hear the form of Aśvinī.
Their eyes are like full-blown red lotuses, and they wear crests and crowns;
clad in white loincloths, they are auspicious and possess a reddish complexion. (1075)
Endowed with extreme youth, moving to the left, right, and around,
they are declared in the fire, among the deities, and as lords of the directions by the names Nāsatya and Dasra.
The form of Aśvinī is known as Ākṛti; by meditating upon it, disease is destroyed.
Its appearance is like black collyrium, and its fangs are like lightning.
Two-armed and with red hair, possessing the graceful play of curved eyebrows and eyes resembling those of a forest elephant, she is adorned with garments and ornaments of red cloth.
Furthermore, he carries a red sacred thread (yajñopavīta) adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, and a trident resembling that of a learned scholar in his left hand. (1079)
Carrying a serpent-noose in his left hand, joined with a curved tongue above it,
and with a crown of matted locks upon his head, he is the terrifier of all.
Now hear of the form known as Yama, which has the appearance of a Rākṣasa:
it has two arms and two eyes, and is clothed in black garments. (1081)
Clad in golden garments, equipped with a sword and a shield,
wearing a white sacred thread and a white upper garment.
The form of Nirṛti is described as being joined with some fangs and accompanied by the coughing of a hungry ghost; now hear the appearance of Varuṇa. || 1083 ||
White as a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, with two arms and two eyes,
he is endowed with all ornaments and resplendent with two earrings.
O Meghavāhana, O Kosala, carrying a noose in your right hand and holding a staff half its length in your left, you may be either seated or standing.
Such would be the form of Varuṇa; now hear the form of Vāyu:
he is black in color, has two eyes, and possesses the playful movement of curved eyebrows. || 1086 ||
Wearing a white sacred thread and white garlands and unguents,
he carries a *kuśa* blade in his left hand and wears a long pendant bracelet on his right.
Endowed with a body of variegated color, mounted upon a deer, in the full bloom of youth,
adorned with divine ornaments, and with a face turned toward departure.
The form of Vāyu has been fully described; now hear the form of Kubera:
he has the luster of sevenfold gold, possesses two arms and two eyes. (1089)
Clad in white garments and adorned with a jeweled crown, he carries a conch in his right hand and bears a radiant lotus in his left. (1090)
Or someone seated upon a lion-throne, borne by men,
or one wearing a white sacred thread, mounted upon a bull, and exceedingly peaceful.
Kapardin has an ash-smeared body, is adorned with the crescent moon,
and likewise holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a deer, and an axe in his hands.
On each side of the south, one should place [the image] clothed in a tiger-skin garment;
it is declared to have the form of Īśāna, or one may also have it made with two arms.
It shall possess the form and appearance of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) and indeed all their auspicious characteristics;
I shall describe it in brief, so listen with a concentrated mind.
Of various colors, of many colors, and likewise blue-colored;
as well as dark like a cloud, and likewise the color of fire. || 1095 ||
Their colors are proclaimed to be like that of Padmanābha, yellow, waterless (clear), resembling collyrium, and red. || 1096 ||
Having two eyes and two arms, peaceful, endowed with a red complexion,
wearing a white sacred thread, and adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with a crown and a casket, beautiful with her hair loosened, she held her weapons upon her head while all [the others] stood with palms joined in reverence. (1098)
The very form of the Vedas, which are the support of life, has been proclaimed;
they are known as the dispellers of fear, the speakers of truth, and the beloved. || 1099 ||
Armed with a sword, blazing, tawny-eyed and large-eyed,
of terrifying form, flaming, and having fire as his own body-born garment.
The younger sister of Pitāmaha, Saṃjñā, together with Pṛthivīdhara;
the mantras for the honor of Indra, and the one known as Cittadayāpara. || 1101 ||
And [the spirits] named Cetopaśāla and Sārasaṃtuṣṭa,
as well as the Kravyādas and Śroṇitas, were struck by Karṇaka with hundreds of sacrificial weapons.
The hosts of pretas and pitṛs are known as Vastravipulāṃsaka;
and Viśālākṣa, Vīra, and Sadbhraṣṭaraṇapriyā.
These eighteen [deities] have two arms and two eyes;
they are extremely fierce, with sharp fangs, hair standing erect, and large bellies. || 1104 ||
Those joined with excessively red hair, possessing the playful grace of curved eyebrows,
holding staffs in their hands, and being formidable— these are remembered as the beloveds among these [goddesses]. (1105)
With broad arms, a massive body, and great strength and prowess, he is proclaimed to possess the very form of the eighteen hosts. 1106.
The Sakala, the Niṣkala, and that which is called Sādākhyam—know Maheśa to be the Sakala; these indeed constitute their threefold nature.
One should know Śiva in this way; that which is called Sādākhya is fivefold.
The first is Śiva-sādākhya, and the second consists of the formless aspects (amūrtīṃś). || 1908 ||
The second is called Mūrtisāda, the fourth is Kartṛsāda, the fifth is called Karmasāda; these are indeed the five Sādākhyas. || 1109 ||
O Mahāsena, Maheśa, however, consists of twenty-five divisions;
joined with these, it issues forth as thirty-one principles.
O Six-faced One, listen as I describe the characteristics of Śiva in brief:
the Great Lord consists of five aspects; this is the characteristic of Śiva.
Śiva is higher than the highest, subtle, eternal, omnipresent, and immutable; he is irreproachable, incomparable, immeasurable, and free from all ailment.
Because of its purity, it is designated as Śiva; it is beyond the supreme, higher than the highest, subtle like space and fire, eternal, and devoid of any agent.
Pervading all, it is said to be omnipresent; for those with unimpaired vision, it is immutable.
It is to be known as stainless, irreproachable, and unlike any other substance, being incomparable. 1114.
It is called the "method of valid cognition" (pramāṇavidhi) and is traditionally known as the "immeasurable" (aprameya).
Endowed with these characteristics, it is here described as the form of Śiva.
For the sake of creating all principles (tattvas), the world is the cause of their origin;
for the benefit of yogins, Śiva is conceived by his own will. (1116)
Within that Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti) is born as a thousandth part;
and from a thousandth part of that Power, the emergence of Ādi-śakti occurs.
In a thousandth part of that power arises the manifestation of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti);
in a thousandth part of this power arise the manifestations of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
These are indeed the five powers, and the Niṣkala is proclaimed as well;
this is declared to be the creation of Śiva, and now the creation of the powers is described. || 1119 ||

Likewise, the deliberations of the yogīs, the Yadus, and the ministers, as well as meditation and worship, may become either manifest (sakala) or unmanifest (niṣkala) for the sake of a specific sign. || 1120 ||
For that form, in brief, is celebrated as being called Sādākhya.
Sādākhya is said to be fivefold; their characteristics are now stated. (1121)
Through the supreme power (parā-śakti) within the powers (śakti), there is the emergence of the one called Sādākhya;
likewise Sadāśiva, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are the presiding deities. 1122.
Brahmā and these five are proclaimed as the divisions of the principles (tattva). Śiva and Sadāśiva are said to be the auspiciousness of the forms (mūrti). || 1123 ||
The form is called Brahmā, and from the perspective of the agent, he is remembered as Īśvara; the action is called Īśāna—thus, that which is one is indeed remembered in two ways. (1124)
Higher than the highest, as well as the supreme, the subtle, the double-subtle,
and the gross— these, beginning with Śiva, are perceived in their proper sequence.
Now, the specific distinction among these five principles is being stated;
there exists a threefold manifestation of the power of the forms of the principles, occurring in sequence. (1126)
The gross and subtle [forms] of Śiva.
Śiva and so forth are said to be the *tattvas*, while Sadāśiva and others are the *mūrtis*.
That form which arises from the union of these two is called an *aṅga* (limb).
It is observed that existence is called "Sādākhya" (the Ever-Designated); because its nature is eternally Śiva, it is celebrated as Sādākhya. || 1128 ||
That which is partless is called the principle (tattva), while that which possesses parts is called the form (mūrti).
The "entire" (sakala) accompanied by the "partless" (niṣkala) is celebrated as "Pratāpa. "Dehi" refers to the partless; "deha" is said to be the entire [body]. || 1130 ||
The connection with the body is known as being of the nature of existence;
for the purpose of meditation and worship for all, it may be both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). || 1131 ||
Having thus understood the distinction between the five principles known as the Sādākhya, one should indeed perform all ritual actions according to their respective origins. 1132.
Śiva, Sādākhyā, Udbhavī, Śāntyatītā, and Parāśakti are synonyms expressing that [reality]. || 1133 ||
The supreme power (parā-śakti), by its tenth part, brings about the emergence of Śiva and Sādākhya;
because she is the source from which the supreme [power] is attained and she is purified, she is called Śivā.
That form which is subtle and known as the form of light,
like the sky in the form of a drop, is directly perceived facing all directions. (1135)
This has been declared as the Śiva-tattva, the abode of all principles (tattvas);
Ādi-śakti and Śānti are its synonymous designations.
The primordial power (Ādiśakti), arising from the first form (Ādimūrti) as its tenth part, is proclaimed as both the primordial power and the root of the forms (damūla). || 1137 ||
Due to its formlessness, that form is devoid of parts (kalās) and is like a liṅga;
it is remembered as having the nature of light, resembling ten million suns. || 1138 ||
The form contained within that is also called the formless and so forth;
these indeed are the divine liṅga, which is here called the root pillar.
Everything arises in the Liṅga, and its dissolution is said to occur in that very place;
Icchā-śakti (the power of will) and Vidyā (knowledge) are synonyms for it. || 1140 ||
Let there be power (śakti) here in a tenth part; it is called the Jyotirmūrti (Light-form). And because of its being a quality of the Icchāmūrti (Will-form), its form is thus illustrated.
Because it possesses a formal embodiment, it is proclaimed as "Form" (rūpa) endowed with its constituent parts (kalā);
its appearance is like that of a blazing fire. || 1142 ||
Because it possesses the quality of being a form according to will, its "form" (mūrti) has been described;
and because it possesses the reality of form, its "aspect" (rūpa) is proclaimed as being endowed with the creative power (kalā). || 1143 ||
Resembling a blazing fire, it takes the form of a divine liṅga;
when one part of its upper portion exists, it is joined with a single face.
The form of the Liṅga is described as having a body of will, three eyes, a beautiful face, and limbs that are lovely in every part, endowed with a face possessing a gentle smile. || 1145 ||
That which is called the Sādākhyatattva of form is said to be the Sādākhyatattva of the agent;
for knowledge, because of its pure nature, is said to resemble a crystal. (1146)
Possessing a divine linga of great length and endowed with the great creeper of weapons,
the Lord, the cause of all, stands in its center in embodied form.
Four-faced and four-mouthed, endowed with twelve eyes;
four-headed and four-nosed, possessed of eight ears. || 1148 ||
Eight cubits and two feet in height, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands.
In his left hands, he holds a noose, a serpent, a bell, and the gesture of granting boons;
he is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of jewelry. (1150)
Thus, that Lord is called the creator of the *liṅga*;
what is called *kartṛ-sādākhya* is indeed said to be *karma-sādākhya*.
Cessation (*nivṛtti*) and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) are synonyms for that [state]. Through a tenth part of the power of action, the *karma* called *sādākhya* arises. (1152)
Action (kriyā) should be known as karma; therefore, it is called "karma" by name. Through the method of the Liṅga and the Pīṭha, there arises that which is called Karmasāda. || 1153 ||
It should be known that Nāda is the Liṅga, and it is remembered as the seat (pīṭha) of Bindu;
the form of Nāda conjoined with Bindu is called Karmasādākhya.
The fourfold form of the agent and so forth is called merely "Sound" (nāda); it should be known as the "Liṅga-Śambhu," and is declared to be the "Pīṭha-Śakti. (1155)
In the form of the yoni and liṅga, it is the cause of the creation and destruction of the universe;
because of that state of union, it is declared to be the nature of karma.
Nāda has entered into the Bindu; within Nāda is Mūrti;
within Mūrti is Tatva; and within Tatva resides Śiva. || 1157 ||
This Liṅga is composed of Śiva and is known as the abode of all principles (tattvas);
by means of this Liṅga, the world—both stationary and moving—is produced therein. || 1158 ||
Therefore, the form of action has been illustrated by means of its specific characteristic:
through the emergence of action there is creation, and at the end of action there is dissolution.
This is the form of the Lord as Karmasādhākhyā, which brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
it is called Karmasādhākhyā by means of the fivefold Sādākhya-yoni.
O Mahāsena, that which is specifically called Śiva-sādākhya is based upon the form of Śiva; for it is indeed formless, and one who relies upon Śiva-sādākhya [attains this state]. || 1161 ||
Because it does not depend on the material forms and so forth due to the non-distinction of its own formal nature,
they know that the form of the Lord of Karma, however, is the substratum of the fivefold manifestation (pañcamūrti).
That which consists of all reality is to be known as the support of all;
this, indeed, being condensed into a formal image, is remembered as the *piṇḍikārtha*. || 1163 ||

Abiding in the aggregate, situated in the midst of the aggregate, encapsulated by the aggregate, and condensed by the aggregate—the aggregate is thus declared to be the very form of the aggregate. || 1164 ||
The wise know this body (piṇḍa) to be composed of Śiva and consisting of all principles;
it is the deity consisting of the five forms and having the five principles as its essence. || 1165 ||
(83) That which is endowed with the qualities of the five-faced ones through the various bodily forms of the embodied beings,
and which brings about their differentiation, is Maheśa and the rest, from whom all the principles (tattvas) and so forth arise. 1166.
From its garments were produced the Siddhas and others by means of the Tantras;
endowed with the excellence of the deity, that is known as the *dhātupiṇḍa*.
One should fashion the vessel with six parts and the six limbs;
it should be complete in all its members and beautiful in all its constituent parts.
Thus, by mere recollection, he assumes a form possessing all aspects; yet upon its cessation, he becomes partless. Therefore, he is both with parts and without parts.
The body, which is not established in its own essential strength (sauvīrya), is said to be composed of flesh and blood;
it is like a rainbow in the sky or like a reflection in a mirror.
Having thus conceived with the mind that which is partless yet the source of all parts, the definition of meditation has been stated; now the nature of its constituent limbs is described.
The embodied forms are proclaimed to be of the nature of qualities (guṇas) and possessed of limbs;
the single bank of this stone-free laughter is divided into two forms.
The mobile [aspect] is said to be Śakti herself, and from that, the very relationship;
the partless (niṣkala) is the agent, while the formed (sakala) is the nature of that which is to be manifested.
One should install the relationship in its form as that which is to be cultivated— the partless Śailaja (the Mountain-born Goddess)—
as well as the kalās, the tattvas, the phonemes, the mantras, and indeed the worlds.
The six steps on the path are specifically enumerated in their proper order:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. (1175)
Peace (śānti) and the others are the five supreme powers (parā-śakti) within this fivefold division.
The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) consist of the path of mantra (mantrādhvan), the path of word (padādhvan), the path of phoneme (varṇādhvan), form (rūpa), and name (nāmaka). || 1176 ||
Thus, the path of reality (tattvādhvan) and the path of limited powers (kalādhvan) together constitute the auspicious plane (pada) of Śiva;
their sequence consists of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Jala.
The form of fire and knowledge are within the sphere of Śānti before the emergence of Ācamana;
and the Śāntyatītā [kalā] is in the ether, along with the five elements that pervade all beings.
One may also enter [the path] from the worlds, or from the twenty-four [tattvas], or from the tattvas;
the path of the thirty-six principles consists of sixteen kalās.
The path of mantras consists of one thousand parts; the path of words consists of eighty-one;
the path of phonemes consists of fifty-one; or indeed, the six paths are beyond numbering.
(p. 84) Regarding the teacher Saṃkara: the characteristics of a teacher—the faults of a teacher. I shall declare the characteristics of a teacher; listen with a one-pointed mind. (1181)
Born into a family of Śiva’s twice-born, he was firm-minded and extraordinary;
he was a knower of the scriptures of the Śiva-siddhānta and an expert in all branches of learning.
Free from disease yet prone to negligence, he was generally seen to belong to a noble family;
O wife, he was endowed with devotion to Śiva and possessed of human virtues. (1183)
One who abides by the conduct of the observance, knows reality, has conquered the senses, and is endowed with all auspicious marks—he is called a Śaiva Ācārya. (1184)
In this regard, there is a certain distinction; O Unborn One, hear that distinction:
for one who has attained [the path] while being devoid of a wife, the ascent via the *arcis* and so forth is as follows.
If the king performs such actions, the kingdom perishes;
the mortals dwelling in that village are then afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other such sufferings. || 1186 ||
Having performed that [penance], one should cause the mind to be purified;
but having committed that action again, one must perform it preceded by expiation.
Vighna, avāmana, dahara, bandha, ciraṃ, khañja, and balā—these are the names of trees;
khalau is to be excluded among them. Jāta, udbhū, and abhidūṣyataḥ are [names of flowers]. Kusumadṛk, mithyāvarākī, and bakabekāpya—in these cases, śivā [is used]. || 1189 ||
One should not perform the ritual arrangement; otherwise, a fault arises. As it has been stated: "But having performed initiation for you according to that Tantra, Śiva [bestows grace]. || 1190 ||
One should perform the rites such as plowing and so forth according to the path taught in this or that particular tantra;
however, there is no fault in a mixture [of practices] provided it is a single part of the Kāmika and other [Tantras]. (1191)
The wise man should perform the beginning and the end entirely according to a single tantra; however, if something is not mentioned there, he should incorporate it from another source as required.
If there is a mixture with another tantra in the supreme *arka* [rite], there is indeed a mixture therein;
by that fault, the kingdom will suffer destruction. (1193)
If this is its characteristic, one should perform it with a single thread for all rites, so that these bonds do not remain and there is the destruction of various fetters. (1194)

One should perform the plowing and other rites, as well as the consecration, according to a single tantra; however, whatever must be performed according to a particular tantra, one should have that performed according to that specific tantra. || 1195 ||

One should have [the rites] performed according to another tantra, especially for those actions not mentioned therein; however, from the initial rite up to the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should have them performed according to that single tantra.
It bestows liberation, indeed it bestows liberation, and one shall attain all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*).
Having first performed [the rite] with one [mantra], it is then performed with another. (1197)
Because of that confusion, O Six-faced One, the king destroys his kingdom; therefore, it must indeed be remedied by his disciple, Vasiṣṭha.
Otherwise, if one were not to act thus, it would cause confusion among the teachers;
and when such confusion exists, the kingdom will undoubtedly meet with destruction. (1199)

The science of action (karmaśāstra) is the highest; the knowledge of action (karmavittama) is the middling; and the science of the characteristics of the arts (śilpalakṣaṇa) is to be known as the lowest—thus it is threefold. || 1200 ||
Just as a sacrifice does not place the embryo with the hand, so too [the deity does not do so];
nevertheless, the deity [is placed] in the womb and in the hand of the preceptor.
Through the touch of contemplation upon observation, birds nourish the action of a mortal from their own bodies, as if from a son, by means of that very condensed mode of subsistence.
Just as an elephant in the forest becomes terrified upon seeing the shadow of a lord of beasts, so too,
upon seeing that body— which is neither a mantra nor an object of worship— one may fall into fear.
A vow, worship, or sacrifice performed without mantras leads to the increase of demons;
such a village, its patron, and its king, as well as the kingdom, shall perish. || 1204 ||
If one has performed the ritual procedure correctly at first, yet performs it incorrectly later, or if the ritual is interrupted, the result may become otherwise than auspicious. (1205)
It renders the master otherwise.
The deity known as Tantrasāda—1206.
The pair of feet should be Kāmika, and the two ankles Yogaja;
the toes of the feet are said to be Cintya, and the shanks should be Kāraṇa.
The region of the knees should be Ajita, the region of the thighs should be Dīpta,
the region of the secret parts should be Sūkṣma, and [the navel] should be Sahasra.
One should place Vīra at the ear-region, Raurava at the mouth,
Makuṭa and Mākuṭa there, as well as the limbs and sub-limbs.
The arms are said to be pure, the chest is like the moon, the orb is [radiant],
and the tongue is described as the manifestor of flavors.
The cheek should be graceful (lalita), and the forehead indeed perfected (siddha);
one should know the lineage (santānakula) as the sacred thread (upavītaka) spoken by Śiva.
The necklace is that of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara), the radiance is the jewel-ornament, they say the garment is the Vātula, and the ointment is the secret of Śiva (Śivamarma). || 1212 ||
In the Siddhānta, there is no offering of oblations, flowers, or garlands;
rather, [the worship] is performed with the body of the Tantrārka, which consists of the form of the mantra. (1213)

Having expounded the vast meaning through the vision of the reality of the mantra's purpose, it is fully declared by the end of the Tantra; thus, the designations "Tantra" and "Saṃhitā" are established.
In the fourth [generation], however, it is ten nights; in the fifth, for a male, it is six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days, but in the seventh, it is three days.
Therein lies the ninefold sovereignty of infinite ignorance, the ninefold wealth, and youth;
likewise, the auspicious Śaiva [nature], beginning with the gentle and ending with the fierce.
The auspicious [breath] is said to be fourfold by way of division: that of the right and that of the left.
It afflicts even the learned, how much more so those who are unlearned? (1217)
And neither the teacher Vaivasvata Yama nor the sages have seen [the fruits of] human efforts;
I consider destiny alone to be supreme, while human exertion is indeed useless. (1218)
Everything is understood to come from the deity, for the divine is the supreme refuge;
just as a frog swallowed by the mouth of a serpent is [rescued] by the deity itself. 1219.
In the same way, the true Guru consumes the human being bitten by saṃsāra;
it is said that the body is like a monkey, while the mantra is known as the life-force. || 1220 ||
This division is remembered as that which establishes the mantra of the Self, the yoga that causes the presence of Śiva, and by which a pregnant woman may give birth. 1221.
This division, excluding the sixty months, fortnights, and so forth, must be performed in all months; and the preceptor [should act] on the day of the ascetic.
One should not cause anger toward one's guru through mind, action, or speech;
for by his anger, one's lifespan, prosperity, knowledge, and merit are destroyed.
By ensuring that the four types of Vedic scholars attain their goals, he makes his own ignorance fruitful;
for by obeying the command of the Guru, he enjoys the perfection of knowledge. || 1224 ||
The Siddhānta is considered to be of two kinds by way of division: Vāma and Dakṣiṇa.
Vāma belongs to Paraśurāma, while Dakṣiṇa is worthy of Bhairava.
The entire Siddhānta and Yāmala, following the path declared by the Primordial Śiva, is fourfold: Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. || 1226 ||
The twenty-eight Saṃhitās are the most excellent Siddhāntas of the Mantras;
in that Tantra, the undertaking begins from the plowing [of the ground] and ends with worship. || 1227 ||
In that tantra, it should be performed; or one may have it performed by means of another tantra—namely, the Saumya, the Ārhata, the Śaiva, and likewise the Pāśupata. (1228)
The Kāpāla and the Pāñcarātra—these six are remembered as the Samāyās.
The followers of Saumya, Arhatamida, Bhākara, Vedānta, Naiyāyika, Vaiśeṣika, and Śaiva—all these householders should perform [their respective duties]. (1230)
O best of the twice-born, [it exists] in the Yāmala, the Mātṛtantra, the Kāpāla, the Pañcarātrika, as well as in the Buddhist and the Jain, and indeed in others as well.
In other paths as well, the Śaivas perform initiations according to their own scriptures and those respective systems, including the installation of their respective liṅgas and other rites.
Because it is primary, the Śaiva [tradition] is both the mouth and the mind;
it possesses authority over all, whereas others do not have such authority in the vision of Śiva.
Therefore, the installation and the worship [of the Linga] must be performed by a Śiva-brahmin solely for the sake of others; for those of other [castes], it is indeed only for their own sake.
One may even perform two omissions of the Lord of Tantra for the sake of others;
however, there is no doubt that the destruction of his kingdom will follow before long. || 1235 ||

Having turned away from the object and having performed the ritual mutilation of the object, it becomes oriented toward the object through the gaze of the Lord; thus was the pavilion and the gate constructed. || 1236 ||
The pedestal consists of the faces of the elements; there are no other faces. Now, the thirty-six principles [beginning with] earth and water— || 1237 ||
Fire, wind, and space; smell, form, taste, touch, and sound; the faculties of mind, anus, feet, hands, speech, nose, and tongue. || 1238 ||

The eye, the skin, the ears, the mind, the ego, and the intellect—these, along with primordial nature (prakṛti), are known by you. Attachment, necessity, knowledge, as well as limited agency (kalā) and time— || 1239 ||
And Mohinī; the Vidyās, Īśvara, Sadākhya, Śakti, and Śiva—thus it is remembered. This is the Nyāsa of the Tattvas and their Lords, as well as the Mūrtis and the Mūrtīśvaras. || 1240 ||
Endowed with [these], he is the Lord of the Three Principles (tattva). The three principles are traditionally known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, and the Sun... || 1241 ||
Jala, Vāyu, and Niśākara; Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, the one called Rudra, and Bhava; and Īśāna and Mahādeva. || 1242 ||
And Bhīma and Laśca are the forms of the Bull (Vṛṣa). The Self consists of five forms; the installation consisting of the five forms [is as follows]: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space. (1243)
In the Khañca-liṅga there are the five forms beginning with Brahmā;
likewise Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa.
Vāyu, Soma, as well as Īśāna, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are the protectors of the worlds;
Daśāyudha, Ananteśa, as well as Sūkṣma and Ekanetra are declared by Śiva. || 1245 ||
Ekarudra, Trinetra, Śikhaṇḍin, and Śikha—
these are the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras), each possessing three eyes and four arms.
The mirror, the full water-pot, the pair of chowries, the Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, and the lamp—these are the eight auspicious objects (aṣṭamaṅgala) of the gods. || 1247 ||
Kumbhakarṇa, Nikumbha, Siṃhasya, Gajavakraka, Jvālāgha, Jālajaṅgha, and Lohaja—these are the threefold [categories]. || 1248 ||
This is declared to be the Deer-Faced [Mudrā]; one should worship it upon the seat.
Dharo, Dhṛ, Somanīla, Pramukha, and Prabhāvaka—[these are the deities]. 1249.
In the Kali age, Bhīma is likewise proclaimed as the eighth among the Vasus;
[the others being] Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yakṣa, Gandharva, and Aindra.
The gentle Prajeśvara is proclaimed as the eighth Brahmā;
[the others are] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Kalavikaraṇī.
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtamanonmanī; Caṇḍarudra, Mahāmoḍī, Vibudha, and Vihalottama. || 1252 ||
Viśvarūpa, Viśālākṣī, Bhūdhara, and Meghavāhana—
these guardians of the celestial chariots should be installed in order starting from the east.
Janārdana, whose form is the bliss of the Imperishable, holds the discus in his hand;
Govinda likewise [protects] the person who has sneezed and my own leader.
And Prajāpati [worships] Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Pitāmaha; as well as Aja, Sṛṣṭimūrti, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Caturmukha. || 1255 ||
Aṣṭaskanda, Skanda, Kumāra, Subrahmaṇya, Kārttikeya, Sena, Ṣaṇmukha, and Śikhivāhana— these are indeed the names of Skanda. (1256)
And the commander-in-chief—these [deities] beginning with the East should be placed in sequence.
[One should place] the ruby, the topaz, and that which has the luster of crystal... (1257).
Coral, lapis lazuli, and sapphire—these seven kinds of gems are indeed proclaimed; one should have [the image] made using the proportions obtained for the jewels. || 1258 ||
The eight seasons: Kulikā, Vaṭaka, Śṛṅga, Gajadanta, Mṛga, as well as Nanda, Abdhi, Hṛdaya, Vallika, and Praṇaja are the seasonal periods. 1259.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Lakṣmī, Tilottamā, Sumukhī, Sumanā, Kumukhī, and Kāmavardhanī. || 1260 ||
These are declared to be the Apsarases who bear the eight auspicious signs;
and the one who knows the mantras, the best among those who know mantras, [attains] the supreme perfection and the garland of lotuses.
Prāñjñā, Īśvarī, and Ambārā are likewise worshipped by the Vatsiddhas;
these are declared to be the Siddhās—now hear their colors. || 1262 ||
Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and likewise Kārkoṭaka;
Śaṅkhapāla, Gulika, Padmaka, and Vāsukī as well. || 1263 ||
She is known as Nāgāsvaṣṭā, possessing two arms and two eyes;
she is in the excellent eastern quarter, and has four faces in the region of Agni (the southeast).
And Kuṇḍodara is in the south, while the Prabodhakas are in the southwest;
Siṃhamukhī is in the west, and Adhomukha is in the northwest.
Some may have one leg, and [one] in the northeast may have eight legs;
these are the retinues of the eight spirits, and one should offer the bali-oblation before them.
The arka, the lotus, the bilva, the nandyāvarta, the pāṭalī, the karavīra, the campaka, and the blue lotus— these constitute the group of eight.
In the eightfold worship,
one should duly worship Vighneśa on the right side above the door,
and one should duly worship Sarasvatī on the left side above the door. || 1268 ||
One should worship Śrīdevī above the middle of the door;
on the right side of the door, one should worship Gaṅgā and Nandīśvara.
On the left side of the door, the wise man should worship Mahākālī, Yamunā, Bhuvaṅga, and Pataṅga, up to the top.
Guha constantly offers oblations to Vimala and Subāhu,
as well as to Gaṅgā, Mahānandī, Mahākāla, and Yamunā. (1271)
O Lotus-born one, Vighneśa is renowned as Stānaka, and Vāgīśa is specifically recited as the Āsana. || 1272 ||
The serpent Bhuvaṅga and the bird Pataṅga were the bed for the lotus-born Brahmā;
all the deities stood at the doorways, gazing at one another.
Having paid homage to the God of gods, one should worship the deities of the doorway:
Gaṇeśa above the lintel, and Sarasvatī to his left.
To the right of Bhuvaṅga, one should worship Gaṅgā, Nandī, and Yamunā, and on his left, Mahākāla. (1275)
One should indeed worship Vimala and Subāhu on the two door-panels;
the wise person should worship Ṛṣabha in front with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Whether the door faces inward or the door-keeper faces outward— for such reasons,
during the worship of the door, at the time of bathing, and at its conclusion— incense and lamps [are offered]. || 1277 ||
At the offering of the food oblation (naivedya), at the conclusion of that, and at the beginning of the Śrī-bali and other rites;
upon completion, and likewise at the beginning of the dance and so forth—at the end of each, one should strike the ritual bell (vāra-ghaṇṭā). || 1278 ||
At the time when the incense, lamps, and so forth [are offered], at that very time one should ring the incense bell. From this ringing— || 1279 ||
The sacrifice beginning with *kṣa* proceeds; its substance and deity are as follows:
[the deity] has five faces resembling the moon, possesses ten hands, and holds a trident in his hand. || 1280 ||

You hold a ṭaṅka, a thunderbolt, and the gesture of fearlessness; in your left hands you hold a noose, the boon-granting gesture, a goad, a jewel, and a fire. You are seated upon a red lotus, O Sadāśiva. || 1281 ||
The essential form: O Goddess, [it is] with the head facing south and the feet facing north, with water held in the arms reaching as far as the Gomukha, situated within the Yoni. || 1282 ||
The form of Sadāśiva, established within the excellent liṅga situated in the center, is the unmanifest (anāmni) essential nature; he has one face, four arms, and [is red] like coral. || 1283 ||
His own form has four arms holding a black antelope, a *ṭaṅka* axe, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
He has a third eye that is white, wears a garment, and is joined by the moon. || 1284 ||
p.
91) With Gaurī upon his crown, with a thousand sons, resembling a jasmine flower, possessing three eyes including the fire-eye, he is the lotus-bannered one (Viṣṇu). || 1285 ||
She has four hands holding the boon-granting gesture and the blue lotus; her third eye is white, she is clothed in a vajra-patterned garment, and Gaurī rests upon her moon-adorned crown. || 1286 ||
He has a thousand sons; his limbs are adorned with various ornaments, his eyes are wide, and he is radiant with a lofty crown that intoxicates the mind.
The essential nature [of the practice] is the meditation on Sadāśiva. First, having fashioned the five faces according to the prescribed rule, through that gateway— || 1288 ||
One should assign KṢa, Trā, and so forth—Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna—in sequence to the head, the face, and likewise the heart. || 1289 ||
One should assign Guhya and the two feet; Īśāna, Puruṣa, Ghoratathā, Vāma, and Sadya. Their color: the color of one just born is like the white of a thorn-apple (gokṣura). || 1290 ||
O Guha, the face of Vāmadeva is indeed like a hibiscus flower;
Aghora resembles collyrium, while Puruṣa has the luster of saffron. || 1291 ||
Īśāna is like pure crystal, five-faced and six-headed;
[five-faced... || 1292 ||
One should place milk-rice (pāyasa) in the eastern direction, likewise kṛsarā rice in the south, mung-bean rice (mudgānna) in the western part, and jaggery-rice (gulānna) in the north.
One should offer pure food and an upward-facing [liṅga] into the five-faced [deity].
Just as the core of the wood-apple fruit is consumed by an elephant,
so too the Supreme Lord should consume all the offerings.
One should place upon the palm of the hand that which is to be drunk, that which is to be dried, that which is to be licked, that which is to be sucked, and that which is to be chewed;
for by the mere sight of food, rice, cakes, water, and so forth, it is taken [as sustenance] by me.
The [deities] beginning with Rasa are on the tongue of the Eater; the one born from the lotus is at the tip of the tongue. On both sides of his own head are the thirty-three forms.
The image, which is the form of the power (śakti) cherished in the heart, resides eternally within stone, water, and metal; that indeed is the living soul (jīva) of the trident. || 1298 ||
In the center—within the two testicles, within the lotus, within the peak, and within the cavity of the *sṛṣṭiliṅga*—is the explanation for the meaning of the *liṅga*. || 1299 ||
To him whose forms are beyond numbering,
whose crest is eternally [adorned], who is dark-hued, the subduer of the wicked, and the restrainer of Time.
And Gaurīśvara is indeed to be carried away; it is the supreme favor bestowed upon Umā.
The dialogue between Gaurī and Śiva accompanied by Umā, which brings happiness; and the Purāntaka (Śiva) together with Guha and Umā, mounted upon Nandin. || 1301 ||
Then [he saw] the Kirātārjuna, Kāla, Umārdha, Harirardhaka,
the three forms of the Dancing One (Nṛttamūrtti), Dahana, and Jāhnavīdhara.
Afterwards, the favor of Caṇḍeśa; beyond that, the Mukhaliṅga;
then Vighna, Kanda, Caṇḍeśa, Kṣetreśa, and Kamalodbhava. || 1303 ||
And Cakrapāṇi, Mārtāṇḍa, Nāgeśa, Vīrabhadraka, Gaurī, Durga, as well as the excellent Mahāmodinī and Sarasvatī. (1304)
One should worship Jāhnavī, Bhadrakālī, Lakṣmī, Pṛthivī, and Mātṛ according to the path prescribed in this scripture, beginning with the primordial Śaiva deities.
Soma-Skaṃdeśvara, Induśekhara, Ṛṣabha, Vāhana, and likewise Naṭeśvara. || 1306 ||
Likewise, [he visited] Keśavāsa and thereafter Bhikṣāṭana;
afterwards, Caṇḍeśānugraha, and to the south, Kālanāśana. || 1307 ||
The forms arising from the Liṅga are divided into sixteen types:
the peaceful form, seated in the lotus posture, bearing the crescent moon upon its crown, and possessing five faces. || 1308 ||
Three-eyed, he carries in his right hands a trident, a face, a sword, and an axe that grants fearlessness; [and in his left] a serpent, a noose, and a bell. || 1309 ||
I bow to the reality known as Sāda, which is joined with a lotus and a goad on its left side, adorned with various ornaments, and resembling a crystal gem. 1310.

Dark-complexioned, three-eyed, two-armed, and posed in the *tribhaṅgī* stance, with her feet bent and positioned to the right and left; holding a blue lotus in her right hand, she has bracelets and breasts. || 1311 ||

That Supreme Goddess has hands reaching down to her knees; she possesses the luster of jasmine, the moon, and crystal, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair. || 1312 || Pañcācana-samā- || 1312 ||
It is endowed with five faces; each face is specifically endowed with three eyes; it has ten arms, one [central] body, and two feet. || 1313 ||
Seated upon a lotus, he holds in his right hands a trident, an axe, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*),
while in his left hands he holds a serpent, a noose, a goad, a bell, and fire.
Endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
the god wearing divine garments, long-armed, and radiant with nails. (1315)
With limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine garlands, this form is said to be peaceful, with a face slightly smiling. (1316)
One should constantly remember this form, which bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation;
this has been declared as the form for meditation, and now its specific details are being stated. (1317)
Vai-kartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama. || 1318 ||
Āditya, Sūryadeva, Aṃśumān, and Divākara—these indeed are the twelve divine ones, endowed with all auspicious marks. || 1319 ||
The Lord of Karma (Karmeśa) shall have his face in the east; the Agent (Kartṛ) shall have his face on the left;
the Other (Apara) shall have his face above; and the Formless One (Amūrta) shall have his face in the north.
Above that, they know the one called Śiva-sadākhya; thus, it is five-faced.
Īśāna is the upper face, and from him the various rites should proceed.
The eastern face has been described; as for the southern one, it is the eighth face.
The upper [face] is to the east, the southern is that very one, while the other is to the west and north. Slightly— || 1322 ||
There is a distinction: that which is facing upward is called "downward-facing," while having contemplated its root, that which faces away [from it] is known as "turned away. (1323)
At the time of worship, having meditated upon her as being worshipped like the mouth of Karma,
and having thus formed the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) according to the rules, at the conclusion of the worship, it should be as before.
And because it consists of these five [elements], it is the cause of all causes;
thus it is proclaimed as Sadāśiva—this is the certainty of the scripture. (1325)
Because this indeed has the nature of action, it is action; yet one should cause action to be performed.
For yogins and mantra-practitioners alike, it becomes a guru through mere remembrance.
That which is endowed with these characteristics is called *karmasādākhyam*.
Beginning with Śiva and ending with Karma, they have been proclaimed in their proper sequence. (1327)
The definition of Sādākhyā has been declared; now listen, O Six-faced One, to the origin of Maheśa from a thousandth part of Karmeśa. (1328)
One should know Maheśa as the manifest (sakala), consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
through twenty-five divisions, the formless (amūrta) consists of twenty-five. (1329)
The god Hara assumes various forms, endowed with diverse distinctions;
he is accompanied by various severed [limbs] and is devoted to manifold divine sports.
Standing, riding a vehicle, seated, dancing, wrathful, and gentle— the God of gods, Maheśvara, is endowed with manifold forms.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, possessing one face and three eyes, endowed with all ornaments, and seated upon a single lotus throne. || 1332 ||
Thus has Maheśa himself been described; now hear of his various forms:
the first is the bearer of the moon, and the second is together with Umā.
The third, however, is mounted upon a bull; the fourth arises from dancing;
the fifth should be known as the one carried on a vehicle; and the sixth is the wandering for alms.
One should know Kalārī as the seventh; Kālābhā shall be the eighth.
Tripurārī shall be the ninth; Jala and Dharā are the tenth.
The eleventh [measure] is Gajāhārī; the twelfth is Vīrabhadraka;
the thirteenth is Harerardha; and beyond that is Tadardhanāri.
The fifteenth would be Kirāta, the sixteenth would be Kaṅkāla, and then the seventeenth would be the Caṇḍabhānu-graha. || 1337 ||
The removal of poison is recorded as the eighteenth, and the true nature of the wheel's breaking is recorded as the nineteenth. || 1338 ||
The Vighnaprāsāda is twenty [cubits], and beyond that is the Umāskanda;
the Ekapāda should be twenty-two, and the Sukhāvaha twenty-three.
The form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is proclaimed to be twenty-fourfold;
the group of six beginning with Indudhārā arises from that which is called Dharmātmā.
The wise know that the removal of poison and other such powers reside in the five [faces] of the belly;
however, those arising from the triad beginning with Suvāsana and ending with Liṅga reside in the one called Śiva.
These forms of Maheśa, arising from actions and so forth,
exist in twenty-five distinct ways, each form being separate.
(95) These, born from Viṣṇu and Brahmā, are portions of ten million Maheśas;
the Sun and Moon arise from Śiva in his right, left, and upper eyes. 1343.

Knowledge arose in his mouth; that which originated from the lord of the throat became the six-faced one; [the knowledge] born in the heart was the god Skanda, and from the navel the gods were produced.
Fifty crores of gods were born from the Mahāṃśa [portion], and likewise crores of sages were born from the hair-pores. || 1345 ||
The emergence of the principles (tattvas) has been declared; now hear of the emergence of the ascetics (yatins).
They are born in succession, each by a tenth part [of the preceding]. (1346)
These indeed are the five powers, the energies of Śiva and the others;
from a thousandth part of Manonmanī, Gaurī then came into being.
Sarasvatī, Durgā, Umā, and Prabhā belong to Śrīdevī; likewise, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Lakṣmī, and Vaiśyā are the Śaktis. || 1348 ||
These indeed are Koṭi, Śakti, and Gaurī, who originated from the God; thus has the specific classification of the Śaktis been proclaimed in brief. 1349.
The tip of the thread is said to be the face; below the thread is called the feet.
The junction of the threads shall be the back, and the two sides of the thread are the two arms.
Or, when seated comfortably in the *prakrama* posture, one should remain in the square *liṅgaka* posture;
the remaining characteristics have already been described, and this is proclaimed as the reclining *liṅga*. || 1351 ||
Regarding the etymology of the word *liṅga*:
"Whatever sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and meritorious shrines (*āyatana*) belong to the earth, they all dissolve (*līyante*) within the *liṅga*; therefore, it is proclaimed as *liṅga*. (1352)
Bhadradala:
Śambhu is in the east in front, and in the north, which is the locus of women. || 1353 ||
That which was asked regarding the western direction, one should worship while stationed on the right;
this is from the section on worship in the *Yogaja*. || 1354 ||
One should meditate on the Lord Puruṣa at the western gate;
Sadyojāta should be in the east, while Ghora and Vāma are as before.
The limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga) are as previously [stated], and the practitioner faces north;
first is that called Śivasāda, and the second is Mūrti. (1356)
The third is called Mūrtisāda, the fourth is named Kartṛsāda, and the fifth is called Karmasāda; these are known as the five Sādākhyas. || 1357 ||
Bali likewise [worshipped] Brahmā in the form of sacrifice, Viṣṇu in his own form, Īśvara in the form of the water-pot (kumbha), and Rudra in the form of fire. || 1358 ||
Sadāśiva, the primary image (mūlabera), is known as the fivefold form (pañcamūrti).
Having recognized that form through the liṅga, one should then prepare the pedestal (sādana). || 1359 ||
The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) should arrange the single-minded divine [seat] upon the arrow;
O child, one should arrange the three seats upon the seat of the Ṛṣis and the Gaṇas.
O child, one should likewise arrange five seats for the human [deities];
[one should visualize her] as having the color of a jasmine flower or the moon, granting boons, three-eyed, and adorned with a diadem.

One should contemplate the Root as the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti), who holds a burden, fearlessness, and fear, as well as a noose and a blade of kusha grass, seated in the midst of a lotus. || 1362 ||
The entire ground of eighty-one squares, situated in the subterranean realm (pātāla),
was occupied by eight nāgas stationed in the eight directions.
Having the luster of a conch shell and other flowers; joined with [a color] resembling neither black nor red;
accompanied by smoke—here, it is possessed of smoke; white like a conch shell. || 1364 ||
With six million eight hundred thousand verses, [he composed] the Anantāsana;
having thoroughly mastered the yoga... || 1365 ||
Together with the ten winds, it is joined with the syllables consisting of the ten-fold self.
Established on the ground, abiding, and arising, fixed and ascending—[the syllable] Oṃ, variegated like a plantain tree, is indeed the giver. || 1367 ||
And that deity is not wealthy. Having placed [the object] upon the pericarp—perfectly circular like the full moon and equal to it—one should [place] Ambikā and the others... || 1368 ||
This is the abode of Śiva, accompanied by the Vādi and joined with Śakti;
it consists of the support, the seed, the sprout, and the stalk, [arising] from bliss within the seats of bliss. || 1369 ||
In the three mandalas, within these three qualities, there is a sequential arrangement: the offering with fresh flowers, the presentation, and the striking. || 1370 ||
(97) The Yoga-lion and the Lotus-seat, which are pure, are in sequence;
the five limbs and six limbs of the seat are known by the names of the three mandalas. || 1371 ||

And it consists of the three qualities (triguṇa). For the rite, there are the seat for invocation, the lotus seat, and the seats of Ananta; the Vimalāsana is joined with the offerings of worship. || 1372 ||
The seat for enjoyment shall be the Yoga-seat; joined with dance, yoga, and so forth, the Lion-seat follows thereafter. It should be made of gold, one cubit in size, and dark blue. || 1373 ||

Adorned with hands holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a banner (*patāka*), the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and a garland; wearing variegated garments and robes, he is endowed with matted locks and a crown, and joined by a rosary (*akṣa*). || 1374 ||
The eye; the form of Keśava endowed with the crown and diadem of the Grandfather (Brahmā); the form of Śiva. || 1375 ||
His face is red-hued and joined with a sky-like countenance;
his hands hold a supreme trident, a goad, and a banner, and he is clothed in black garments. || 1376 ||
The form of Śiva has the son of the Moon (Mercury) as its head, is endowed with eleven eyes (the number of Rudras), possesses one face and four arms, and resembles coral. || 1377 ||
He may have four hands holding an earring, a sword, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons;
he wears garments of blue and white, and is joined by the moon. || 1378 ||
The crown bears the form of Lord Śiva; it is the form of the Supreme Goddess.
