She possesses the luster of lightning, has a face like the full moon, and has tongues and eyes extending everywhere. || 1379 ||
She stands in the midst of all wombs, possessing two arms,
with hands extended holding blue lotuses, and endowed with the nine syllables beginning with *Prāṇa*.

In whom are they smiling? It is said that it is indeed the circle of fire; it is also said to be the circle of the sun. [He is] the one whose splendor has departed, whose face is like a lotus. || 1381 ||
She has two eyes, two arms, and she moves with outstretched lotuses;
her breasts are full, she is adorned with golden earrings on her ears, and she possesses the radiance of the sun. || 1382 ||
Situated above the solar wheel, that which was described as the solar mandala is now called the lunar mandala; it possesses a white radiance. || 1383 ||
Adorned with golden armlets on their two arms, holding lotuses in the palms of their hands with long-reaching fingers, they possess two eyes and faces graced with beautiful earrings. || 1384 ||
Thus joined, she is perfectly established within the sixteen digits (kalās) in the east and the other directions;
such is the invocation described, which one should perform at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā). || 1385 ||
Prajāpati said:
From the time of its installation onwards, Śiva remains present within the liṅga.
"From where was it brought forth, into what, and who [brought it]? Tell me, O Śaṅkara! (1386)
Īśvara said:
What you have spoken is indeed true, O one with a slightly smiling face;
there is no such thing as "invoking" [a deity], for he remains present even from another region. || 1387 ||
By means of the mantra, Śiva remains facing oneself at the conclusion of the ritual;
there is no formal dismissal (udvāsana) nor movement to another location. || 1388 ||
Just as fire exists within wood and is made manifest by friction, and just as that blazing fire may be covered over by ashes; 1389.
Just as a fire is made to blaze by fanning away the ashes with the wind,
so too the Lord, who is steadfast like that fire, is kindled by means of His very mantra.

There is no invocation (āvāhana) or dismissal (udvāsana) in the case of a consecrated liṅga (śiṣṭaliṅga), especially when it is of the Prajāpati type; however, for that which has two faces (dvimukha), there is a formal dismissal at the conclusion.
Just as fire contained within a vessel may be made to blaze by means of the wind, so too does the Lord Śiva arise through the mere presence of the *liṅga*. || 1392 ||
That linga which has been installed by gods and sages is called a Śiṣṭa-linga; it is the cause for the presence of Śiva. || 1393 ||
Therefore, there is no invocation, nor is there any rite of dismissal. O God, whence could there be an invocation, and likewise, whence could there be a dismissal?
They forget the invocation through mere remembrance and forget the dismissal; indeed, the invocation is the Liṅga itself, for it is remembered as the very form of the Liṅga. (1395)
Having placed a mirror in the presence of the Ācārya, one should worship in due order;
though lamps and thousands of lamps [are offered], the root lamp is not defiled.
For whom the worship of the deity is the Liṅga, the root-Liṅga is not a mere smearing;
though there are many colors in the state of the cow, milk alone is the source of their origin. || 1397 ||
A single mantra arises, yet the tantra appears in many forms; it is seen in various shapes, just as clay on a potter’s wheel takes on diverse forms. || 1398 ||
Having meditated upon the Teacher with the mind, the Supreme Goddess, difficult to perceive,
remains present within his mouth as a mass of light from many rows of lamps.
If [the self] exists as something that obstructs those things which are formless by virtue of their qualities, then what can be said regarding that which is itself formless? || 1400 ||
(99) Wherever deities are fashioned in stone, clay, wood, or painting,
the deity of the self is unconstructed and self-luminous. || 1401 ||
Then, one should invoke Agni from wood and Īśa from the moon in the jar;
having worshipped whichever deity [is appropriate], one should contemplate that very deity as oneself.

Having wiped the liṅga and the pedestal with darbha grass and washed them with the mantras of the five limbs and six limbs, one should [worship] the liṅga with the Prāsāda mantra and the Hṛdaya mantra. || 1403 ||
Touching with both hands joined in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Liṅga is known as the "Liṅga-form" (*liṅgamūrti*). Just as [in the case of] fire... [1404]

Or, having performed the *tarpaṇa*, having made [the offering] suitable and having removed [impurities], and having placed his hands in *añjali* at the heart while reciting the *Prāsāda-mantra* with flowers— || 1405 ||

Through devotion, the practitioner, having attained a state of aesthetic relish (*rasībhāva*) within the sphere of the partless (*niṣkala*), should meditate with valorous stride upon his own power within its abode. || 1406 ||

In the *nāda* and likewise in the *bindu*, that which has emerged sequentially into the abode of one's own power (*sva-śakti*)—such is the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the elements (*bhūtānām*). || 1407 ||
And likewise, the portion ending with *bhūtānta* and that very same [portion] ending with *tānta*; mounted upon Śiva and Viṣṇu, this is here called the Śiva-mantra. [This is] the *prastāra*. 1408.
The line arising from space is the second, the half-moon;
the third is curved in shape, and the fourth is joined with fire. (1409)
The fifth has the form of a banner, and the eighth faces downward;
the seventh is joined with a bindu, and the eighth is called the nāda.
That which is joined with eight lines is called a *prāsāda*;
its *prastara* [is as follows].
He whose body consists of five syllables is of the nature of a temple.
He who understands this constantly is indeed the Guru, the Lord;
he is the twenty-fifth, the fifth of the fourth, the quintessential twenty-fifth.
The fifth pair of the eight [syllables] is endowed with the fire-seed (ra); Medhā is situated in the second seed-syllable, preceded by the element (dhātu) in due order. 1413.

Or the mantra may be the combined form of Śiva's *lāñchana* (the bull), consisting of the sound (*nāda*) and so forth, the peak syllable (*kūṭa*), the letter of Time (*kālārṇa*) joined with the letter of Earth (*pārthiva*). (1414)

The letter of Varuṇa (va) joined with fire (ra), the sixth vowel (ū) endowed with the vowel (a), and at the end of the vowels, enriched with the bindu and nāda—those who know this nine-syllable essence as Śiva. || 1415 ||

(100) He who is the soul of the creation and dissolution of the universe proclaimed the mantra of Śiva: having extracted the syllable of sound (nāda), it is joined with the letter 'da' and the fourteen [vowels]. 1416.
It is joined with the Bindu and Nāda, preceded by Nāda and accompanied by the first [vowel];
likewise, it is the first of the eight groups (aṣṭavarga) conjoined with the third vowel. || 1417 ||
Having extracted the first letter of that class and conjoined it with the first vowel,
this five-syllabled mantra of Sadāśiva is thus formed.

In the Kauṣaṣṭīvi verses, [the mantras] consist of a dot (bindu), a crescent moon, three eyes, an eye, the sun, and sound; O Sītā, they are joined with a dot on the seat of the younger brother. || 1419 ||

Having unified the [elements] born of creation, such as the humpbacked belly, one who is not hindered by [worldly] action (karma), having pierced through the accumulation of the *kalās*, proceeds according to the sequence. || 1420 ||
We abide in that which is eternal, stainless, called "the sale," unmixed with the innate (*sahaja*), and [characterized by] internal regulation of the channels (*nāḍī*). || 1421 ||
The Brahma-aperture is suspended like a garland, intensely opening toward the heart as it brings forth the peace of the Lord of the Self— the inward-facing light.
Victory to him whose forehead and eyes are clearly visible, who, though his expansion is merely a pretext, pervades the entire world, O you who bear the moon upon your crest! 1423.
He is skilled in the expansion of the supreme syllable, having attained mastery in its dissolution;
he is free from the bonds of yoga regarding the extensive unfolding of the lineage of the determined manifestation.
Exertion! Having found rest in that which is eternal through those [practices], and having seen Śiva as innate prosperity, may there be happiness here; let there be no delusion. || 1425 ||
The Guru [resides] in the ocean of palaces of snow;
having mentally recited [the mantra] from the root lotus up to the twelfth [digit], one should [proceed] for the benefit of men. || 1426 ||

The moon of the nectar of Śiva’s union with Śakti, the poison of the Lord of the vowels (Ha), the drop (Bindu), the half-moon, the triangle, and the dot—these are situated in the center of the Ni-yama [cakra]. || 1427 ||
Having gone to his own forest-dwelling friend, he performed the crest-gesture of the emanation of the womb of the pair of the humpbacked ones [Kubjika] and the trident. || 1428 ||

Preceded by the *prastāra* [of the mantra], and having crossed over [the ocean of existence] with the *nistāyaka*, this is the partless state, free from the notion of "I" (*ahambhāvanā*), and devoid of attachment. || 1429 ||
The lotus-like face of the Lord, which is like a peaceful lake where the tumultuous waves of all powers have subsided, brings forth bliss through its profound stillness. || 1430 ||
He is the supreme Śiva, who has crossed over the great river of worldly existence, and who resembles hundreds of thousands of moons at the end of the night. || 1431 ||
Having entered again and dissolved the states of existence into the setting [of the sun], one should contemplate this: at the *mūlādhāra*, one should remember the letter *ra*. || 1432 ||
One should visualize the Creator (Brahmā) together with fire, moon, and sun within the *kuṇḍalī*;
Viṣṇu is declared to be in the navel; and Rudra alone is in the cavity of the heart. || 1433 ||

Maheśvara is at the root of the ear; that which is called Nāda is at the root of the tongue; Bindu is at the tip of the nose; and that which is called Nāda is in the middle of the eyebrows. || 1434 ||
One should know that the one named Śakti is on the forehead; at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate Śiva as the "Dance Above" (ūrdhvanṛtta). || 1435 ||
In the midst of the white and the red, it exists in the form of a drop, higher than the highest;
situated within Śiva, it is peaceful, beyond peace, and higher than the highest.
One should meditate upon these as Śiva: "the God who is higher than the highest," the primordial moon, the moon-fragment that is the ornament of death, and the pinnacle of qualities.
The rising sun possesses the fragrance of a jewel-less plow; the moon-faced one has the form of a plowshare; the trident has two circular discs. || 1438 ||
May Śiva—the Sakala, the Parāsakala, and the Niṣkala—protect you; having ascended the Prāsāda temple via the path of Kalā. || 1439 ||
O Sukeśī, beholding the entire phenomenal world below, one should savor that which is intensely concentrated with bliss within the supreme nectar of light.
O Destroyer of Smara, on this day, one who has fully transcended the series of steps known as Sadāśiva—
which are difficult to surmount for those of inferior intellect— reaches the pinnacle of the temple.

Those who, having abandoned the remainder of even the slightest pleasure, meditate upon the auspicious mind that transcends all limbs; they attain the state of the mere temple [of liberation]. || 1442 ||
Some fortunate ones, by means of the reality and through the power of the method, having led the moonlight to the gateway of Śiva, cause it to enter the consciousness. || 1443 ||
The lute of delusion, being without support, would produce existence within non-existence;
having offered salutation with a mindless state, one should not think of anything at all. || 1444 ||
Although I previously uttered "Haṃsa" and subsequently "Om," I alone know this fully—
the "I," the "Tvam," and Śiva as well.
If it is called formless, it is intention (ākūta); if it is embodied, it is the embodied one.
The fire has two bulls, and the power belongs to the sun; in both, there is manifestation and non-manifestation.
Between the sky and the water, he meditated upon the temple,
whereby the turbidity of the wave of the six paths subsided. (1447)
It consists of the *vimasta*, *masta*, and *tama* [states], pertaining both to the temple and to the supreme [deity].
Indeed, that which serves for the enjoyment of these two is composed of Śiva and Śakti. (1448)
Thus, I am the Supreme Śiva, bearing the body of Māmariśa, which is full by means of the Śrīvidyā; I am the Prāsāda-mantra, the Heart, the Will, the Breath, and the Exhalation. || 1449 ||
This great medicine called "The Palace," which grows upon the mountain of the palace, is the great medicine for those bitten by the serpent of saṃsāra. (1450)
Enough, enough with this fatalism! For one who has attained the state of ultimate reality, what need is there for us for a palm-leaf fan in the heat of worldly existence? 1451.

The meditator, through the pervasive relationship with the objects of meditation—which are the supports for the fruits of worshipping the worshipful and the non-worshipful—perceives each respective object within the resonance of the mind. || 1452 ||
The *mātrālayas* [are established] within the *mudrās*; they consist of the limbs, faces, ornaments, bodies, colors, parts, powers, darkness, means, and the goal to be attained. 1453.
And having recollected the vehicle, one should worship Śambhu; [offering] much wine, meat, and the enjoyment of women, one should worship the descent [of the deity]. 1454.
This undertaking of the yoga of the sixty-four [deities] is well-conceived;
I am Bhairava, renowned among the common folk, who has taken refuge in Bhairavī—I am Śiva. || 1455 ||
Behold the ordinance like the Suṣumṇā channel, fashioned neither by the individual nor by the Lord, but proceeding from the Lord; it is the immeasurable flower of bliss. || 1456 ||
Nor do I favor the fourfold Vedic altar when it is sprinkled with water, accompanied by the sounds of divine festival instruments, and urged forward by those devoted to the gods. (1457)
Therefore, one should grasp that which is struck by the body, and it should be worshipped just as this [body] is;
yet there is no non-difference between the moving finger and the fire-mandala below. 1458.

The second [cakra], located at the root of the navel, is said to consist of the foundation of the Kula; it has the color of a kadamba flower, possesses eight petals, and is triangular in shape. (1459)
Shaped like a serpent’s coil and consisting of eight circles,
the great channel named Kuṇḍalā is called the solar orb.

At the tip of the crest [of the head] is the twelve-finger span; on both sides of the neck of the lute (vīṇādaṇḍa) is the Suṣumnā, and likewise, in the center of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is a hollow.
Joined with the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa), it moves among those [channels];
indeed, at that time, it circulates while remaining established within the foundational supports (ādhāras). || 1462 ||
That which is to be supported and that which is impelled by it are thus situated within the meditative absorption;
and the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs] are on both sides of the neck of the lute.
The *upāna*, the *pādukā*, the *jagatī*, the *jaṅghana*, as well as the *kukṣara*, the *kumuda*, and the *bāhulāṅka*. || 1464 ||
The *kaṇḍa* should be known as the ear; it should be positioned lower and lower. The *mahāpaṭṭi* should be the forehead, extending to the edge of the hair where the *ghṛtavāriṇī* [ends]. || 1465 ||
One should purify all parts of the seat (pīṭha) according to the Pāśupata [tradition];
this is known as the purification of the seat, and the site itself is purified by means of the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
The leaf is Brahmā, the fruit is Viṣṇu, and the flower is indeed Īśvara;
these three gods are the purpose for the cutting of the head and other rites of worship.

The water left over from fish is said to be *matsyocchiṣṭa*; that which is left over from the tongue is *jihvocciṣṭa*, while that which is left over from a calf is like salt (*kṣārābha*), and that which is left over from a bee is the former (*pūrvaka*).
The substance of the remnants of food is for the purpose of worship;
this remnant, the offering made to Śiva, is the sustenance for the deceased.
These five, produced from the paste of *kākapiṣṭa*, constitute the purifier (*pavitraka*):
the thumb has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and likewise the index finger has Keśava.
The middle finger has Brahmā as its presiding deity, likewise the ring finger has Īśvara;
and the little finger has Sadāśiva—these are the presiding deities of the fingers.
Female, male, and neuter:
the thumb is female, the index finger is male, and the middle finger is neuter. || 1472 ||
On the ring finger and the little finger of men likewise;
she is the Earth Goddess (Bhūmidevī), two-armed and two-eyed, adorned with a basket-shaped crown. 1473.
An eight-petalled white lotus, situated upon the pericarp and filaments;
the Goddess, seated in the center of the lotus, adorned with a golden complexion. (1474)
Having invoked the Sadyo mantra, the preceptor should worship the Goddess from that [mantra], even if she is devoid of limbs due to defects such as physical deformity. || 1475 ||
One who has severed his own *svayambhū-liṅga*, one who is deficient in limbs, or one who possesses faults;
likewise, a charioteer who is joined with only one wheel [is defective] for a great chariot.
Having fashioned the Sun-god in human form, accompanied by seven horses,
with his hair either slightly visible or entirely gone; (1477)
Or else, he has a crimson crown and is endowed with a halo of light;
he wears a red cloth as an upper garment, is red in color, and is in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a white sacred thread,
he is seated upon a lotus throne in the midst of a circle of radiance.
Having two arms and two eyes, and holding lotuses in his two hands—
thus established in a chariot, such is said to be the form of the Sun.
Form indeed is said to have the appearance of the sun, like that of a weaver's shuttle and so forth;
O Teacher, listen with a concentrated mind to this summary of the body. (1481)
He has two arms and two eyes, is dark-complexioned, and composed;
he wears a tunic, bears the characteristic marks, and has a white sacred thread.
Adorned with bracelets on the ears and joined with necklaces and armlets,
he may wear either a crown, a tiara, or a headpiece of beautiful hair.
Alternatively, he may hold a jewel-encrusted crown together with a ring;
in his right hand a kumuda lotus, and in his left hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Alternatively, the staff may be held inverted or crooked on the left side;
or the water-pot may be in the left hand while the right hand is extended. || 1485 ||
Or he may hold a goad in his left hand, or it may be joined with a rosary;
for the rite of pacification, he is a hero, a knower of the Vedas, a student of the Vedas, and one who is purified.

In the *śayana* (reclining) posture, the left foot is extended while the right foot is drawn up; it is positioned over the corresponding knee and joined with the graceful hand (*vilāsahasta*). || 1487 ||
If he is endowed with four arms, let there be a vajra in the right hand and a staff in the left;
[this is] the Vidyā Mohinī, and the son is Śuci.
The Teacher has fully explained the nature of the body; now hear concerning the form of Skanda, as well as that of the Guru, the books, the Nāgas, and the host of devotees. 1489.
O Śivā, neither the remains of offerings (nirmālya) nor cows, land, gold, garments, jewels, gold ornaments, and the like belong to the Yakṣas or Mātṛs. || 1490 ||
Having set aside the remaining offerings, one should present them to Caṇḍeśa;
likewise, the oil, the powder, the ashes, and the place where the betel was kept.
Thus the rule for the colors has been declared; one should then dismiss the *nirmālya*.
The gross *liṅga* is the temple (*vimāna*), and the subtle *liṅga* is Sadāśiva. (1492)
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), the auspicious liṅga (bhadraliṅga), and the triple-liṅga (liṅgatraya) are thus declared.
Furthermore, one who [builds] a temple with its shadow over the shadow of the liṅga... [1493]
This is declared to be the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), remembered as the "Five Liṅgas" (pañcaliṅga);
[this is] the Liṅga in the Sūkṣma-tantra, and now follows the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the center of the nine squares, milk should be placed;
in the eastern direction, curd; in the direction of Yama (the south), ghee; and in the western direction of Varuṇa, two [portions] of cow dung.
In the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, one should place this fivefold cow-product (pañcagavya) along with a powder made from *piṣṭāmalaka*. || 1496 ||
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter—these five [substances] should each be placed individually in the east; each is prescribed separately.
Having bathed with these mixed together in a single vessel according to the domestic ritual, one should place the special ingredients: cow urine in the east and likewise cow dung in the south. (1498)
The preceptor should place milk in the region of Varuṇa (the West) and curd in the region of Soma (the North);
he should place everything in the center with their respective mantras.
One should place a jar of milk in the center, preceded by curd;
having placed ghee in the south, one should place cow's urine in the north. (1500)
One should place cow dung in the west, flour mixed with water in the southeast, turmeric in the southwest, and place myrobalan in the northwest. 1501.
In the northeast, one should prepare [the site] with flowers using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya):
cow urine has the bull as its deity; cow dung has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Milk has the gods as its deity; curd likewise has Gaṇapati;
clarified butter has Rudra as its deity; and these are the deities for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should consecrate the five products of the cow with the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*;
[these are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (1504)
One should place [the substances] beginning with *sadya* and ending with *īśāna* upon cow-dung and other materials;
one-quarter *prastha* of clarified butter is prescribed, and two-quarters are said to be curd.
Two parts of milk are prescribed, the fourth part is cow-dung water, and six parts of cow-urine; thus there shall be one āḍhaka of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
(106) The best [measure] is said to be one *prastha*, the middling is two *kuḍavas*, and the lowest is one *kuḍava*; these are called the measures of substance. || 1507 ||
Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, these are for the two excellent vessels;
others, however, say the vessel may be of bell-metal, while for an iron vessel, one of clay is prescribed.
Regarding the colors: from a tawny cow comes cow’s urine; from a red cow comes cow dung;
it is said that from a black cow comes milk; and from a white cow, curd is prescribed. (1509)

In the case of a smoke-colored cow, curd should be taken; for the Upāsana rite, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be used. Alternatively, everything may be from a tawny cow (kapilā), or repeatedly from cows of various colors.
As a result, for thousands of millions of kalpas, he is honored in the world of Śiva;
such is the merit from consecrating the Lord of the Gods with the five products of the cow.
One should pour a hundred parts of milk into ten parts of water;
this cow’s milk will destroy sins and eliminate all misfortunes.
For purification from impurity, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are especially recommended;
specifically, one prastha of ghee and two prasthas of curd.
Three *prasthas* of cow’s milk, four *prasthas* of cow dung, and six *prasthas* of cow urine constitute the supreme [mixture], O Prajāpati. (1514)
Half a *prastha* of ghee, one *prastha* of curd is prescribed;
half a *prastha* of milk is mentioned, and likewise two *prasthas* of cow dung.
O Prajāpati, three measures of cow urine constitute the middling amount;
beyond this, I shall explain the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For the sake of destroying all evil and for the sake of attaining all accomplishments, it is said:
"The *droṇa* [measure] is thus the best, while the *kūrcaka* is the middling. (1517)
Half of that is known as the lowest; thus it is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
[The offering] made with the ghee of a tawny cow is called "cow-butter," while that from a white cow is called "cow-milk. (1518)
The wise one should collect milk that is yellow in color, cow dung that is red in color, and cow urine that is black in color. || 1519 ||
Clarified butter indeed has Rudra as its deity; curd has Soma as its deity;
milk has Śukra as its deity; and cow dung has Arka as its deity.
Cow’s urine has Agni as its presiding deity, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have the same deities;
likewise, ghee is said to belong to Kaśyapa, and curd to Kauśika.
The milk belongs to Bhāradvāja, and likewise the cow’s ghee to Gautama;
the cow’s urine belongs to Ātreya; and thus the sages have been proclaimed. (1522)
One should take cow's urine with the Sāvitrī mantra, cow dung with "Gandhadvārām," milk with "Āpyāyasva," and curd with "Dadhikrāvṇo. (1523)

"Thou art semen, thou art light, thou art vigor; by the impulse of the god"—with these words, [he offers] water with *kuśa* grass. He should give cow's urine with "From that Savitṛ... (RV 3.62.10). 1524.

May the cow-dung, fragrant, the gateway, the invincible Śrī, and the curdled milk (*dadhikrāvin*) deliver me across. The clarified butter (*ājya*) is pure light—this is the water of *kuśa* grass. "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ... This is the cow-urine. In the middle... [1526]
Having first placed cow dung, one should place milk in the south;
having placed it in the west, curd is prescribed; and in the north, ghee. || 1527 ||

Having established [the deities], one should establish them in sequence. Having constructed a pavilion in front of Śiva, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) consisting of five squares, or [place] cloths upon each square. || 1528 ||
The wise one should worship the mantras as before; having placed milk in the center, curd is prescribed in the east, and likewise ghee in the south. || 1529 ||
One should place honey in the west; in the north, the placement of sugar is prescribed.
This is called the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). The deity and the ritual act should be performed with the three syllables. || 1530 ||
Then there shall be the ancestral rite (pitrya). For householders, one should properly perform the purificatory rite with two-day intervals. Of the great year... || 1531 ||
One should perform the circumambulation of the Liṅga at the proper time with constant celebration, avoiding theft and strife; this is the tradition of the Guru and the Lord. || 1532 ||
The teacher (ācārya), the preceptor (guru), and the master (svāmin) are threefold according to their sequence:
the teacher is one who instructs the child, and the preceptor is the one who wears the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra). || 1533 ||
For in this manner the procedure for instruction is ordained by its Lord, together with the lineage, the sphere of activity, the trees, and the constituent parts of the monastery. (1534)

A twice-born who is devoted to Śiva [should avoid] a tree that stands in the place of a guru, or its destruction; likewise, he should avoid one who has fallen from the milk [of purity], an atheist, and those who revile the sacred tradition.

One who steals the property of Śiva shall be afflicted with leprosy and other diseases; likewise, one who steals the property of a guru or commits treachery against a guru is joined with [the fruits of] such sins.
One who possesses many seeds is afflicted by that [defilement], while one who is seedless is devoid of sight.
One should act for the sake of the unseen; once seen, worship is fruitless. (1537)
Whether in that village or elsewhere, through the absence of [false] cognition, there is the destruction of the wealth of grain;
the contemplation of reality in all directions brings protection and grace to transmigrating beings. (1538)
Because it possesses the nature of protecting through reflection, it is here called by the word "mantra.
Mantra should be understood as being of two forms, distinguished as the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka). || 1539 ||
That which has the form of speech is declared to be the signifier (vācaka), while that which consists of meaning is considered the signified (vācya).
Furthermore, in some cases, the purpose of both the signifier and the signified is held to be the resonance (nāda).
Sound (nāda) is declared to be mantra; that sound arises as Parā.
From sound, the Bindu is produced, and from this Bindu, the Svara (vowel) arises like the roar of the ocean.
Therefore, from the two vowels of Fire (Ra), there are thirteen variations for them;
from the vowel [A], sixteen; and those called the Jīvas, beginning with Ka, are born from the lotus of the body. 1542.

In number they are thirty-four; their consonants indeed consist of two groups, [the labials and dentals], by which alone everything is pervaded on all sides through the distinction between the hand (pāṇi) and the drink (pāyi).
The scripture composed by them alone is divided into higher and lower;
it consists of nine sections called Nāda, according to the distinction of the fifty phonemes.

The transformation known as the "elemental beings" (bhūtabhūta) is equal in number to the gods and lords of gods; through the letters of the Khaṇḍā [alphabet], these ninefold [principles] are thus formed by the letters. 1545.
O Brahmin, that sound is described through its various states, beginning with the primordial;
it is recited as being threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme. || 1546 ||
Consisting of the continuous flow of verbal cognition, she resides in the hearts of all living beings;
she is differentiated into fifty powers by the fifty Rudra deities. (1547)
O Brahmin, this Mātṛkā should be understood by those practitioners who perceive reality; its dwelling place will be explained later during the description of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).
O Blessed One, the living beings in this world have their lifespan diminished to four hundred years; they are possessed of greed, hatred, and the like, and are deluded by false doctrines. || 1549 ||
O reservoir of compassion, you should explain in many ways the true nature of the mantras according to their sequence, for those who are incapable as well as for those who are capable. (1550)
In whatever manner may bring happiness to human beings, in that very manner I shall speak in brief. (1551)
Beginning with *jīva* and ending with the fifth [vowel], joined with the preceding cause and effect, *vāyu*, this mantra known as *Cintāmaṇi* is a designator of Śiva. (1552)
The Earth, the Head, the Spear, the Armor, and the Weapons are the preeminent sages; Sadyojāta and Dayāvān are also [deities], as are both their respective locations. (1553)
Then, according to the distinction of those colors, they should perform the conceptualization of the mantra-deities;
or else, the definition of mantra is stated in another manner. || 1554 ||
Together with the Sun (the *sāntārka*), through the conjunction of the seed-syllables (*bīja*), [one places them] on the feet, heart, secret place, and head;
then the heart, crest, mouth, armor, the upward-rooted [eye], and the weapon-mantras.
The practitioner of mantra should sequentially extract the weapon-mantra (astra) together with its flaming tip;
or else, [he should visualize it] as the syllables mounted upon the seat of fire, radiant like the moon in the sky.
Through the union with the seed-syllables of earth, water, fire, space, and so forth, this mantra constitutes the primary division; indeed, its arrangement of limbs is generally based upon this.
It is the cause of the union between the reality (tattva) and the categories (pādārtha);
it is the innate seed (khabīja) residing within the root-seed (mūlabīja), that white atom (sitāṇaka) located in the primary cause.
That is called Sṛṣṭi; it is joined with the word Śiva, preceded by the Tāra (Om), and its slender-bodied seed-syllable is also for the one who pervades the sky (Ha). || 1559 ||
This is generally declared to be the root mantra for purification;
therein, the arrangement of the Brahma-mantras and limbs is performed both in direct and reverse order. (1560)
"Now, I shall here describe the characteristics of mantra according to the nature of Time," so it is said in the *Kāmika*.
"Likewise, within the supreme and subtle Śiva-tattva, the Bindu arises. (1561)
From the Bindu, Nāda was produced; from Nāda, Śakti was born;
from Śakti, Vāgbhava arose; and from Vāgbhava, the sixteen Kalās were born.

From the kalās and other [principles], the manifestation (vyañjana) was born; from that manifestation, all the scriptures arose through the mode of Śiva and Śakti, originating from the bindu and nāda.
That which is called the "sound from the finger-tip" is known as the seed-syllable *bindu*;
that seed is said to be the *kanda*, the supreme essence consisting of all powers.
At the time of that seed and sprout, there arises a garland of vowels beginning with 'a';
from the vowel 'a' up to the letter 'kṣa', it is produced by means of the seed-syllable of the mouth.
The *a*-group, the *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, and the *ṭa*-group;
the *ta*-group, the *pa*-group, the *ya*-group, and the *ṣa*-group. || 1566 ||
This group of eight has been declared; now the classification of these groups is stated here: the 'a'-group is the group of Śiva, while the 'ka'-group is the group of Brahmā. (1567)
The *ca*-group is the group of Viṣṇu, while the *ṭa*-group is the group of Rudra;
the *ya*-group is the group of Vyoman (the Ether), and the *śa*-group is the group of Śakti. || 1568 ||
This has been declared as the nomenclature of the groups; now listen again to their divisions:
the *a*-group, the *i*-group, the *ṛ*-group, and the *ka*-group. (1569)
The *ca*-group, the *ya*-group, the *ṭa*-group, the *nṛti*-group, the *ta*-group, the *varuṇa*-group, the *pa*-group, and the *vāyu*-group. || 1570 ||

The *y*-group, the *soma*-group (*sa*-group), the *śa*-group, and the *īśa*-group (*ha*-group)—this is declared to be the classification of the groups; now the classification of the *kīla* (stake) is being described here.

One should join the first, the middle, and that which consists of the seed-syllable of Māra situated in the middle; this is remembered as the *kīla*, and whatever its essential nature may be in the subsequent [mantra]— || 1572 ||

One shall obtain [the fruit] through the utterance of the entire mantra and its conjunction with the script according to the proper method; thus, one should recite the mantras for the successful accomplishment of the ritual peg (kīla). || 1573 ||
Having joined all of that together and understood it through this application of the *kīla*, one should perform everything. (From the *Kiraṇa*, verse 1574)
Devoid of the Praṇava:
that mantra which is devoid of the Praṇava is life-taking.
Indeed, for all mantras, the Praṇava is said to be their life-force. (1575)
The deity of the Praṇava is Agni; its form is that of the Supreme Brahman;
O Goddess, its metre is Gāyatrī, and its seer is proclaimed to be Brahmā. || 1576 ||
I shall now explain the Praṇava in brief, and not in detail:
the letter A, the letter U, and the letter M, together with the Bindu and the Nāda. (1577)
The syllable *a* has Brahmā as its deity; the syllable *u* is said to be Viṣṇu;
the syllable *m* has Rudra as its deity, and the *bindu* has Īśvara as its deity.
Nāda is declared to be Sadāśiva and is remembered as consisting of five divisions:
it resides in the heart of the letter A and in the ear of the letter U.
The middle of the palate is the location of the letter *ma* and the *bindu*; above that is the place of the *nāda*, which is thus proclaimed. (1580)
They know the Praṇava to be the name of all letters and to consist of all the gods;
Sanatkumāra is its seer (ṛṣi), and the Oṃkāra is white in color.
It is said that its meter is the Gāyatrī because of its nature as Śiva;
all yogis declare the single syllable "Om" to be Brahman. || 1582 ||
In the manner of *bindu* and *nāda*, it has the form of the *praṇava*;
indeed, that which has the form of the *praṇava* is said to be the origin of the *praṇava*. (1583)
First, the sound (nāda) arose; second, that which originates from the throat-syllable (galika).
The third arises from the coil, and the fourth originates from the crest. || 1578 ||
That which is proclaimed as "nāda" is known to consist of five divisions;
the letter *u* is to be understood as the circle (*valaya*), and the crest (*culikā*) has the form of the bindu.
The anusvāra and the letter *ma* are proclaimed as the five colors;
for the purpose of creation and maintenance, the wise one should pronounce them facing downwards.
The syllable known as *praṇava*, which is designated as the "mouth" of all living beings, is proclaimed;
the practitioner of mantras should utter it first for the purpose of purifying the mantra.
One should hold in the mind that mantra which is the destroyer of saṃsāra, which consists entirely of Śiva, which is the mantra of the essential siddhānta, and the king of all mantras. || 1582 ||

The mantra of the Transcendent (Tīta), the mantra of the sovereign powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the mantra consisting of Amṛtaśiva for the purpose of destroying death, and the single-syllable *Oṃ*. || 1583 ||
The mantra that bears the Upaniṣads, the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," is the five-syllabled supreme Brahman— pure and the destroyer of sins.
One should constantly contemplate this with the mind; one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The salutation is yellow in color; its location is traditionally said to face the east.
Indra and the other deities are its presiding divinities; Gāyatrī is remembered as its meter; Gautama is its sage;
the syllable "M" is its form; its color is black; and its location is indeed facing south.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the seer is Atri, and Rudra is said to be the deity.
The syllable ŚI is its color, smoke-colored; its location is indeed the western face. || 1587 ||
Viśvāmitra is the seer, the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī is the meter, and Vi�ṣṇu is the deity;
the syllable is "va," its color is golden, its location is the left shoulder, and its direction is the north. (1588)
Its deity is Brahmā and others, its metre is Bṛhatī, and its seer is Aṅgiras;
the letter Ya is red in color, its location is the upper face, and it is Virāṭ.
The seer is Chaṃdas, Bhāradvāja; Skanda is said to be the deity.
Thus [end] the udātta, anudātta, and svarita [accents]. 1590.
The first [note] is udātta, and likewise the second of the fourth [group];
the fifth is indeed svarita, and the middle one is known as niṣadha. || 1591 ||
The letter *na* is declared to be feminine, while the three letters [nā-ka-ra] constitute the masculine gender;
the letter *ya*, however, is neuter, and thus it is here called the "five-syllabled" (pañcākṣara). || 1592 ||
The heart begins with *aja* (the left), the *śikhā* is *aghora*, and likewise the *śikhā*;
*puruṣa* is the *kavaca*, *īśāna* is *śiva*, and the eye and weapon follow in sequence. (1593)
p.
112) Of that [mantra], the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon—these are proclaimed as the six limbs in their proper sequence. || 1594 ||
The [mantras] from the heart to the eyes are proclaimed as being joined with the nasal drop (bindu);
the weapon-mantra (astra) is joined with the visarga and endowed with the six cognate letters.
The syllable Oṃ is the first seed-syllable, while the syllable Ma is the second; the third seed-syllable is the letter I, the cause of all causes. (1596)
The fourth seed-syllable is Ū, and VYO would be the fifth;
MA would be the sixth, and likewise VYĀ would be the seventh. || 1597 ||
The eighth seed-syllable is *vikāra*, the ninth is *nekāra*, and the tenth seed-syllable is *oṃkāra*; this is here called the mantra of Śiva. (1598)
It is joined with the letter *sa* and the letter *ma*, endowed with the sixth vowel, combined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and preceded by the *praṇava*. || 1599 ||
At the time of installing the *liṅga*, one should place the mantra in this manner according to the sequence;
however, at the time of worship and recitation, one should join it with "to Śiva. (1600)
The five-syllable [mantra] is said to be female, male, and neuter; it is called Nāda and Gaganam, and its Bindu is Śiva. || 1601 ||
The syllable *ha* is said to be the heart, the syllable *mau* the two arms, and the syllable *oṃ* the feet; [this is] "Salutation to the seat of the Prāsāda. || 1602 ||
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"One should place the syllable *a* on the crown of the head and the syllable *ā* on the forehead;
the syllable *la* on the right eye and the syllable *ī* on the left eye. (1603)
The letter *u* is in the right nostril; the letter *ū* is in the nostrils of the sky (the bridge of the nose).
The letter *ṛ* is in the right ear; the letter *ṝ* is in the left ear. (1604)
One should place the syllable *ḷ* on the right cheek and the syllable *ḹ* on the left cheek;
having placed *e* and *ai*, one should place *o* and *au* in the middle of the palate. (1605)
Having placed *aṃ* at the root of the palate, one should place *aḥ* at the root of the palate;
the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left hand.
The *ṭa*-group [of consonants] is on the right side, and the *ta*-group is on the left side;
*pa* and *pha* are on the right side, while *ba* and *bha* are on the left side. (1607)
Having extracted the eight syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *ha* at the region of the navel, that which resides in the heart indeed expands. || 1608 ||
One should place the letter *la* in the region of the anus and the letter *kṣa* in the secret place;
[one should likewise place] five, five, four, five, and five times five.
The sixth [syllable] consists of five fives; beyond that is the seed-syllable of Māyā.
The seventh and the fourth [syllables], conjoined with the second vowel, [form the next]. (1610)

The Śiva-mantra joined with the seed-syllable of Marut is now declared here: it consists of the letter at the end of *ya*, the letter at the end of *ma*, and the letter at the end of *va*, conjoined with the third vowel. (1611)
That which ends in *lāṃ* is endowed with the tone of the *pakṣa*; that which ends in *māṃ* is known as the five-syllabled mantra.
His body consists of these five syllables, and his vital breaths consist of the *ṛc*.
He who constantly understands this is indeed the Lord Guru.
The letter *a* is to be known as earth, and the letter *kha* is said to be water. (1613)
The letter *ga* is said to be fire; the letter *gha* is called air;
the letter *ṅa* is declared to be space; and the letter *ca* is called air. (1614)
The letter *cha* is said to be *praṇi*; the letter *ja* is called *pāda*.
The letter *jha* is said to be *vāyu*, and the letter *ña* is indeed *upastha*. (1615)
The letter *da* is said to be the ear, and the letter *ṭha* is called the head;
the letter *ḍa* is said to be the eye, and the letter *ḍha* is designated as the tongue. || 1616 ||
The letter *e* is said to be the nose, and the letter *t* is sound itself;
the letter *th* is declared to be touch, and the letter *d* is called form. || 1617 ||
The letter *dha* is said to be taste; the letter *na* is called smell.
The letter *pa* is said to be speech; the letter *pha* is called space.
The letter *sa* is said to be giving; the letter *bha* is called emission (*visarga*);
the letter *ma* is said to be bliss. One should install these as the imperishable syllables of the principles (*tattva*).
The letter *ya* is said to be the wind; the letter *ra* is called fire;
the letter *la* should be known as earth; and the letter *va* would be Varuṇa.
The syllable *śa* is said to be the bulbous root (*kanda*); the syllable *ṣa* is the equal one (*sama*) that has fallen away;
the syllable *sa* is said to be power (*śakti*); and the syllable *ha* is remembered as the Person (*puruṣaka*). || 1621 ||
The letter *la* is made the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the letter *kṣa* is said to be action (*karman*).
The letters beginning with *a* have been proclaimed in brief. (1622)
For the sake of the emergence of mantras and the origin of the phonemes,
there are fifty-one syllables beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
These phonemes are praised as bestowers of desired objects;
they exist in the form of female, male, and likewise neuter (udbhava) forms.
And all of them assumed the forms of deities.
The seed-syllable of the color, the color itself, and the mantra for attracting the seed-syllable of the gender.
These indeed are their auspicious names, which express synonyms for their respective classes;
for they [describe] the difference in form and likewise the portion of those who have arisen from them.

(114) Furthermore, [it explains] the distinctions such as the *tattvas* and mantras, as well as the fruits pertaining to the presiding deities (*adhideva*), the gross and subtle forms, and specifically the manifestation of the individual soul (*jīva*). || 1627 ||
O Six-faced One, hear this division in brief and in summary:
within the supreme, subtle Śiva-tattva, the form of the Bindu is born. (1628)
From Bindu, Nāda was produced, and from Nāda, Śakti was born;
from Śakti, Śabda is born, and from Śabda, Udbhava arose.
In the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], the collection of digits (kalās) arises, and from those digits likewise arise the sub-digits (vikalās);
the mantras that express it and those mantras themselves are not distinct at all.
The sequence of emanation has been declared; now their characteristics are described.
In the process of emanation, the Supreme Power (parāśakti) takes the form of the Bindu, and from it arises the Nāda, which transcends it.
Power (śakti) is to be known as the oblation of will (icchā); here, it is said that the knowledge of sound (śabda-jñāna) is [the result]. || 1632 ||
Speech would be the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and the sixteen vowels;
their forms are likewise declared to be both primary nature (prakṛti) and modification (vikṛti).
The seven syllables are the primordial nature (prakṛti), while the nine syllables are the transformation (vikṛti); these are the letter A, the letter Ha, the letter U, and the letter Ṣa. || 1634 ||
The letter *u* and the letter *ū*, the letter *ṣa* and the letter *ṣṭra*;
the letter *ḷ* and the letter *ḹ*, and the arising of the letters *e* and *ai*.
The vowels *o* and *au* should likewise be known to arise in their respective order;
these indeed are declared to be the primary forms (*prakṛti*) among the phonemes beginning with *a*. (1636)
These sixteen vowels, beginning with *a* and ending with *ḥ*,
are indeed the measures of time (*kalā-mātrā*), the vowels, the living beings, as well as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*).
The vital breath, the self, and the body are likewise synonyms; this is declared to be the division of *kalā*. Now hear the division of *vikalā*.
The letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa,' as well as the final phonemes, are known to be incomplete;
however, the five letters beginning with 'a' arise within the letter 'a'. (1639)
By means of the *ca*-group [consonants], the five [vowels] arise in the letter *i*;
however, the group of five beginning with the letter *da* is produced from the letter *u*.
The five syllables beginning with *ta* arise within *ma*,
while the five syllables beginning with *pa* arise within *ka*.
Arising from the syllable Oṃ, the letters beginning with Ya are established according to the scriptures;
these are indeed remembered as five groups of five, each consisting of five syllables. (1642)
p. 115) Masculine gender:
the body as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the physical frame, the field (*kṣetra*), the substratum, and likewise the form (*tanu*).
The consonant is that which denotes the power of differentiation and is a synonym for the *bindu*. || 1643 ||
And the *kalā* of the *vikalās* shall be declared as three fortnights; likewise, there are thirteen lunar days (*tithis*), namely Śiva, Agni, Bhūta, and Rudra. (1644)
These indeed have been proclaimed as the tastes and colors, as well as the masculine gender; the essence of the Ikṣu-veda is Bhānu, which is the cause of the seed-mantras and so forth.
These six are indeed called seeds, as is the feminine gender;
the four sounds ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are traditionally known as neuter.
The letter *ka* and the letter *ga*, the letter *ca* and the letter *ja*;
the letter *ṭa* and the letter *ḍa*, and the letter *ṇa* and the letter *da*. || 1647 ||
The letter *pa*, the letter *ma*, the letter *ya*, and the letter *ṣa*—these are proclaimed as the masculine gender among the twelve vowels. || 1648 ||
The letter *kha*, the letter *gha*, the letter *cha*, and the letter *jh*;
the letter *ṭa*, the letter *ḍa*, the letter *ṇa*, and the letter *da*. || 1649 ||
The syllable *pa* and the syllable *ma*, [and so forth], the syllable *ṭha* and the syllable *ḍha*, the syllable *tha* and the syllable *gha*. || 1650 ||
One should designate these as the solar seed-syllables (bhānubīja) in the feminine gender;
one should know the remainder to be neuter; thus the threefold division is traditionally taught.

One should designate the three letters beginning with *a* as space (*vyoma*), the three beginning with *ī* as wind (*anila*), and the letters beginning with *da* as the seed-syllables of fire (*tejas*). (1652)
The three vowels beginning with *e* (e, ai, o) are Āyā; the three beginning with *au* (au, aṃ, aḥ) are Mahī.
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while the form (*mūrti*) is called the transformation (*vikṛti*). || 1653 ||
Those who are deficient in power are thus described; these [categories] are of three kinds. Nature is said to be luminous, while modification is called form.
The letter *a* has one measure (*mātrā*), while *ai* has two measures;
*o* has one measure, while *au* has two measures. || 1655 ||
The anusvāra and visarga are endowed with one mātrā;
[the vowels] from the letter *a* up to *na*, as well as the letter *la* and the sound *lakāra*. (1656)
On the earth, the letters beginning with *śa* are to be known as the group of five;
likewise, the letters *va* and *sa* are traditionally remembered as the portion belonging to water.
The syllable beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *na*, and the syllable beginning with *ta* which is the first letter;
the vowel *a* belongs to all deities and is red, effecting the subjugation of all. (1658)
The other power of the letter Ā is the white [syllable] which is an attractor. The letter La has Viṣṇu as its deity; it is dark blue and brings about protection. (1659)
By me, the syllable *rī*, which is yellow and brings women under control, has been drunk;
and the syllable *u*, whose deity is Vasu, which is black and brings kings under control. (1660)
The syllable *ukāra* is the goddess Earth, dark-green in color, who brings the world under her control;
the syllable *ṛkāra* is to be known as Brahmā, yellow in color, the destroyer of the fierce.
The syllable KĀRA, the form of Śrīkaṇṭha, destroys the fever of Mañcara;
and the syllables Ḷ and Ḹ, white and red respectively, belonging to the two Aśvins, remove fever. (1662)
The letter *e* is Vīrabhadra, who is yellow and bestows the accomplishment of all aims;
the letter *ai* is Ādiśakti, who is like crystal and supports the Gaṅgā.
One should know the syllable Oṃ to be the Lord (Īśvara), the light that bestows all fruits; the syllable Au is the Primordial Power (Ādiśakti), the white I who grants all accomplishments.
The syllable *Aṃ* is Maheśa, red in color, the bestower of all happiness;
the syllable *Aḥ* is Kālarudra, liberated, the cutter of time.
The letter *ka* belongs to Prajāpati; when visualized as yellow, it brings about sight.
The letter *kha* should be known as the Jāhnavī (Ganges); resembling a razor, it destroys sins. (1666)
The syllable *ga* should be in the form of Gaṇeśa, red in appearance, and the destroyer of obstacles;
the syllable *dha* is to be known as Bhairavī, which bestows victory and grants wealth. (1667)
The letter *da* is to be understood as Time (*kāla*), which brings victory over all;
the letter *ca* is of fierce form (*caṇḍarūpa*), the destroyer of ignorance and of enemies. (1668)
The syllable *cha* is auspicious; *kālī* [is associated with] *syād*, which bestows victory upon the king. At the syllable *ja*, Jaṃbhalā is to be known; she is red-hued and brings victory. (1669)
The syllable Jha belongs to Ardhanārī; it is yellowish-red and brings victory. The syllable Jña is to be known as Koṭarī; it is yellow and destroys disease. (1670)
The syllable Ṛ, which is Bhṛṅgīśa, is red in color and brings all happiness;
the syllable Ṭha has the form of the moon, is white, and destroys death.
The syllable Ḍa has one eye and is yellow; it destroys the defeat of Time (Kāla). The syllable Ḍha is the seed-syllable of Yama; it is blue and brings victory over Death.
The syllable *ṇa* is the seed of Nanda; it is red in luster and bestows the accomplishment of wealth. The syllable *ta* has Vasu as its deity; it is white and brings about total victory. (1673)
The syllable *tha* is to be known as belonging to the Atharva Veda; it is white like a jasmine flower and bestows victory.
The seed-syllable of Durgā is the syllable *da*; it is dark blue and grants the accomplishment of all aims.
One should know the letter *Dha* to be the giver of wealth (*dhanada*), yellow in luster, and the bestower of the accomplishment of goals.
The self-manifested (*svayaṃbhu*), the divine (*daivika*), that of the Goddess (*devya*), the human (*mānuṣa*), and those of the Rākṣasas and Bāṇa—thus the *liṅga* is said to be sevenfold. (1676)
A banner appearing tattered, the form of rudrākṣa beads, clarified butter or the scent of honey, and a mountain-like form rising from the underworld. || 1677 ||

The characteristic of these has been declared; the self-arisen linga is said to be long in shape, distinguished by a head, and possessing a luster that is even despite its depressions and elevations. (1678)
It should be joined with lines and hollows, with a stream at the opening raised by one barley-corn;
it should be held in the palms in the shape of a casket, free from the Brahma-thread.
The characteristics of these have been declared; such is called the divine *liṅga*.
It has the shape of a *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit or the form of a *mātuluṅga* fruit. (1680)
The Gāṇava-liṅga is said to have the shape of an urvāruka fruit, the form of a kapittha fruit,
and the appearance of a palm fruit.
The root-liṅga is thick at the base, that of the middle is like a barley grain, and that of the pipīlikā is thin;
the middle liṅga has a thick head—thus the fourfold division declared by the sages.

Whether it be the measurement of the door, the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha), or even the measurement of the liṅga; whether it be the measurement prescribed in the treatises on architecture (śilpa-śāstra) or even the measurement of the cubit (hasta). || 1683 ||
Or, according to the measurements prescribed in the treatises on craftsmanship, it should have the shape of an umbrella with its top rising upward;
at its base and at its tip, it should be multiplied by one-eighth of its own width.
In the case of a Linga belonging to the rainy season, it should be properly square with the Viṣṇu-portion;
[the gems used are] ruby, ruby-red (padmarāga), lapis lazuli, and topaz.
Sapphire, diamond, coral, crystal, and likewise emerald—
these are known as the nine gems, O Saṃkalpa, by means of their characteristic marks.
One should know that the māṇikya bestows fame, the padmarāga bestows prosperity,
the vaiḍūrya bestows long life, and the puṣyarāga bestows victory.
Indranīla brings nourishment; coral brings subjugation;
crystal brings the increase of sons; and all [gems] bestow emeralds. (1688)
In this world, one shall obtain liberation from the body here in Pilāsva.
A linga made of ripe fruit shaped like a *sūpha* fruit, and a pedestal made of gold—1689.
If the male organ is excessive, death will occur; if the vulva is excessive, there will be loss of wealth. One should make them equal in size, for that brings all prosperity and happiness. (1690)

(118) One should avoid [hair that is] like the rays of the sun, rough, thin, thick, and so forth; likewise, that which is long-shaped, white, tawny, wounded, or of various other [unfavorable] forms. || 1691 ||
And it is clearly endowed with lines, dots, and the marks of a deer;
it is excessive in its power, or joined with a *liṅga*, or cracked at the tip of the trident. || 1692 ||
By a householder, all auspicious things should be dedicated to me;
on that day, other items unfit for sacrifice [should also be offered]. || 1693 ||
A wise man knows that all external appearances are but dense trunks ending in their respective functions, while the inner essence within the cavity is the true form of the person.
All external forms are said here to be the form of a woman;
at the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should avoid the woman, for the man knows that [the state] ends with absorption into her (tallaya).
One should apply this sequence of punishment, with some specific distinctions made by those who possess [knowledge];
one should know that the word "ut" means "risen," while "magha" is traditionally remembered as meaning "self."
That which arises spontaneously is therefore called a festival;
it is worshipped by all limbs, and knowledge is born within the self.
Because it is born from the Purāṇa, it is called "Pūrjā.
The conch has the moon as its presiding deity, and the belly has the Gaṅgā as its presiding deity. (1698)
At the beginning, Prajāpati and Brahmā were the presiding deities;
they went together with all the gods to the assembly of the day, which is dear to the hosts.

The wise one should raise the banner. That which is said to be the third, situated within the essence, is known as the Vāma weapon; likewise, the terrible *bimba* beginning with *kāṣā* and ending with *vidyā* is the Tatpuruṣa [face]. || 1701 ||
The principles beginning with Earth and ending with Nāda are said to be presided over by Īśāna and the others;
the principles beginning with Kāṣṭhā and ending with Varadā-Śakti are situated within each respective principle.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Gautama, and likewise Kāśyapa; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, and Sādākhya as well. (1703)
O lotus-eyed one, the [mantra] of the seer, the meter, and the deity has been declared according to the sequence beginning with Īśāna, following the path prescribed by the Vidyā. (1704)
Having assigned [the offerings] to the respective places of the deities and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the wise practitioner should,
while merely observing the substances, recollect them in sequence with their respective mantras.
p.
119) One should protect that substance, having established the presiding deities of the vessels;
as stated in the *Dīptatantra*:
Having invoked the seat and the form, [one should place them] upon the heads of these three.
Having understood [the relationship] through the state of pervasion and the pervader, one should begin the sacrifice;
[visualizing the deity] seated, pure, ending with Vidyā, within the range of the Mūrti and Śakti.
Having invoked Śiva as the embodiment [of the deity], one should worship him from head to foot;
according to the Suprabheda, he has two eyes, two arms, and wears a crown of fierce rays.
Whether wearing a crown or a tiara, or even having his hair tied up,
he is endowed with all ornaments and possessed of blazing feet.
She was draped in garments of fine linen, silk, and divine raiment, as well as in variegated cloths;
she was complete in all her limbs and endowed with every auspicious mark.
Either the right arm is bent at the elbow with the left hand hanging down, or the left arm is bent at the elbow with the right hand hanging down. || 1711 ||
There, one should carefully mark the thread according to the measurement of the nose;
the form of Gaurī is indeed said to have the shape of Bhavānī.
She has two eyes and two arms, is dark-complexioned, and possesses full, elevated breasts;
she is dark-hued with full cheeks and eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus.
One should again perform the ritual placement of the hand-gestures (karanyāsa) for her as before;
the form of Bhavānī has been described, while the form of Gaurī is as previously stated.
It is taught that at the beginning of a mantra there is *sūtaka*, and at the end of a mantra there is *pretaka*.
*Pretaka* serves to satisfy the ancestors (*pitṛs*), while *sūtaka* is of the nature of a *rākṣasa*. || 1715 ||
The middle [offering] shall be for the destruction of death; one devoted to Śiva should avoid [these] at the three times of day.
[One should offer] milk from a tamed [cow], ripe fruit, sacred sesame, flowers, and food. || 1716 ||
A well-constructed snare.
The *karavīra* [flower] [is used] for a day and night, while the lotus (*paṅkaja*) [is used] for six months. || 1717 ||
For two months, one should worship with tulasī and bilva leaves;
among all varieties of flowers, karavīra is especially recommended. (1718)
Washing with a leaf is prescribed, as is sprinkling with a flower;
likewise, sugarcane, fruit, and root are used for washing and cutting.
The origin of the Śaivas is known as the *kuṇḍagola* of the *liṅgas*.
Ādi-Śaiva is Śiva; Rudra is the essence of pure Śaivism, whose nature is Śiva. (1720)
Therefore, the Śaiva rite must be performed from the consecration until the conclusion of the festival;
it should be carried out by an Ādi-Śaiva, both for his own sake and for the sake of others.
p.
120) It is said that "the primordial Śaiva" is Śiva himself, the Brāhmaṇa teacher;
[for him] there is no impurity from birth or death, just as if he had died at the time of worship. || 1722 ||
One should not observe impurity (āśauca) on that occasion; rather, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
This applies likewise to celibate students (brahmacārī), householders, ascetics (yatīnām), and spiritual teachers (deśika).
One should not observe impurity, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water;
even during birth or death, one should not cause the suspension of sacred rites.
The individual soul is like a bubble on the water; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga.
A woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga becomes purified by her menses after giving birth. || 1725 ||
The sun, fire, and wind possess purity increased ten million-fold;
likewise, the state of Śiva and the twice-born remains pure for ten days. (1726)
For a Vaiśya, it shall be twelve days for the king alone; for a Śūdra, it shall be fifteen days; and for one month for a Śūdra—this is the summary for the four castes. || 1727 ||

If a Śiva-dvija, while performing the consecration festival or the installation ceremony, should encounter an impurity (āśauca) arising from a death or birth occurring in the interim, [the following applies]: || 1728 ||
Having summoned his son or disciple, that twice-born Śiva-devotee should begin that rite; whether it be the worship of a *liṅga* or a *kautuka*, he should perform the daily worship.
Impurity due to birth or death and the like is purified in a single day;
however, for Brahmins purification occurs in ten days, while for a king it is in twelve days.
Likewise, a Vaiśya should observe purification for a fortnight, and a Śūdra for a month;
this applies to all rites such as sacrifices, and one should observe the vow for the sake of performing a sacrifice.
The twice-born who have been initiated, ascetics, and celibate students should not observe the two-fold impurity, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water. || 1732 ||
Furthermore, there may be impurity (āśauca), yet one is purified by mere bathing.
In the *Vidyāpurāṇa*:
"Upon the death of a maternal grandfather, a paternal grandmother, or a maternal uncle... (1733).
One who has conceived a child should bathe his own guru, his teachers, these mothers, his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his own sister.
In the Smṛti statement:
"If the servants die within twelve daṇḍas [of the master's death], one should perform the purification (śiva) after abandoning them and carry out the daily and occasional rites. (1735)
In the Great Mouth (Mahāmukha):
"The individual soul is Śiva; Śiva is the individual soul; the individual soul is said to be Śiva.
By virtue of the terms 'bound soul' (paśu) and 'bond' (pāśa), the individual soul is [distinguished from] the supreme Śiva who is liberated from bonds. || 1736 ||
The four-footed form is that of the Veda, while the horn-like form is that of Agni;
likewise, the cowherd-bird is Āditya, and similarly, it is Rudra.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— this bull-nature is called the Bull (Vṛṣa).
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, and [the world] has perished or been consumed by fire once again, || 1738 ||
Having subdued the vehicle of Śruti by means of the form of a bull,
the Vedas, like dogs, slowly and gradually sniffed at his lotus-like face.
I bow to that Supreme Lord, whose feet are to be meditated upon,
who is both auspicious and inauspicious, and who carries both the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs, as well as the moon and sun, and all the gods, were likewise cut down by me. (1741)
Therefore, that vehicle is indeed called the dog-vehicle.
In the *Kāmika*: "The thirteenth [tithi] on the new moon day, and the fourteenth in the month of Māgha... (1742).
One should worship on the night presided over by the fourteenth day, for that is Śivarātri;
the fourteenth day is declared to be Śivā, while the new moon (amāvāsyā) is Śiva himself.
A wise person should perform the conjunction of these two on the Śivarātri night;
by constant recitation, the deity, being fulfilled, becomes pleased. || 1744 ||
With faces appearing serene and well-proportioned, they are thus described as eternal;
yet they are terrifying to yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, grahas, serpents, and the like.
When all that has been recited at the end has been completed, O best of sages, I shall speak of Śivarātri, which brings fear and anxiety to an end; one should perform its worship.

In the Kṛta age, as well as in the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—one should worship Guha after having performed worship in each respective age; indeed, one should sacrifice to Guha specifically in the Tretā age.
In the Tretā age as well, one should worship Vighneśa, and thereafter Acyuta;
in the Kali Yuga, however, one should worship Brahmā, Indra, and the sages.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, on the fifth day when the moon is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, on the seventh day when it is in the Aśvinī constellation, and on the eighth day of the dark fortnight when it is in Kṛttikā. (1749)
On the twelfth day of the month of Ārdrā, and likewise on the eighth day of the month of Puṣya—
having thus worshipped throughout the year, one should observe Śivarātri.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, the Śivarātri vow yields excellent fruit;
it lasts for one month and two fortnights, specifically during the night of the additional fortnight.
May that fruit of performing Śiva-pūjā throughout the night be granted to me;
for one entire fortnight, one should worship Śiva during the first part of the night.
If, however, it occurs on the male lunar day (*puṃpakṣa*), the king perishes along with his kingdom.
It should be performed during the first watch of the night; one should not cause it to be done at any other time of night. (1753)
Therefore, with every effort, especially during the first part of the night— and particularly during the fortnight when the nights are longer— one should perform the ritual worship of Śiva. (1754)
That night should be for the worship of Śiva, O God, and there shall indeed be his presence;
however, a night during the waning fortnight likewise brings about all manner of defects.
Therefore, with every effort and in the sequence of all months,
one should observe Śivarātri daily at the conclusion of the twilight rites.
One should perform the worship of Śiva especially during each watch of the day;
furthermore, the ritual offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed on the ninth, seventh, or fifth day.
Thereafter, one should offer sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, on the day prior to that, one should purify the pavilion.
Having worshipped with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then bind the protective amulet (kautuka).
Having worshipped a bilva leaf which is infused with all fragrances... (1759)
The wise one should wrap the bilva fruit with a cloth for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
At the clear dawn, the wise preceptor (deśika) should perform his ablutions.
Having observed that people perform libations in the forenoon, circumambulation at midday, and worship in the evening, one should observe the vow accordingly.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, as well as Śiva-devoted twice-born men and all living beings alike, should observe the fast. || 1762 ||
Indeed, for all living beings, fasting and likewise sleeplessness performed by women is said to accomplish all undertakings. || 1763 ||
It bestows longevity, spiritual accomplishment, and likewise complete liberation;
for men who observe fasts that are otherwise inauspicious, this very birth becomes auspicious.
And being celibate, he should diligently observe a sleepless fast and worship the four junctions of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Then the preceptor should meditate upon the region as being devoid of Brahmā, Indra, and the sages;
he should first worship Vighneśa, and after that, the worship of the Sun.
Having prepared rice with śāli grains, one should then have the auspicious day (puṇyāha) proclaimed;
first there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and in the second [case], there should be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 1767 ||
In the third watch, he should bathe with honey, and in the fourth, with the essence of sugarcane;
the most excellent preceptor should perform the worship specifically during each watch.
In the first [rite], the ritual bathing is prescribed to be one hundred and eight;
in the second, the ritual bathing likewise consists of twenty-five, less one.
In the third [watch], one should perform the ceremonial bathing and fill nine new jars;
specifically, at every watch, one should cause the bathing to be performed below.
Having performed worship during the first watch of the night, one should honor with bilva leaves;
in the second [watch], with lotus flowers, and in the third, with jasmine flowers. (1771)
Having worshipped the Nandyāvarta, one should worship during the four watches;
one should perform worship at the four twilights, for the bilva leaf yields great fruit.
The first consists of rice with mung beans, the second is milk-rice (pāyasa),
the third should be rice with sesame and peas (kṛsara), and the fourth is pure rice.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla specifically during each watch of the night; one should perform the great worship specifically during each watch of the night. (1774)
The guide should worship there with garments, gold, and rings;
he should honor the Brāhmaṇas there and worship the devotees of Maheśvara most excellently.
One should honor the attendants with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
this brings prosperity, victory, merit, and increases longevity and health. (1776)
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
that Śivarātri occurs on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha.
Between the months of Māgha and Phalguna, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the fortnight shall be equal; thus, one should perform the ritual on the fifteenth day.
One should perform the sacrifice in the four directions before the setting of the sun;
it should be completed on the fourteenth day at the very end of the waning of the moon.
One should worship Śivarātri, which is joined with the end of the month of Māgha;
that lunar day (tithi) on which the sun has set is to be known as the entire [observance] day.
That lunar mansion is the day-and-night during which the sun has risen;
thus ends the ritual for Śivarātri in the great tantra known as the Vijaya. 1781.
The fourteenth mixed with the new moon, the seventh with the eighth, and the tenth mixed with the eleventh destroys previously accumulated merit. (1782)
The night on which the fourteenth day predominates is considered Śivārātri;
[it occurs when] the thirteenth day lasts for three watches of the night and the fourteenth day for one watch. (1783)
The thirteenth lunar day is desirable when mixed [with the fourteenth], but not when joined with the new moon;
however, the nourishment (poṣaṇa) is on the fourteenth, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is also on the fourteenth.

That night on which the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) is complete and the fourteenth (caturdaśī) lasts for one watch (yāma), shall be endowed with the grace that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The thirteenth [digit] has the form of a vulva, and the fourteenth has the form of a linga;
the ascetic woman, joined with the new moon, should be honored by the householder.
p.

124) Then, the height of the *liṅga* is made of twenty-four parts, of which the portion of Śiva is four parts; in the *brahma-bhāga*, it should be eight parts; and again, in the middle, the portion of Viṣṇu— || 1787 ||
One should divide the *vasu* (eight) part by nine parts and the *śiva* (eleven) part by ten parts to obtain the *vardhamāna*.
In the Dhārāliṅga and in all liṅgas, there are eight points at the inner base.
The Yugāgra [type]; above that, the Jit, Dviguṇya, Sudhāra, and Dhārāliṅga are recommended for all castes on a mountain of pure stone. || 1789 ||

With the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one [offering] is for the full moon; thirteen [offerings] are for the first day of the lunar fortnight, and one ghaṭikā is for the fourteenth day. One should then perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*).
Having performed the entire ritual placement (karanyāsa), one should meditate on the hollow body as being in the center;
having restrained the vital breath with firm resolve, one should contemplate the blazing syllable *huṃ*.
The syllable *huṃ* is joined with that very *recaka* [exhalation] at the knot. || 1792 ||
Then, having formed the five knots, one should determine the primordial nature from that; having grasped the individual soul with the liberation mantra at the top of the *huṃ* syllable.
Accompanied by the kumbhaka [retention], one should lead the upward-moving breath;
having it stationed within the gateway of the teeth, one should unite it with Śiva.
This should be the self-yoking; thereafter, one should purify the elements.
Earth and wind, water and fire—these pairs should be purified of one another.
The manner in which the elements are to be purified through their mutual opposition is stated as follows in the *Sūkṣmatantra*:
"The elements, beginning with *nivṛtti*, do not constitute any other complete locus. (1796)
Having realized that these [elements] are pervasively established, one should purify them;
or else, there is the burning away of the elements, or their mutual purification.
The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) taught here has the maṇḍala and so forth as its presiding meditative absorption (samādhi);
it is free from the stain of otherness regarding that which is to be purified, and is established as a mere fraction [of the ultimate]. (1798)
Having reflected upon the purpose of the divine body, one should lead [the breath] into the immersion in nectar,
having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī power whose sole nature is nectar.
One should meditate upon the divine portion (devakalā) being sprinkled by the flow of nectar arising therefrom;
having prepared a seat within the heart, one should cause the self in the form of the deity (mūrti) to enter into it.
Having performed the replenishment once more, one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
It is considered the threefold duty of recitation to chant the root mantra ten times for each of the limbs.
When an action is performed even without the thumb, it yields its fruit;
likewise, [the merit of] supporting the head, the ear, and ten crores [of other acts] is likewise fruitful. || 1802 ||
Bound at the neck with a hundred crores and bound by the month for a thousand [years],
Pārvatī, having become the sacrificial oblation, sang through the attainment of knowledge. (1803)
The *uttamottamaka* consists merely of the connection with *jñāna*; it measures eight *tālas*, is characterized by feet repeatedly bent, and features the left leg extended upward.

The Karaṅka gesture is performed with the left hand; that movement which is turned back by those who know the rules should be employed in the *navanīta* (butter) circular motion (*vṛtta*) [in the *sūkṣma* dance]. || 1805 ||
It has been described in various ways, specifically regarding internal and external [forms];
among the liṅgas and temples, each superior type is proclaimed as the most excellent.
Having performed circumambulation within the womb [of the temple], one must not do so outside, as it would involve many faults;
for within the womb, there may be the shadow of the Liṅga, the remains of offerings (nirmālya), and impurities.
Having avoided the *somasūtra*, the *mūla*, and proximity to a deity—if all of that is indeed conducive to every fruit. (1808)
Within the area of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala), there is also the Soma-line;
it may be equal in measure to the temple, or exactly the same as the temple itself.
Even amidst a heap of discarded flower offerings, the shadow of the temple remains;
having avoided all such things, one should then perform the circumambulation.
One should perform the circumambulation by way of the left and the right, moving upward;
or rather, the circumambulation should be performed by way of the left and the right.
The region of Caṇḍeśa should be on the left, and the other, the Soma-sūtra, on the right;
one should perform the circumambulation by way of both the left and the right, or [alternatively] by way of the right alone.
The left side should be the region of Caṇḍa, and the other the Soma-thread;
one should perform [the practice] with gentle movement along the paths of the right and the left.
In this manner, there should be circumambulation to the left and to the right for the sake of the eternal internal festival;
and there is another circumambulation of the limbs, which is endless from its rising to its setting.
The merit of these two shines forth, yet it cannot be fully described due to its many qualities;
one should know that to be the majesty of the sacred field (kṣetra), and that shall be the fruit for the gods.
