The line for the expansion of the *dhāman* should be equal to the line of the *soma*; it should be situated in the direction of the *soma* of the *soma*. Beyond the line, there should be no overstepping. || 1816 ||
A man who passes through the shadow of Shiva’s temple or through its precincts does not incur any fault, even if he has committed a very grave transgression. || 1817 ||
He who covers a Liṅga with his shadow, or a temple with his shadow, while the Liṅga is in the shadow of the temple, shall undoubtedly go to hell along with his wife and his sons. (1818)
This is declared to be the pedestal for offerings (balipīṭha); here the five liṅgas are described, belonging to both women and men who are devoted to Śiva without pride. (1819)
One should first recite the mantra of Śiva beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the respective name for each;
however, one should place one's own name in the middle of that Śiva-mantra.
Uttering the third mantra, "Śiva," for the sake of his devotees—
he recites it for the rite of pacification (śāntika) in the morning, and for the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) in the evening.
One should perform the optional rite during the midday; one should not step over the shadow of a dwelling.
In the case of an optional circumambulation, one should perform it clockwise along one's own path.

O Brahmin, it grants success within six months; through the rite of pacification (śāntika), there is great fruit, while the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) is proclaimed to yield results within eight months.

Having performed the worship for one year, which fulfills all desires and grants the accomplishment of every goal, the remainder [of the recitation] is performed in the midst of the assembly of the Gaṇas, in the sequence beginning with Aries (Meṣa) and ending with Virgo (Kanyā). The mantra consisting of twenty-eight [syllables] is known as the Mālāmantra. || 1825 ||
The garland of mantras bestows success in old age; the mantras themselves [bestow success] in youth;
those consisting of more than five syllables bestow success in childhood; and all others [bestow success] at other times.
Those ending in *strī*, *ntrā*, *vahni*, and *jānta*, as well as those ending in *namas*, are feminine;
the neuter [mantras] are those ending in *napuṃsaka*; and the remaining ones are said to be masculine. Thus ends the section on the classification of genders. || 1827 ||

The classes of mantras; the goal to be accomplished; for the sake of success in recitations and other rites, there is the worship of the three [deities] and the libation performed by those born [into the lineage]; well-accomplished through the mantra of recitation, it serves the purpose of the practitioner. || 1828 ||

The enemy is destroyed; the Smṛti states that [mantras] with the color of the enemy destroy the mantras. Susiddha: the rites of recitation, worship, and so forth are accomplished by the mantra. || 1829 ||
For that supreme practitioner, all mantras constitute half-accomplishment and grant success everywhere; through the mastery of even a single-syllable mantra, one attains ten lakhs of recitations.

Regarding the recitation and so forth: one should perform the recitation of the syllables and the rosary according to reason and in due order. In this way, one should perform the recitation of the seed-syllable; likewise, it should be doubled. || 1831 ||

By way of number: those ending with "svāhā" and "namaḥ" are known as feminine; those ending with "namas" are neuter; and those ending with "viśeṣa" are masculine. For the rites of subjugation, eradication, and inciting enmity, as well as for minor magical acts, masculine mantras are prescribed.
The Revatī [constellation] removes diseases, while the Karṇikā [constellation] elsewhere renders one impotent.
One should know that recitation performed at home yields an equal result, whereas in a temple it becomes a hundredfold.
In a meritorious forest or a grove, it is said that the merit is a thousandfold;
on a mountain, the merit is ten thousandfold; by a river, it is declared to be a hundred thousandfold.
(127) It is declared that in a temple of ten million deities, [the worship] is infinite in my presence;
likewise before the sun, before the Guru, before Indra, and before the lamp and water. || 1835 ||
In the presence of both Brahmins and cows, by his splendor, that [image] facing eastward was worshipped, as was the southern one with eight attendants. || 1836 ||
One should know the western [direction] as *dhanaya* and the northern as *śāntika*.
She wears a turban and a bodice, with her hair loose and covering her neck.
One who has performed an impure act, one who is pure [after bathing], or one who has applied ointments should never recite [the mantra].
Likewise, one suffering from thirst, fatigue, hunger, or exhaustion, nor one who is terrified by a formidable forest. || 1838 ||
One should avoid looking at corpses during the practice of recitation; if they appear while one is fasting, one should remember this verse with a composed mind.
One seeking liberation should employ the thumb; for malevolent rites, the index finger; for nourishment, having placed the middle finger; and for rites of pacification, the ring finger.
The drawing-in of the little finger is taught, or likewise that of the ring finger in all cases;
one should employ all these for cruel rites at the time of rain.
In summer one should perform the rite of causing enmity; in the rainy season, it becomes the rite of expulsion;
in the winter one should perform the rite of killing; likewise, when the sun is in Virgo.
Having uttered the *japāṃśu* (the portion for silent recitation), one should employ the *teja paiśācika* (fiery spirit-force) in the rite of *homakarma*;
however, when the mantra is recited [audibly], it is declared that this applies to all mantras. || 1843 ||
Recitation is said to be fourfold for all who desire to perform recitation: mental, that which reaches the ears, whispering, and the clearly articulated. || 1844 ||

The audible (vyakta) is ten times [the value of] the whispered (upāṃśu); from that, the lip-muttered (aṣṭaka) is a hundredfold; the mental (mānasa) is a thousandfold compared to that; now hear about the finger-counting and other forms of recitation.

In the detailed classification: counting with the fingers, with knots on *kuśa* grass, or with a container—these are equal in their fruit. Through such recitation, one should constantly [worship] the deity. 1846.

If one performs it oneself, [the merit] becomes pleasing; it is said to be sixfold when performed by the thumb, tenfold greater when performed with blades of *darbha* grass, and a hundredfold when using *kuśa* grass with knots. || 1847 ||
With coral, [the merit is] one thousandfold; with gems, ten thousandfold;
with pearls, it is said to be one hundred thousandfold; and with lotus seeds, it is multiplied by ten million.
With rudrākṣas, however, none [of those defects] exists. Now listen as I describe the origin of the rudrākṣa; it occurred after thousands of divine years. || 1849 ||
The eye was opened by me; it releases, it releases from the eyes—therefore it is called *rudrākṣa*. A single vajra is Śiva himself. || 1850 ||
The fruit resulting from its retention is infinite. Wherever that practitioner dies, he goes to the supreme goal. It is said that the two-faced one is Śakti. || 1851 ||
The three-faced is indeed Nāda; the four-faced is Bindu;
the five-faced is Sadāśiva;
the six-faced is declared to be Īśvara; and Rudra is remembered as the seven-faced. || 1852 ||
Likewise, for Viṣṇu it is eight lotuses, and for the Four-faced One (Brahmā) nine lotuses;
from nine faces down to one face, the fruit increases a hundredfold at each step.
By applying the sacred ash to the hands, throat, and head, and by maintaining it on the neck,
one is liberated from past sins and attains union with Śiva.
The sight of it destroys sin, while its touch bestows all perfections;
one should always wear the Rudrākṣa, which is meritorious even when first gathered before being consecrated.
By consuming Rudrākṣa at the three junctions of the day at the time of departure, one attains the state of Rudra; there is no further rebirth.
Thus it is said in the Vijaya-tantra:
"Twenty-five [recitations] are for the sake of liberation; twenty-eight are for nourishment. (1857)
The rosary for recitation should be made with thirty beads for the attainment of wealth, fifty for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), and it should be consecrated in every way by all the *Śambaras*.
From drawing together the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, the highest accomplishment is attained;
from the union of the thumb and the index finger, the middling accomplishment is desired. (1859)

From the joining of the little finger and the thumb, the least accomplishment is said to be attained; the recitation for the ancillary mantras should be performed at one-tenth the measure of the root mantra—this is the view of the three [traditions]. (1860)
When an action is performed without the thumb, it yields its fruit;
[if performed] with the head, it is ten millionfold, and at the ears, it is one hundred millionfold.
A hundred crores bound around the neck and a thousand bonds of fetters—therein lies the fruit. || 1862 ||
One should know that a line [of sesame seeds] yields eightfold merit; with lamps for sons and fruits, tenfold;
with conch-shells and gems, a hundredfold; and with coral, a thousandfold.

A rosary of pearls yields a hundred thousandfold merit, one of lotus seeds is said to yield ten millionfold, and a rosary of rudrākṣa beads likewise bestows infinite fruit upon the recitation of mantras.
Through constant recitation, the deity becomes pleased after a hundred measures; once pleased, the eternal state described in the Udyāga is attained through the initial ritual procedures. (1865)
That which was inhabited by terrifying yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, house-snakes, and the like,
has now become entirely endowed with freedom from fear.
(129) That specific merit which was performed through recitation for the destruction of evil throughout successive births— by that recitation, one conquers diseases and attains liberation. || 1867 ||
Through recitation, one attains both accomplishment and liberation;
this [practice], which consists of grace, has been taught for those with passion within the home.

Having offered the herd of cows to the pen, and likewise having accepted what was not to be taken from the house, he took the best portion of the vessels and went to the tavern to procure liquor. || 1869 ||
If the lord of the field is benevolent toward the house of another's wife, he brings constant and unshakeable happiness; if he is neutral, there is a single waist-belt in the middle. || 1870 ||
Having written this supreme wheel of grace in a year, one should worship it;
therein, with all one's soul, one should diligently apply safflower [to the drawing], and one becomes the most excellent of all. || 1871 ||
In the world of men, he comes under one's control; one should place [the deities] on the left and right sides of the surface of Kāma and Indra, honored by the Three Forms (Trimūrti).
In the space between those arrows, one should draw the seed-syllable of Śrītārā; then, surrounding it on all sides, [one draws] an eight-petaled lotus. || 1873 ||
In the lotus mandalas of the [deities'] hands, one should place in reverse order: *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ* at the tips of their petals, *oṃ yūṃ* on the outer edges, and *śrī* at the three abodes. || 1874 ||
The syllable *hrīṃ* should be in the center of the moon, above which is a circle complete with sixteen vowels; on the outside, there should be the form of a lotus, like the sun.

It is accompanied by the *sānta* (the letter *s*) and joined with the *yānta* (the letter *y*) and so forth; outside of that, it is encircled by the sun, accompanied by Hari and Hara, and joined with the root mantra. || 1876 ||
I bow to the King of Yantras, which directly brings the three worlds under control and removes all poisons; it has one hundred, twenty, nine, and eight petals. || 1877 ||
Immediately after that, one should place the seed-syllable of Madhyendra, followed by a thousand "jaḍa" syllables accompanied by vowels, and the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center of the moon. || 1878 ||
The moon of wisdom is the discus; it rests upon a perfectly clear lotus, held in both hands along with two full vases. || 1879 ||
Holding a Veda and a rosary in his two lotus-like hands, and carrying at the ends of his arms two jars filled with blue [lotuses], he listens while resting his head upon them.
May she, who bears the moon-digit as her kinsman and assumes the form of the two gods (Śiva and Viṣṇu), enter you all, bestowing the glory of the entire multitude of kalpas. 1881.
The prosperity that has emerged from the mouth of the Bindu is the cause for attaining sovereign power over one's own domain; it is perceived here day after day. || 1882 ||
O noble one with the three-cornered [forehead], it is impossible for men to ever perceive or even conceive of the tree that can be climbed by you during the days of sacrifice. || 1883 ||
Having drawn two sets of sixteen and fourteen spokes,
a lotus with sixty-four petals, and three circles as its limbs, one should place a triangle in the center.
I bow to the Cakra. The Śrīdevī then states the following verse:
"One should write one [syllable] as before, in each of the directions starting from the exterior. (1885)

One should write [the syllables] separately; then [the syllable] ending in *vaṣaṭ*, followed by *moda* and the *mātrā*. [This] is situated in the middle of the jar (*ghaṭa*), and again placed within the hollow of a lotus (*padmapuṭa*). || 1886 ||
In all rites for pacification, this wheel which is benevolent in nature is the most excellent of all wheels; [it should be drawn] on white cloth or birch bark. || 1887 ||
Or else, on a beautiful cloth, when there is an auspicious conjunction of day and lunar mansion, one should draw the wheel with parched grain or saffron. || 1888 ||
Having become firm, he [faced] the direction of the Lord of the Gods; having made Rudraḍaṃ his finger-guard, it was praised as being like a lac-colored finger-ring. || 1889 ||
That by which this is constantly meditated upon does not approach that man with death;
having uttered "hāṃ hrīṃ," it always bestows nourishment and power against irregular fevers. (1890)
One should specifically perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
it is prescribed that one should worship [the deities] beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namaḥ."
They hold skull-bowls and tridents, and are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
they have the appearance of dark blue clouds, possess three eyes, and have the moon as their crest-ornament.
The goddess who removes all obstacles has been described, as well as the other eight Bhairavas,
[who dwell] in these villages, cities, towns, and houses.
In crossroads, cremation grounds, and halls, he beheld the elephant-riding one—
three-eyed, eight-armed, fierce, with hair standing erect and prominent tusks.
Raudra is of a blackish hue and possesses contentment; he has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, holds a human head and a dhattūra flower, and wears a snake as a sacred thread.
In his right hands, he holds a conjoined pair of leaves, a discus, a spear, an earring, a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, and a Pināka bow. || 1896 ||
In his hands, he holds a skull, a bow, a bell, and a noose;
he is adorned with all ornaments, steadfast, and indeed possesses a banner and a garland.
Seated upon a matured pedestal, joined by Nāgas and Nāgāmbaras—
thus indeed shall the true form of Kṣetrapāla be described.
One should perform the application and worship with the mudrās at the end of the mantra: the lotus, the trident, the bud, the *niṣṭūra*, and the vulva-conch. || 1898 ||
p.
131) The meditation on Mātaṅgī: Her fingers, like sprouts, are dancing according to the *tāntra* [rhythm], and she is adorned with *tāpiñca* [flowers].
O Lord, Mother Prabhā, adorned with a crest-jewel of youth— || 1899 ||

O Mother, who possesses all splendor, whose heavy braid of hair is filled with swans, cranes, and peacocks, and who brings about the destruction of worldly existence—[protect] the two sons of Mata and Śamataṅga. || 1900 ||
They behold her with splendor; [I] behold Vārāhī’s mantra, with three eyes, a crystal water-pot, and a rosary. 1901.
Her four arms are adorned with the splendor of books and rosaries;
she wears white and black garments and is graced with white perfumes and flowers. || 1902 ||
I bow to Vāṇī, who is seated upon a white lotus,
who is tranquil, whose waters are known as the Śāta, and who possesses the vast splendor of a sprout.
Her form in the assembly inspires confidence; her speech is gracious, sweet, and pleasing to those in distress. || 1904 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain King, the eighth [letter] with its third [consonant], conjoined with the fourteenth, is indeed the manifest form of Chinnovī. 1905.
This indeed is called the *daṇḍakuṇḍala* [mudrā] of Sarasvatī;
I shall now describe the meditation on the Goddess, which accomplishes the fulfillment of all purposes.
Seated comfortably in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, she possesses a pure smile,
is red in color, exceedingly gracious, and adorned with all ornaments.
She has three eyes and a beautiful crown, adorned with the crescent moon as an ornament;
she shines with necklaces, anklets, armlets, and high waistbands.
Adorned with pearls, rubies, and lapis lazuli, accompanied by elephants,
wearing jeweled ornaments, and decorated with gemstone earrings.
She wears various jeweled bracelets and beautiful, multicolored bangles;
she holds a noose and a goad, and is intent upon granting boons and fearlessness.
She held a rosary of seeds and, out of compassion for living beings, was being fanned with two chowries; she was Caṇḍikā, adorned with a parasol.
She was served at the soles of her feet by the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma;
thereafter, she took up the great sound which was the color of fire.
This supreme mantra, which bestows the activity of speech and accomplishes all desires and goals, was proclaimed and spoken by Śambhu in the past.
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā; its meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
Ambikā is declared to be the deity, and Mahādeva is the presiding divinity. (1914)
They say that Brahmā is the first, and Viṣṇu immediately after him;
beyond him, they indeed speak of Mahādeva as the deity. (1915)
Some say the deity is Durgā, while others say it is the Mother-goddesses; others speak of her as Vāgdevī, and likewise others know her as Lakṣmī. (1916)
Others say he is Āditya; others praise him as Jyeṣṭhā.
What is the use of saying more on this matter? Śiva consists of all the gods.
Having one hand or four hands, adorned with all ornaments,
with broad hips, a slender waist, and elevated breasts.
Having meditated upon Manonmanī, who is endowed with the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and possesses auspicious characteristics,
the wise one should worship her for the sake of bringing joy to the world.
O you whose eyelashes are dark like a young leaf, would your eye be like a lotus, with its hand-like rays extended and lofty? || 1920 ||
O best of beings, listen to that which is renowned as the Śaivika Śāntika.
The left hand of the God is joined to the hip of the Goddess;
furthermore, Gaurī should hold a lotus in her own right hand.
The left hand is indeed hanging down; this is the certain conclusion regarding the specific [feature].
This is known as Umāmaheśvara, and it is called the dialogue with Gaurī. || 1923 ||
One should perform everything as previously described; the specific detail is now stated:
with the right hand of the god, he enters the breast of the goddess.
O twice-born one, listen with favor to this dialogue between Umā and Śiva, which is joined by inner devotion and concerns the intermediate state between those two. 1925.
Indeed, there is some slight distinction between Umā and Maheśa;
for that [part] of the God which is in his right hand resides in Bhavānī, while [the part] in the moon resides in [himself]. 1926.
In this [context], the grace of Umā alone has been clearly proclaimed for everyone;
thus, the fourfold division of Candradhara has been celebrated. 1927.
He who is called Candraśekhara is also said to be Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Dakṣiṇeśa; listen to the two-fold [teaching]. 1928.
Three-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, of gentle form, with a smiling face;
wearing a black antelope skin as a garment and an upper cloth of tiger-skin;
and having joined together two flowers—the moon and the sun—as a lion’s mouth.
Whether joined together, scattered, or bound with bamboo joints.
He is endowed with glossy locks of hair, or else possessed of matted locks;
in his left hand, he holds a book that is one long finger-breadth in size.
In the right hand there is a rosary, while in the left hand there is fire;
the left hand is joined with the right hand which holds a rosary in the form of a prayer-bead string.
When the subtle body is established, the vital breaths (prāṇas) remain; meditation joined with this brings auspiciousness.
When one is somewhat joined with this, strength is united throughout all the limbs. (1933)
Lying with the right foot, knee, thigh, and head upwards, accompanied by the left foot—this form has been fully described; now hear about the *laṃbasūtra*.
One should arrange them one above the other, extending to a length of twelve finger-breadths:
Agastya, Pulastya, Viśvāmitra, and Gautama.
One should cause the light of yoga practice to shine forth according to the prescribed rules;
thus one becomes Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Now hear about Gaiyamūrti.
The left hand with the bracelet is called the *nāgayajña*;
likewise, the left hand with its face turned upward is so designated. (1937)
One should place the right foot upon the top of the thigh, positioning it there in two parts;
the entire hand [should rest] on the hip, and the left hand above that.
The left thigh is said to be one *kalā* in measure, while the portion from the hip upwards is known as the length of the staff (*daṇḍāyāma*); its width should be one *kolaka*.
The mouth of the *lāmbu* should be six finger-breadths in height;
the bamboo staff (*vaṃśaka*) should be at the wrist-joint (*kaṭaka*), and the *hikkā* should be immediately after the middle.

It is said that it measures five or six finger-breadths; the wise one should know that the distance from the navel to the binding of the cord on the right side is equal to the length of the face. (1941)
One should again visualize [the deity] as seated, standing, or even mounted on a vehicle;
thus is the specific mantra taught, while the remainder of the explanation is like that of the [Mūla-]mūrti.
Now listen to the description of Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the form of a bull;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Bull-vehicled One (Vṛṣavāhana).

The wise practitioner should place the God, accompanied by Bhavānī, upon the pedestal; He is mounted on a bull, is of two forms, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the Brahmins. 1944.
Having placed the bull behind him, [he is] endowed with the characteristics as before, four-armed, three-eyed, and joined with matted hair and a crown. 1945.
Right here is the substance-ornament, endowed with all ornaments;
it has a white sacred thread, a peaceful form, and a smiling face.
Having grasped an axe in the right [hand], one should place a deer or a piece of meat;
or alternatively, a bracelet on the left hand or on the forearm of the left hand.
In that hand, however, one should hold the wing or the banner facing downwards;
the tip of its middle finger shall be level with the line of the navel.
One should perform it thus for the sake of enjoyment; now, that which is for the sake of liberation is described:
[the deity] has three eyes, four arms, is peaceful, and is endowed with all ornaments. (1949)
With a braid-like arrangement [of the hair], one should fashion a crown; then, either to the south or in front of the temple, one should again cause a pavilion to be constructed. (1950)

Or, according to the measurement of the extent of the hearths (dhiṣṇya), one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule, either half of that, double that, or in the middle of the footprint on all sides.
One should construct a square pit in the east, one shaped like a bow in the south,
a circular pit in the west, and a lotus-shaped pit in the north.
In the middle of the three [fires], one should fashion a circular primary altar for Īśāna; or, according to the rule, it should be in the center of the eastern fire-pit's altar or in the fire itself.
The Vāstu-homa should be performed; carry out the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa). At the conclusion of that, having cast the bali-offering, [present] pure food combined with curd.
One should sprinkle with the *puruṣa* mantra and again perform the *puṇyāha* rite.
The *śiva-kumbha* (Śiva-pitcher) should be in the center, while the *śakti* (pitcher) is to its left.
In the eastern pitcher during the month of Kārtika, one should worship Maheśvara in the southern pitcher,
Murāri in the western pitcher, or indeed Ardhanārīśa.
In the ritual arrangement of Madhyamārīśa, the distinction regarding the water-pot (kumbha) is stated here:
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with its proper characteristics upon the Vardhanī vessel.
One should place Brahmā in the northern pitcher along with the Śaktis and their companions;
then, from the east to the northeast, one should install the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their soldiers.

She also [offered] three water-pots filled with water, containing *kūrca* grass, grains, and cloth; and on the back of the one released from the interval between the staffs, the five-fold [mantra]. || 1959 ||
Outside the base of the interval between the staffs; or else, the establishment of the banner within that space of six staffs for the ten [deities] is thus described. || 1960 ||
If the base is thick, it is a woman; if the tip is thick, it is a eunuch;
and if it is equal from base to tip, it is a man—such is the characteristic by means of the *darbha* grass.
Kuśa, kāśa, as well as dūrvā, vrīhi, mocchiya,
viśvāmitra, and uśīra— these are proclaimed to be the seven types of darbha grass.
A vessel for receiving guests should be made of *darbha* grass, eighteen finger-breadths in length and equal [in width];
here, a knot of four finger-breadths at its midpoint is considered superior, middling, or inferior according as it is half that size.
The *kūrca* [bundle of grass]: one should know that Brahmā resides at the root of the *kuśa* grass, Keśava in the middle of the *kuśa*, and Śaṅkara at the tip of the *kuśa*. || 1964 ||

The deities are the intellect (dhi). It is recorded in the Smṛti that one should fashion a *kūrca* from twenty-five blades of *darbha* grass; it is made with ten and five [blades] in the middle, and with nine *darbha* blades.
One should place the *kanyasa* [finger] upward;
from there, the *kūrca* [hand-gesture], and the *antaḥ-kūrca* must be performed—this is indeed the meaning of the *arthāma*. || 1966 ||
The *kūrca* should be known to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and likewise [inferior].
For a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), it consists of two *darbha* blades; for householders (*grahastayaḥ*), it consists of three *darbha* blades. (1967)
For a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), five kuśa blades; for a mendicant (bhikṣuka), seven.
This is declared by Dakṣiṇāvarta as the ornament for the hand that holds the purifier (apavitra). || 1968 ||
The ring is said to be two finger-breadths [in width], the knot should be one finger-breadth;
at the tip it is four finger-breadths, and [the rest] seven... 1969.
The deities of Sarasvatī and the other Śaktis are declared by the wise to be "adaiva" (without a presiding deity). || 1970 ||
In the left nostril, on the left side of the bathing pedestal, likewise in the left navel, the right thigh, and the middle of the right ankle. (1971)

One should obtain an equal division from the line; however, on the left side, there should be a portion from that line to the middle of the breasts, which is proclaimed to be three finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the thread, four finger-breadths to the south is the middle;
from that thread, four finger-breadths to the south of the knee is the center of the altar. || 1973 ||
From the right thumb of that [hand] along the thread, it is traditionally taught to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
from the left thumb along the thread, it shall be seven and a half finger-breadths.

while the circumference of the left hand at the wrist is four finger-breadths on the outside.
Śroṇa, the distance from the wrist to the end of the forearm should be two finger-breadths plus one finger;
[she has] plump thighs, plump * * * * * * * and a slender waist. (1977)
Whether seated or standing, even when not explicitly stated, one should follow the sequence as previously described;
one should increase [the measurement] threefold from the hairline, the ears, the knees, and the soles of the feet.

on the thighs, one should increase the distance by four barley-corns, avoiding the regions that must be excluded.
One should always arrange the three-fold measurement for all [types of] stones;
it should be twice the height of the liṅga, and [the measurement] from the material should be sixteen parts.

One should take the auspicious qualities from the inferior; one should properly perform everything, including that which is joined with the base and the minor, as well as what is superior to curd and that of the Goddess. 1981.

thereafter, the height of the Āryā-devī in the primary image (mūlabera) shall be— || 1983 ||

Then, having obtained materials such as stone or clay, one should fashion an image;

O Goddess, according to the prescribed rule, one should determine the height starting from the ground-level (sudhāmādi); that should be done either by the *sadyāda* finger-measure (*mānāṅgula*) or by the *mātrā* finger-measure (*mātrāṅgula*), and one should thus fashion the shadow of the house for all of them.

The goddess is clothed in fine linen (dukūla), adorned with a jeweled crown, joined by two hands in the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā), and holding a noose and a goad. || 1994 ||
Having two arms or two eyes, and endowed with hanging hands, she is described as being at the time of commencing the act of seizing a full-blown flower. || 1995 ||
As previously stated by the Sage regarding the purification of the eyes:

Lavaṅga, karpūra, and the three fruits (phalatraya), powdered in equal proportions and combined with honey and sugar—this is dear to Śiva, a destroyer of sins, and purifying. || 1999 ||
He dwelt there in that supreme, stainless place.
Liṅgamudrā, Namaskārā, the one called Nālā, Śaṅkhamudrikā, Surabhī, Mukulī, Avāhinī, and Niṣṭhurā. (2000)
Having personally witnessed that which was proclaimed,
one should perform the auspicious rites in due order, including the golden auspicious threads and the peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma).

One should perform [the ritual] for me, beginning from the conclusion of the *kautuka* and ending with the conclusion of the sacrifice;
it has six lineages, one heart, four faces, and four supports. (2003)
On the earth, they know the Vāstupuruṣa to be bent over with his head toward the east; the deities known by the names mentioned by Ārya are to be understood as residing in his head. (2004)
The right arm of Savitrī is called the *kūja*, while the armpit (*kakṣa*) of Savitrī is said to be the *tāpavatsa*; that same *kakṣa* is the left arm.
The right side is to be made as Viśvasvī, the left side as Mahīdhara, and the center as consisting of Brahmā; O Mitra, this is prescribed as the first procedure.
Indra and Indrarāja are said to be the right foot; Rudra and Urujayī are the left foot, and likewise Śaiva is the face. (2007)
In the middle third of the site-plan, the Vaśa [deity] faces the six directions, east and north;
in the center of the site are the protective enclosures (varmaṇi), and Brahmā is said to be the heart.
The Niṣkuṭa and Aṃśasvaras are to be known as such; likewise, among these, the Pūruṣa is the lord who brings about auspicious and inauspicious results for men in every house. (2009)
One should not cause the knowledge of those limbs to oppress the limbs of the house;
for they, when properly maintained, attain their respective masters according to their numerical order from the very beginning.
Therefore, a wise person should by all means perform the propitiation of the forty-five deities within the enclosure.
The manifestation of the face of the river along with her consort is here called *āvāhana* (invocation);
the settling of the devotees therein is declared by the wise to be *sthāpana* (installation). || 2012 ||
(138) One who, though devoid of the twilight rituals and the like, should thus abandon his body while fully absorbed in meditation;
Having extracted [the mantra] beginning with "kulasvajanam" and so forth, one should worship Śiva.
One attains a state adorned with faith equal to that [merit] through Maghā, even as it is filled with riches;
for among all beings, consciousness is said to be sound. || 2014 ||
For the sake of realizing that which exists as consciousness—whether in the form of sound or otherwise—for one who abides within the limbs of the self of Śiva. || 2015 ||
One should perform that rite with the sound of beating a drum,
just as one sprinkles water upon gold to bring out its brilliance of molten gold.

[otherwise] the twilight rite would be devoid of its lamp. || 2017 ||
If the twilight rite is performed without a lamp, one should then plant [the offering] twice as much;
otherwise, by such transgression, the entire mantra becomes fruitless.
Then, having performed the *śāntihoma* (peace-offering), one should recite the root mantra a hundred times. O Kāraṇa,
if the offering of food and other requisites is omitted, famine will certainly afflict the land.
If one is devoid of the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*), one should give that substance doubled;
and if one is devoid of both twilights, one should perform the auspicious consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
On the first day, when free from grief, perform the consecration with droṇa-measures of milk;
on the fifth day, perform the *śakti*-oblation; and on the tenth day, perform the ceremonial bath.
If more than a month has elapsed and [the image] is deficient, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa).
Having performed the ceremonial bathing (snapana), one should then carry out the worship as prescribed.
If one has died without the lamp of nirvāṇa, one should perform the rites prescribed for the world;
if it was deficient by one cause, one should then plant twice as many.
Perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) on the fifth day and the ceremonial bath (snapana) on the tenth day;
if the worship of the gateway is omitted, there will be the destruction of the crops.
One should recite the mantra of the deities stationed at the door one hundred times,
and worship them as before with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
If the daily offerings and festivals are omitted, one should deposit grain [in the image];
if even the twilight rites are omitted, one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having recited the root mantra one hundred times, perform the festival as before;
and when the two junctions [of time] have passed, one should perform the two rites of pacification.
If the five-day festival is deficient, one should perform the *mūrtihoma*;
one should cause the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) of Śambhu to be performed and worship him with special care.

139) In the monthly festival, whether it be deficient or complete, [the worship is performed] with musical instruments, the five Brahmans, the six limbs, the primary seed-syllables, and the ten-syllable [mantra]. || 2029 ||
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred times for each [item], that substance shall become twofold [in efficacy].

for if the ninefold food offering (navanaivedya) is omitted, famine arises upon the earth.
Then, having performed the *mūrti-homa*, one should feed the Brahmins;
having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite of worship, one should offer abundant sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
If the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) is omitted, a great plague breaks out;
therefore, having performed the ten-fold oblation (dāśāhoma), one should cause the bathing of the Lord to be performed.
If the Pavitrārohaṇa rite is omitted when it ought to be performed, the wise man [should know the omen];
if the Kṛttikās are devoid of lamps, there will be drought. (2035)
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śānti-homa), one should cause the bathing of the Lord to be performed;
having worshipped Him thoroughly according to the prescribed rites of worship, one should present abundant sacrificial oblations.
When the month of Āśleṣā arrives, one should perform the Kṛttikā-lamp rite;
a black lamp made of stone is recommended, while one made of gold is most auspicious and beautiful.
On a black stone, a red dot; on a black stone, a black [dot] removes all defects. On a black stone, [dots] that are red, yellow, white, and likewise yellow [are effective]. (2037)

On a white mountain, [the stone] should be white or yellow; on a white [mountain], it should be white, and there will be happiness. On a black mountain, however, according to the doctrine of Vṛddhamaya, it should especially be three-colored. || 2038 ||
Resembling the leaf of the *kharjūra* palm, it is full, auspicious in form,
with the circumference of its linga and pedestal equal to the breadth of its span, extending as far as the range of an arrow's flight.
The *tuṅgaka* [is so called]; then the *vistṛtārtha*; then the *gomukhāyata*; then the *gomukhānta*; and then the *karṇanāsa*. || 2040 ||
Having divided the eightfold measurement of the *liṅga*—excluding one part from the *rāla* and the *tantu-liṅga*—there is *bhoga*. || 2041 ||
It is better that this be accomplished by oneself; indeed, liberation is equal to the *liṅga* itself, arising from the center of the pericarp situated upon this [seat]. (2042)
Four-armed and three-eyed, resembling a thousand suns,
wearing a tiger-skin garment and likewise smeared with ashes. (2043)
A mass of tangled matted hair, beautified by its own agitation;
likewise, the *dhuddhūra* flower, the *arkapuṣpa*, and the *lakṣmapuṣpa*. || 2044 ||
One should always place the *dhātṛ* on the path, *dakṣagaṅgādharahara* on the head,
*kara* in the middle of the forehead, and *vahabandhana* on the brow.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and even ear-ornaments, as well as with delightful anklets on her feet, she was beautified by various flowers.
He has the sacrificial thread as his upper garment and is endowed with the application of sacred ash;
he holds a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in his right hand and likewise a fire in his left hand.
In his right hand he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and in his left hand a staff-like arm;
his right foot is white, and his left foot is likewise raised.
Yogis who have perfected the qualities of meditative concentration and have reached the further shore of reality should always meditate upon the God whose form is supreme bliss.
The hundred-thousandfold [scripture], which is supreme, infinite, and a form of the supreme dance;
wonderful, immortal, true, most secret, auspicious, and beautiful. (2050)
It is the supreme, the infinite, the form of the supreme dance;
it is the wonderful, the immortal, the truth, the most secret, the auspicious, and the beautiful.
"Salutations to all at the time of twilight; this is the extraction of the supreme dwelling.
Thus one should worship the God, and the kingdom shall become most beautiful. (2052)
Thus, this secret bath is prescribed for all the gods for one who possesses a serene mind, who is righteous, and who has offered oblations into the fire.
The Īśvara-cakra is the support, and the Liṅga is called Sādākhya. It is said that the Nada of the Śaktis, who are the consorts, is the producer of bliss. || 2054 ||
It is also said that he was born from Śiva by the name Tāṇḍava. || 2055 ||
In the *Śrīmadviśvāsakārikā*: "When, at the time of ascending, the fruit faces toward the height of one's hope... (2056).
If it is obstructed at the ascent, O Guide, then the fault lies with the step.
The leaf is Brahmā, the betel nut is Viṣṇu, and the lime-powder is Maheśvara;
O God, you are pleased by that, for the gift of tāmbūla is supreme. (2058)
A celibate student, an ascetic, and a forest-dweller are inauspicious;
chewing betel-leaf and giving sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are equal to the eating of cow-flesh.
Having taken refuge at Īśakarṇa, Vāsukī [is located] to the east of the god's face, and Pavanāśana is the Kṣetrapālaka in the northeast.
The deity faces south, whether in the field or in the region of the wind;
the door is to the west of the deity, and the guardian of the field is in the southeast.
The gods face north, while Kṣetrapāla is in the southwest;
this location should be established, for other locations lead to destruction. || 2062 ||
"Having established the sacrificer among the directions beginning with the east, [one effects] the destruction of the king and his kingdom"—thus it is stated in the Kāmika-tantra. || 2063 ||
If the deities are invoked into the consciousness that exists in the form of the liṅga, then upon their entry, do they enter into the interior of that deity? (2064)
Just as fire arises from the friction of the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*) when the fuel is well-prepared, the deity dwells there through the mental disposition of the teacher (*deśika*). (2065)
By means of a cloth, a wooden staff, a rope, or a garland of darbha grass, why would one cause [the deity] to enter through a single door above the pedestal? What is the purpose? || 2066 ||
Divided by twenty, with sixty-four parts increased by four [yugas], there is a lotus; outside, there are four walkways in every direction.
In the *dvārāṃśa* and *vasvaṃśaka*, on its side is the *vasuliṅgaka*; the *giripada* and *giripada* are joined with the *vedas*. In the corners— || 2068 ||
Having trimmed the creepers, one should make them very beautiful, just as in the illustrious Śvetapura, O Brahmin, [there were] two hundred of the best of Brahmins. (2069)
These ten, indeed, were enumerated for the sake of Śiva by the Sacrificer himself:
the cow, the eater, the alms-offering, the protection of the *sāla* tree, and the bird on the branch. || 2070 ||
And the rearing of deer; and at night, [he should avoid] children, those who are not desired, trees, the depositing of wealth, and the tending of cattle; [and] procreation... || 2071 ||

The family physician who protects and nourishes, who removes the thorns [of disease] and provides relief; he avoids persistent afflictions, is like gold, and gives the oil of the *kappaṭa* plant. (2072)

The protection of the helpless, the wretched, the blind, and the distressed; the education of princes; the establishment of the rules of conduct; and the treatise on the investigation of the meaning of the ancient Dharma. || 2073 ||
Exegesis and the study of the Vedas are Dharma; these they know to be the thirty-two-fold Dharma that comprises all the worlds. || 2074 ||
In Śrīmadvyāghrapura, in Śiraḥpura, in the illustrious Kumārāpura, situated in the glorious Brahmapura, in Arjunavana, in Śvetāvana, and in Kuṅtaka. (2075)
From Puṇḍarīkapura, the illustrious friend previously brought back twenty-five of the best of twice-born men, according to the supreme enumeration. || 2076 ||
There were thirty Brahmins counted as being established in the Veda, and fifty in number were called the Kumbhanāthas. 2077.
O Prince, the best of the twice-born known as Subhaga, who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures, [described] the white form as being six more than forty.
In that land where Haras, the Supreme Soul Śiva, was present in person,
he [instructed] twenty-eight Brahmins, both virtuous and non-virtuous.
The celestial chariot is radiant and divine, extending from its own world to the supreme abode;
from that [world], it is reckoned as eightyfold in terms of its qualities.
The most excellent among beings initiated the six Brahmins born in Brahma-purī, who were his own *ṣaḍvipras*, into the mouth of Śiva known as Sadāśiva; they were of the Kauśika lineage. || 2081 ||
They were worthy of receiving water for the feet; they were born from those sages in due order according to the prescribed rite.
They bore the names Śiva and Brāhmaṇa, and resided at Vṛddhādri and Kamalālaya. || 2082 ||
In Sitavana, Chāyāvane, and Mandara; likewise in Madhupura, Janavane, Paṭṭīśvara, and Hīśvara. || 2083 ||
One should know Śiva to be at the forehead; one should contemplate him performing the upward dance.
[He is located] in the foundation (ādhāra), the linga, the navel, the heart, the head, and the palate.

At the root and on the forehead are two petals; on the sixteen-spoked and twenty-petaled wheels, and on the twelve-and-a-half and four-spoked wheels, [the letters] va, sa, ante, bā, la, ma, dhye, sa, pha, ka, ḍha [are placed]. || 2085 ||

I bow to that radiant form of the syllable *Haṃsa*, endowed with all aesthetic qualities, situated here in the middle of the *vala* constellation within the support (*ādhāra*) of the jewel-abode. || 2086 ||

The self-sign (ātma-liṅga), resembling [the sun], situated within the lotus of the heart in the city of Māyā, [is purified] by the consecration of the water of the pure mind from the river of faith. || 2087 ||
Yogins constantly meditate upon the syllable Oṃ, joined with the Bindu, by means of the flowers of meditative concentration for the sake of non-rebirth. || 2088 ||
Salutations again and again to Oṃkāra, the bestower of both worldly desires and liberation;
the sages bow to the God, and the hosts of celestial beings bow to him.
Men bow to the Lord of Gods; they do not bow with their hands alone, but offer salutations again and again to Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the bestower of great grace. || 2090 ||
Salutations again and again to the God who removes great sins, to the letter *ma*;
to Śiva, the peaceful Lord of the World, the cause of grace for all beings. (2091)
Salutations again and again to the auspicious God who is solely devoted to the welfare of others; and salutations to the bull, his vehicle, which was offered by Indra, the enemy of Vāsava.
Salutations again and again to the Lord who holds the power of the left (Vāmaśakti), to the letter Va;
salutations to the God, the all-pervading Lord, who is situated here and there. || 2093 ||
This is the supreme singular deity; salutations again and again to the letter Ya.
Whether it be made of metal, wood, clay, or stone— || 2094 ||
One should perform the reattachment of fingers, the tip of the ear, or the tip of the nose;
however, one should employ a doubtful case that is fit for reattachment, but not one that is unfit.
The joining of severed limbs and minor members is prescribed;
then, another [form] has five faces, wrathful, with the heart and throat displaced.
The navel and the belly; the back, chest, anus, penis, and likewise the pair of thighs, as well as the pair of knees, and the two buttocks. || 2097 ||
The hips, the pair of sides, the two hands, the nose, the head, and the region of the arms— these are the limbs of Śiva’s body, which are the source of all arts.
In the performance [of the rites] for the eight groups of thirty vidyās,
one should subsequently recite the mantra for the increase of longevity on the eastern side of the palace, according to one's specific capacity.
One should know that in the southeast there is strife, while on the south [side] there is the attainment of the knees.
In the Rākṣasa direction is the cause of liberation;
in the Vāyavya direction is attraction, while in the North it bestows prosperity.
O Goddess, I perform the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*); in the middle [position], it bestows the accomplishment of wealth;
before Śiva, for the sake of all accomplishments—thus are these [mantras] for recitation. (2102)
Two types of lingas have been fully described: the mobile and the immobile.
The mobile is renowned as being made of consciousness (pratīti), while the immobile is composed of earth.
Maheśvara always dwells there indeed, filled with affection;
one should perform the purificatory rites of the mantra, and thus it surely increases.
That which is called "division of limbs" (aṅgabheda) is said to be fourfold;
it consists of the limbs, the minor limbs, the complete limbs, and [the fourth], which thus becomes four.
The head, the face, the heart, and the limbs are thus proclaimed;
likewise, the eight [parts] are the two ears, the two breasts, the two arms, the navel, the private parts, and the belly.
The eyes, nose, ears, hands, feet, palms, fingers, thighs, knees, shanks, and the minor limbs—these are proclaimed [as the parts]. (2107)
Garment, sacred thread, garland, weapons, ornaments, as well as the lower garment and the upper covering— this is proclaimed as being with all its limbs (sāṅga). || 2108 ||
In her lotus-like hands, she holds the vessel of fearlessness and the boon, as well as a ladle, a bow, and arrows;
she is the Goddess Annapūrṇā, who incessantly bestows food, the essence of Śiva.
I pay homage to Pāṇḍarā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Moon-wheel (Candracakra), which is very difficult to obtain.
One should draw a wheel with eight circular segments, provided internally with two divisions.
In the center of the pericarp of the lotus is the great-faced one in the form of a *piṇḍa*;
following that is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa ending in *ṭa*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*). || 2111 ||

Drink [the mantra] consisting of the letter *ṣa*, the third [letter *ga*], and the letter *va* joined with fire (*ra*), endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*au*), and joined with the bindu and nāda. 2112.
One should place Bhuvaneśa in the middle of the four oceans;
one should write this great mantra, the Piṇḍa, in the center of the pericarp.
One should first place the *kalās* upon the sixteen petals; then, on the second row of petals, one should place them with respect to each petal of the third row.
One should write the fourth vowel in the third petal-side, and the letter 'da' (dānta) in the fifth petal; one should then inscribe the seed-syllable of Varuṇa.

Having placed the letter ending in 'ṣa' (ṣa) in the sixth [cell], and having placed the egg-shaped syllable (aṇḍaka) along with the bindu situated in the seventh [cell], one should also place the vowels outside of that.
One should place the sixteen vowels joined with the bindu;
on the petals, one should write the eight groups of eight [consonants] and the Lord of the World (bhuvanādhipati).
The flame of the moon, conjoined with the seed-syllable *svadhā*, is said to be within the fingertips;
this divine [mantra] is proclaimed to be in the lunar faces. || 2118 ||
This bestows all desired fruits especially at this particular time;
the syllable *hrīṃ* is in the center of the moon, while the sixteen letters are in the upper layer.
The outer [mandala] should be complete in the shape of a lotus; it is joined with the sun at the end and also endowed with the final [letter]. Outside that is the solar enclosure. || 2120 ||
Accompanied by Harihara and joined with the root mantra, it is the sovereign of all yantras, which directly brings the three worlds under control and removes all poisons. || 2121 ||

O King, [one should draw] a vessel with twenty-nine parts out of a hundred; then, in the centers, the seed-syllable, followed by the vowels, *ja*, *jha*, *va*, *sa*, *ha*, and *hrīḥ*. One should place Indumatī in the center, and the arms should be adorned with the syllables of the life-force of the stakes and the Bandhūka flower.
The luster of her body is as crimson as a cluster of flowers; she possesses full breasts and is intoxicated with passion. || 2122 ||

With lotus-like eyes rolling, she is the Fortune of the Lord of Lakṣmī, bestowing all that can be granted by the gods; she is the sharp goad for the lineage of those whose noses are bent by her crooked cry. || 2124 ||

O Sage, he beheld those two divine Śaktis of Hari, who were endowed with three eyes and possessed a wonderful state of being, while they were being observed by Jīvanakara with his copper-colored [vision]. || 2125 ||

One should contemplate even with the mind: having placed the water for the feet (pādya) upon the soles of the feet, the water for sipping (ācamana) upon the hands, and the respectful offering (arghya) upon the head. || 2126 ||
One should apply the fragrant unguent as anointment; place the flower upon the head, the incense in both nostrils, and having assigned the lamp to the eyes, [offer] the food and other items.

One should place [the water] in the palm of the hand. The *pādya* (water for the feet) shall be the destroyer of sin; the *ācamana* (water for sipping) brings prosperity; and the *arghya* (offering of respect) is for the sake of pleasing the deity. || 2128 ||
Fragrance is known as that which brings delight to Brahmā; the flower is likewise known as that which is dear to the sages.
The *ārārtika* lamp is dear to Jayā; the mirror is known as the bestower of knowledge; the parasol is the manifestation of sovereign command; and the fly-whisk is the destroyer of enemies.
There may be that which is to be sung... [omission]. Prosperity may consist of water, which is the characteristic of life. || 2131 ||
I pay homage to the supreme pair of Sound and Word, which transcends the sphere of Vāmana,
which is differentiated by white and red radiance, and whose nature is Śiva and Śakti.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Controller;
having looked upon his devotee Vyāsa, he who is a treasure-house of compassion, O sages.
To the silent teacher, one who is concentrated in the state of silence, with silent meditation and absorption—if here the meaning becomes clear. || 2134 ||
*Tāraṃ khaṃ ṣāṃ* is the *kūṭa*; *bharala bhararayūṃtāra* preceded by the nasal bindu and *nāda*, followed by *huṃ phaṭ taḍaṅgau* together with *varṣaḍpi*. || 2135 ||
One should strike that with *vauṣaṭ*. *Vāk*, *śukra*, *dhvani*, *śiva*, *ṛṣi*, *klīṃ*, and *dunāda*—these two are said to be the *bindu* and the *śakti*. (2136)
The resonance (dhvani) indeed [arises] from the emission of the *śālikā*;
it emits the void (*kha*) or the syllable *vāḥ* with a bindu, and the resonances follow the sound of the parrot. || 2137 ||
As one desires, the sound of the *hṛṃ* and *bindu*, the resonance of the *bindu* and *nāda*, and indeed the *bindu-nāda* itself—thus it is for me. || 2138 ||
Endowed with a dark complexion, possessing a neck like a conch shell, and having a large belly;
wearing red garments, she is peaceful and joined with the banner of longevity.

Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by a daughter and a son, one should fashion the arms of that [image]; the girl and the boy should be placed in order [on the left and right] respectively. (2140)
The first is Soma-dhārī, the second is Śiñcatī together with Umā, the third is mounted upon a bull, and the fourth is in a dancing form. Vai-vāhya— || 2141 ||
What is the fifth? The wise one should know the sixth to be wandering for alms;
he should know the seventh to be action, and the eighth to be the time of death.
The ninth shall be Tripurāri, and the tenth is Jalandhara;
the eleventh shall be Gajāri, and the twelfth is Vīrabhadraka.
The thirteenth should be Hari; after that, Ardhanaari;
the fifteenth should be Kirata, and the sixteenth would be Kankala.
Then the Caṇḍeśānugraha [chapter] shall be the seventeenth,
and the Viṣāpaharaṇa is traditionally known as the eighteenth.
The essential nature of Cakratāna is recorded as nineteen;
Vighnaprasāda is the twentieth, and after that is Umāskanda.
The twenty-two-fold [form] consists of one foot; the twenty-three-fold is the *sukhāsana*;
and the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is proclaimed as the twenty-four-fold.
The garment [consists of] the streams of Indra, while that which arises is called armor;
these are distinct, each according to twenty-five varieties. || 2148 ||
The *sṛṣṭiliṅga* is for the sake of Gaṅgā; its description is associated with the *saṃgeyamūrti*, having the *aśvattha* tree as its crest and possessing a grasp of both radiance and time.
The Gaurīśvara-vārāhya, the supreme Umā-graha, and the joy-bestowing dialogue between Gaurī and Umā. || 2150 ||
The secret one, together with the one whose form is wealth, the destroyer of cities;
the Kirāta and Arjuna, Time, the half of Umā, and the half of Hari. || 2151 ||
Afterwards, there should be the three dance-forms (nṛttamūrti), as well as Dahana and Vidhara; then Caṇḍeśa, Anugraha, and thereafter the Mukhaliṅga. || 2152 ||
Vighnaskanda, Caṇḍeśa, Kṣetreśa, Kamalodbhava, Cakrapāṇi, Mātaṇḍi, Nāgeśa, and Vīrabhadraka. (2153)
Gaurī, Durgā, as well as the excellent Mahākoṭi, Sarasvatī, Jāhnavī, Bhadrakālī, Lakṣmī, and Pṛthvī are the Mothers. || 2154 ||
Then, according to the path taught in that scripture, one should always fashion the forty-limbed form of Sadāśiva, who is pure and beloved by Śakti, from the *kālāgni* [substance]. || 2155 ||
p. 147) Just as one should recollect Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, and the second quality (guṇa),
[so too] the womb, mind, ear, skin, palate, nose, speech, and hand— 2156.
One should meditate upon the feet, the lower part, the sign, the sound, touch, form, taste, smell, earth, fire, water, and air, by means of the *iḍā* [nāḍī]. || 2157 ||
The bimba [fruit] has sixteen [parts], and the wind is sixty-four;
one should abandon the abode of Piṅgala, not the hair. || 2158 ||

By means of ten places [of articulation] and two [additional ones], through the resonance and sound of the syllable *oṃ*, one should extract the blue beginning, which has the wind as its object and ends in the heart. || 2159 ||
In that regard, no fluctuation is made. Arising from the phonemes (varṇa), when the supreme, subtle Śivatattva is reached, then the Bindu is produced; from the Bindu, the Nāda [arises]. || 2160 ||
From the arisen *nāda*, *śakti* was born; *nāda* is called the "little finger" (*aṅguṣṭha*), and it is remembered as the seed-syllable *bindu*. || 2161 ||
That seed-syllable is said to be the "Ka" (the difficult), which is auspicious and composed of all powers.
From the power [of Śakti] arises the Vāgbhava; from the Vāgbhava come sixteen digits (kalās). || 2162 ||
From the *kalās* and other elements, the consonants (*vyañjana*) were produced; from the consonants, all the scriptures arose.
At the time of the sprouting of those seeds, the letter *a* was born from his mouth.
From the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, these are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) born from the mouth;
the letters beginning with *ka* are those born from both [the eyes and the ears];
those beginning with *pa* are born from the organ of desire (*kāma*), and those born from the *bindu* arise in sequence. || 2165 ||
One should place beans that are not smaller than the measure, as well as sesame seeds; having cast in the *vivasvat* and other [grains], one performs the worship with curd in the *mitraka* [vessel].
Milk is produced on the mountain; the oblation (bali) is known as the lowest.
Ghee belongs to Parjanya, while Indra's [portion] consists of fresh butter, rice-grains, and flowers.
One should give *koṣṭha* and *puṣpa* to Indra, *madhugandhā* to Bhāskara,
*sadya* and *madhuka* [to Candra], and fresh butter (*navanītaka*) to Bhūśa.
For Agni, an offering of burnt ghee is desired; for Śambhu, milk-rice with sugar;
for Brahmā, parched grain; and for Rākṣasa, a cold offering is prescribed.
For Śiva, it is food with wine; for Gandharva, all types of perfumes;
for Bhṛṅgarāja, it is without meat; and for Jhaṣa, they know it to be fish-rice.
In the dance, there is the merit of sesame seeds (*tila-puṇyāha*), the seed-gatekeeper (*bīja-dauvārika*) offering,
the *modaka* for Sugrīva, nourishment, perfumes and flowers, and then water.
Having placed milk-rice (pāyasa) for Varuṇa, and having dried blood even with the gods,
one should offer fish to Rāgāsya along with sesame seeds and rice grains.
Having well understood the prohibition regarding the self today, and having weighed the fire of the scales,
the root-rite of pacification (*śāntipūjā*) is indeed prescribed with curd and whey. (2173)
One should offer rice mixed with jujube fruits and curd to Bhallābhā;
and during the month of Śukla, one should give sweetmeats (modaka) to Devamātṛ in the constellation Mṛgaśīrṣa. || 2174 ||
It rises with the consumption of sesame; it ends with the razor at the conclusion of all cold [offerings].
With parched grain and rice, there is the Sāvindra [offering]; with the Sāvindra, there is the fragrant water.
In the month of Rudra, in the month of Rudrajaya, one who has sweated for a month [attains the state] of the two sinless ones. || 2176 ||
Kumuda, fish-meat, conch, Kha, and Padmaka—
these are the offerings for the east, while the offering for Indra is in the south.
One should offer to Pūtanā a smile, a garland, an upper garment,
a common oblation (sādhāraṇabali), pure food, clarified butter, and curd.
One should offer perfumes and other such items to all the deities as well; a maiden, a solar deity, or a courtesan are suitable for the performance of the bali offering.
One should perform the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* for the deities, beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, according to the sequence, while bestowing fearlessness upon them.
After performing the worship, one should subsequently offer the common *bali*;
thereafter, the wise one should offer the appropriate *bali* for each [deity] with water.

And having thus heated the villages and so forth, as well as the frog, the foot, and the supreme *śādhika*, outside [the body], by means of the previously mentioned procedure in sequence, the deities [should be invoked]. (2182)
Then he should dismiss the deities; let them be established there as they were. He should place the Brahmins and the external deities in their respective positions as prescribed. || 2183 ||
They are not prescribed for the purpose of constructing a temple, nor for the purpose of a door;
thus it is said "from the village," and this is declared as another secret.
The state of one established in the fast of the well is the goal;
being serene and possessing a purified body, he takes hold of the digits. || 2185 ||
One should properly perform the specific and general offerings for men daily, as prescribed; thus says the Mayamata, verse 2186.
The heart of Sadāśiva is Śakti, and Śakti is the heart of Śiva;
there is no difference between the two, even as there is none between the wind and the sky.
From the union of Śiva and Śakti, the Mother-Śakti and the Grandfather [Brahmā] arise;
therefore, with every effort, it is said that fire originates from them.
Now I shall speak specifically of Śivarātri;
one should worship it at the rising of the lunar mansions and lunar days, and during the gathering at a sacred ford (tīrtha). || 2189 ||
One should worship Śivarātri on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha;
however, according to that Tantra, the fourteenth day is said to begin from the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī).
On the fourteenth night of the lamp-offering, *huṃ* and *phaṭ* are praised;
both of these fierce [syllables] should be employed by the practitioner when worshipping the collyrium. (2191)
That which completes the ten of four [groups] is the fourteenth;
the Lord chose that very night associated with the fourteenth. (2192)
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: "If the fourteenth day is joined with the new moon on the thirteenth day, that night of the fourteenth day is known as Śivarātri. (2193)
In the Vāyu Purāṇa, in the section on the Vision of Time (Kāladarśa):
"When the sun sets on the thirteenth lunar day, one should observe the vow of Śivarātri there for the sake of bestowing prosperity, even if it spans only three or four nāḍīs. (2194)
In all cases, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is desired at every [observance];
otherwise, there would be a loss of merit, except for the breaking of the fast [at the conclusion]. || 2195 ||
If today, on the thirteenth day, the great night should be pervaded by spirits,
one should perform the Śivarātrī vow and likewise keep a vigil there.
If the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) consists of thirteen nāḍīs at sunset,
one should perform the Śivarātrī vow and likewise observe a vigil.

In the morning, one should offer prepared cow-products; likewise, the five nectars at the two junctions of the day; having worshipped with honey at the three junctions, the essence of sugarcane is the fourth.
The people should especially honor the teacher, Piṇḍita, and Janārdana;
on that day, they also behold the sacred silk cloth there.
During the royal consecration, the initiation, the mid-rite, the consumption of food, the sprinkling, and the eightfold binding; (2200)
One should cause the application of the *jātikāpāla* paste for the sake of a fruitful conception.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the bull-vehicle (*vṛṣabhavāhana*).
The deity mounted upon the bull is said to be of two kinds: that which bestows enjoyment and that which bestows prosperity. A wise man should install the Lord together with Bhavānī above the bull.
Having placed the bull behind him as before, accompanied by Dakṣiṇā,
he is four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with matted hair and a crown.
Thus [he is] endowed with divine ornaments and all manner of jewelry;
he wears a white sacred thread, possesses a peaceful form, and has a smiling face.
In his right hand he holds an axe, and in his left hand he displays the gesture of granting boons;
he is dark-blue in complexion, and his garment is of the color of a young doe.
Having raised the right hand with the hands [in the gesture of] fearlessness, one should place the left hand upon the lap and let the right leg hang down over the seat. || 2206 ||
The dance known as Vṛṣabhavāhana is also declared to be for the sake of peace.
She possesses the nature of the enemy of bees (a lion), is clothed in a tiger skin,
and likewise holds an egg-born [creature], a shaven-headed one, and a *ro* and a *matha*.
And by one who has not grasped the essence of the *ācāma*, there is the fault consisting of the nature of the mantra;
this occurs when the practitioner and the preceptor, together with those who endure [the practice] until the end of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), [are deficient]. (2209)
One should perform all rites, both daily and occasional;
for those who remain at the door of the fire-chamber, the best of the twice-born partakes of their food.

The ritual sipping of water (āpośana), the drinking of liquor, and the eating of beef—these are [prohibited] even when [the leaf] has a handle or is made of plantain leaves, or even if its tip is on the left side. || 2211 ||
One should likewise sit upon a cold seat, and having eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Facing east or facing downward, one performs sacrifice; facing south, one enjoys prosperity;
facing north, one enjoys liberation; and not facing [any of these], one does not enjoy [the fruits of action]. || 2213 ||
When a learned scholar who has completed his Vedic studies and vows arrives at his house, she plays with him;
she, whose supreme goal is the desire to sport with everyone, is my [mother]. (2214)
Whether the water be pure or impure, or whether it be small or even very small—whatever water is in the presence of Śiva is renowned as being within the Śivaliṅga. (2215)
For men, the days from Sunday to Saturday yield results in sequence that are inauspicious; even by taking away fame, they bring death and misery. || 2216 ||
And for a son, there is destruction and death; for life, there is the fortune of death;
for prosperity, there is disease and extreme suffering; and for wealth, there is its depletion. || 2217 ||
One should state the loss of wealth; the days of the week, beginning with Sunday, shall yield results in sequence;
one should declare the bitter oblation (kaṣāya-huti); and having taken [the portion] from Āśauca... || 2218 ||
Avoiding those in bronze and bell-metal vessels, he partook of food in the middle of the assembly;
during vows and fasts, he was not one who had mastered the Vedas. || 2219 ||
Blue in color, with two eyes, two arms, and two feet,
he bestows fearlessness and grants boons, and is adorned with a crown and a diadem.
The invocation of Vāyasa, accompanied by the one clad in blue garments;
the ornament of iron, and Śanaiścara of peaceful form.
For the purpose of performing a special sacrifice for the God of gods,
the most excellent of preceptors should set aside one-eighth part of the rice for the sake of side-dishes.
The lion, the tiger, the boar, the donkey, the elephant, the buffalo, and the cock—these are the vehicles of the Saṃkrāntis. || 2223 ||
Pakṣakṣobha, pravāla, barkakārpāsa,
kambala, and kambala— these are the garments for the Saṃkrānti.
The lute, the sword, the winnowing basket, the staff, and the wielder of the bow; likewise, the serpent-staff weapon—these are the weapons of Saṃkrānti. || 2225 ||
Mudga-rice, milk-rice, rice with molasses, and likewise rice with ghee; a handful of curd, and fasting—these are the meals for the Saṃkrānti. (2226)

If it is a lion, there will be the loss of the kingdom; if a tiger, the destruction of Brahmins and the best of the twice-born; if a boar, there will be the destruction of crops; and if a donkey, the destruction of Vaiśyas.
If an elephant appears, there will be the loss of the king; if a buffalo, the destruction of the Śūdras;
and if a cock, the destruction of everything—these are the characteristics of the Saṃkrānti.
Those two gods, whose hands are adorned with conch shells and skulls, who wear garlands and bone ornaments, have their abode in Dvāravatī and the cremation ground. || 2229 ||

May Sarasvatī reside in your home along with Lakṣmī; live long!
Just as Brahmā is with Sarasvatī and Īśvara is with Girijā... [2235]
Padmaja with the gods, Gaṇeśa with his hosts along with the daughter of Puloman, and Bhūdevī with the foremost of the Maruts, fire, and water— || 2236 ||

With a body consisting of fifty distinct letters arranged as her face, arms, feet, eyes, and wings, she shines with a single verse for her young child.

At the root of the palate, on the forehead, on the two-petaled, sixteen-spoked, twenty-two-petaled, and ten-petaled [lotuses], on the twelve [spokes] above, on the four [spokes], at the end of the abode, and in the midst of the child. || 2288 ||

I bow to the well of syllables, which is joined with the vowels in the middle of the ears along with the *ḍakka* and *kaṭha*, endowed with the meaning of the principles (*tattva*) as *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, and possessed of all its petals. || 2289 ||
Of this mantra for the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās (aspects), Īśāna and Sadyojāta are the seers; Gāyatrī, Si, Bhūri, and Tā are the meters. || 2290 ||

Amṛ—svāhā to the head. Oṃ haṃ huṃ, to those with flaming crests; oṃ haiṃ, to the wielder of the vajra; to Svatantrā; oṃ hrāṃ, to the undiminished; oṃ, to Paśu. || 2292 ||
Phaṭ! Meditation. Bhi Bhraṃ Nām.

[Repeated Mantra]. Then, having offered to Tripurā betel nut (*pūgīphala*), betel leaf (*nāgavallī*), and scented substances combined together, one should perform the lustration rite (*nīrājana*). || 2294 ||
Having worshipped with eight flowers, one should pray to the Supreme Deity;
having obtained permission from Kāmeśvarī, one should worship the nine enclosures.
Coconut, ghee-cakes, and sweets mixed with molasses;
refreshing drinks, pieces of sugarcane, plantains, honey, and parched grain.
One should offer milk-warm water mixed with *śilā* and *vāsana* in the midst of each of the ninefold offerings. || 2297 ||
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should pray to Caṇḍikā within the heart;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā up to the water [element], one should worship in due order.
Filling the joined palms with flowers, one should invoke the Supreme Deity.
One should worship the services beginning with the seat using their respective mantras;
then, having offered incense and a lamp, one should present the food offering (naivedya). || 2300 ||
Milk-rice, rice with milk (pāyasa), rice with mung beans,
and rice with black gram— these, along with fried cakes (vaṭaka) and sweetmeats (apūpa), constitute the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer *śaṣkulī* cakes, sesame sweets (*tilamoda*), and milk electuaries;
likewise, water with syrups, as well as curd, milk, and ghee.
One should offer it, accompanied by condiments, to Caṇḍikā.
For one who was thirsty and eating, [the mouth] was split open facing the east.
From the mouth [arises] the palate... the tongue is produced from that. || 2304 ||
From that, various tastes were produced, which are perceived by the tongue.
Then, within the body, there is space; in that [space], activity— || 2305 ||
In that state, for one who is engaged in various activities, there exists *ojas*, which is the power of the faculties; because it consists of power (*śakti*), it is of a subtle nature. || 2306 ||
The great chief named Praṇasutras is the vital breath (*asu*) of all;
he demonstrates their greatness—that the vital breaths are the senses, ending with the vital breath itself. || 2307 ||
Performing these activities, they breathe after [the breath], performing the activity;
manifesting that activity of the downward breath (*apāna*), they breathe out and relinquish that activity. || 2308 ||
Like servants following their king, the stars, being cast down and shaken, moved along with the Virāṭ and Jīva constellations as previously described. || 2309 ||
It was stated for the purpose of meditating upon [the Self] through differentiation: "He who is born" means he who desires to eat (*jakṣatam*), that is, to consume; first, at the outset—|| 2310 ||
It was divided and became differentiated; the palate is the locus, the tongue-faculty is the instrument, various tastes are the object, and Varuṇa is the deity—thus it is known. 2311.
In all cases, this fourfold set—namely, the pervader, the locus, the deity, and the object—is to be inferred even if not explicitly stated; it is presented here by way of illustration. || 2312 ||
From the *bhūman*, that which was brought by fire and wind arose from those two;

As he desired to grasp that [sound], his two ears were split open;

He displays the jewel. When the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) in the sky [of the heart] is intensely vibrating, he speaks incoherently; there, in the nose—that is, in the nostril—|| 2317 ||

Golaka-kuṇḍa arose from the origin of Golaka Śaiva;

Having performed the recitation of the mantra, no fault is found.
